Brazil: when public wealth and power moved into private hands

A profile of what marks such a deal, and the record from 1500 to 2026. Built from the data files by build.py. Disasters are on a separate page. Timeline charts: full-size page.

The story in pictures

Five centuries of transfers on one page. Each chart says its point in the title; tap a dot or bar for detail.

More charts: the signs, money by era, and on the disasters page. The full-size timeline charts have their own page.

Who was president, and who were the appointed people who could decide these transfers?

Done: every term from 1822 to today now lists its ruler and decision-makers, on the timeline page.

The data maps 196 people across 52 terms and the colony years. Each case below now has a "Decided by" line with the people linked to it.

Who counts as a decision-maker

The ruler, the money ministers, the ministers over the assets, the heads of the state banks and of the companies being sold, regulators and sale councils, and the negotiators with foreign powers.

What each record shows

Posts with dates and who appointed them, work before and after, foreign ties, the role in each case, and investigations with their outcome exactly as recorded. Every entry has its own status pill; unverified ones stay visible and marked.

Where to see it

  • Every term: scorecard, decision-makers and the cases that started.
  • People on both sides: government, then buyers, foreign firms or lenders.
  • Foreign counterparts by country.
Most links are "in office at the time". Only 70 of 608 person-to-case links name the person acting in the case. The rest say who held the post when it started.

How can we analyse political power in every term?

Done: each of the 52 terms has the same six-question scorecard, set next to the money and inequality data. See how it is scored.

  1. Who ruled, and how did they get there?
  2. Who could choose them? (registered voters as % of the population)
  3. Who backed them?
  4. What checked them? (V-Dem democracy index)
  5. What did they hand over? (the cases that started in the term)
  6. Who gained and who lost? (change in minimum wage, Gini, state-company investment, public debt, V-Dem)
Patterns, not proof of motive. Seats in Congress are missing for every term; see the data gaps.

Can we see it on a timeline, crossed with purchasing power and wealth concentration?

Done: the timeline stacks every term, case and data series on one year axis, 1822–2026, with the colony cases above it.

  • Public patrimony: public and state-company investment, privatization money by year, state-company counts, public debt.
  • Purchasing power: real minimum wage, household income, GDP per person.
  • Concentration: Gini, top 1% and top 10% shares, land Gini, labour share.
  • Political power: democracy index, voters, company campaign money.

Hover or tap a year to read every value and who was in power.

What did the double-check find?

Fact-checkers re-opened the sources for about 1,126 figures. About 567 held up, 233 needed a correction, now applied, and about 293 could not be confirmed.

The research also grew. Gap-filling notes added 154 new entries or additions to existing ones. This page now has 186 entries (it had 116), and the disasters page has 94 (it had 60).

Still open: 323 of 832 figures on this page are unverified and 96 are disputed. Each figure keeps its own pill, so you can see which is which. Hover a pill to read why.

The biggest corrections

  • Vale 1997: the price of R$ 3.338 bn is about US$ 3.0 bn, not US$ 3.3 bn. See Vale.
  • Eletropaulo: it sold at the minimum price, not above it, and the AES default was in 2003. See Eletropaulo.
  • PROER: the per-bank amounts were wrong. They now follow the CPI Proer report. See PROER and its cross-cutting entry.
  • Grampo do BNDES: the tapes came out in Nov 1998, and the TCU puts BNDES help to Telemar at R$ 686.8 mn. See the case.
  • EBX and JBS: R$ 10.4 bn for EBX was approved, not paid out. The R$ 5.08 bn JBS figure is a TCU audit estimate, and a later TCU ruling found no debit. See EBX and JBS.
  • Eletrobras: R$ 46 bn is only one part of a TCU minister's undervaluation argument. His full gap is about R$ 63 bn (R$ 130.4 bn against R$ 67 bn). See Eletrobras.
  • Correios: the Treasury rejected a R$ 20 bn loan and authorized R$ 12 bn on 18 Dec 2025. No R$ 10 bn figure exists. See Correios.
  • Volkswagen ranch: the investigation rests on at least 42 victims and 11 witnesses. The "1,000 victims" estimate is not in the cited pages. See the case.
  • Colony: Loronha's 400–500% profit figure is in a source after all (one secondary source), and the first Banco do Brasil's capital is now 1,200,000$000. See Loronha and Banco do Brasil.

The short answer

Brazil moved public land, resources, money and markets into private hands in every era. The record has 186 entries from 1502 to 2025.

  • The profile has 13 signs in 4 mechanisms. The most common: public money, private control (39), exclusive privilege (35), bailout (31), subsidy or tax break (30), law rewritten for the deal (28).
  • Highest scores: Siderbras steel: Cosipa, Acesita, CSN (1993), Acominas (5 of 13), Belo Monte dam (Xingu, Pará) (5 of 13), Terra Legal: prices charged versus market value, and the TCU audits (5 of 13). See all scores.
  • The pattern shifts over time: monopolies in the colony, public money behind private control from 1985, rewritten laws since 2016. See signs by era.
  • 413 of 832 figures are verified or corrected. Amounts are never added up across currencies or eras.

What a public-to-private transfer looks like: the profile

A transfer is a deal where public wealth or power ends up in private hands: land, a monopoly, a company, cheap money or a debt the public takes over.

Across 500 years the same 13 signs keep showing up. They fall into 4 mechanisms: hand over the asset, put public money behind private control, bend the rules, and let the losses go public.

A deal does not need every sign. The more signs it shows, the closer it is to the pattern. Each card below has a one-line test you can run on a new deal.

1. Hand over the asset

Public land, rights or markets pass to a private holder, often on thin terms.

Land or resource grant

Public land, forest, subsoil or water rights go to a private holder.

Spot it: Does a title, lease or concession cover land or a natural resource? How many hectares, for how long, at what fee?

Cases: e1-19 (1852) e2-09 (1906) e3-01 (1950) e5-05 (2006) x-20 (2009) e6-06 (2016)

Tagged in 21 of 186 entries. By era: Colony 3 · Republic 5 · Dictatorship 1 · 2003–2016 2 · 2016–2026 1 · Cross-cutting 9.

Exclusive privilege

One holder gets the sole right to trade, run or extract in a sector or place.

Spot it: Is there a monopoly or exclusivity clause? For how many years? Who is barred?

Cases: e1-19 (1852) e2-08 (1906) e3-10 (1967) x-15 (1999) e5-15 (2010) e6-15 (2020)

Tagged in 35 of 186 entries. By era: Colony 12 · Republic 7 · Dictatorship 2 · 2003–2016 4 · 2016–2026 6 · Cross-cutting 4.

Below-value or no-contest price

The price is far under other estimates, or the contest was skipped, thin or built on a seller-friendly method.

Spot it: Compare the price with the seller's own base case and outside valuations. Was there one bidder, or a renewal with no auction?

Cases: e3-14 (1974) e4-05 (1991) e5-07 (2007) x-20 (2009) e6-16 (2021)

Tagged in 14 of 186 entries. By era: Dictatorship 2 · 1985–2002 2 · 2003–2016 3 · 2016–2026 6 · Cross-cutting 1.

2. Public money behind private control

The public side carries cost and risk; the private side keeps control and upside.

Public money, private control

State banks, funds or pension funds supply capital or credit while private owners keep control and upside.

Spot it: Who put in the cash? Who votes the shares? Who is paid first?

Cases: e1-20 (1852) e3-14 (1974) e4-05 (1991) x-10 (1995) e5-15 (2010) e6-13 (2020)

Tagged in 39 of 186 entries. By era: Colony 1 · Republic 1 · Dictatorship 2 · 1985–2002 13 · 2003–2016 13 · 2016–2026 2 · Cross-cutting 7.

Paid in paper or cheap credit

The buyer pays with discounted securities, long instalments or loans from a public bank.

Spot it: What share of the price is cash on day one? Who lends the rest?

Cases: e2-08 (1906) e3-15 (1974) e4-05 (1991) e5-09 (2008) x-20 (2009)

Tagged in 20 of 186 entries. By era: Republic 2 · Dictatorship 2 · 1985–2002 9 · 2003–2016 4 · Cross-cutting 3.

Guaranteed return

The state promises the investor a minimum return or payment whatever happens.

Spot it: Is there an interest guarantee, a revenue floor or a minimum-payment clause?

Cases: e1-19 (1852) e2-08 (1906) x-06 (1974) e3-17 (1975) e4-11 (1995) e5-20 (2012)

Tagged in 16 of 186 entries. By era: Colony 2 · Republic 4 · Dictatorship 1 · 1985–2002 3 · 2003–2016 5 · Cross-cutting 1.

Subsidy or tax break

Tax waivers, cheap power or subsidised credit lower the private cost.

Spot it: Is there an exemption, a special tariff or a below-market loan? What does it cost per year and what did it buy?

Cases: e1-19 (1852) e2-14 (1927) e3-15 (1974) e4-17 (1996) x-15 (1999) e5-22 (2012)

Tagged in 30 of 186 entries. By era: Colony 4 · Republic 2 · Dictatorship 7 · 1985–2002 2 · 2003–2016 5 · 2016–2026 3 · Cross-cutting 7.

3. Rules bent to fit

The legal frame, the overseer or the valuer is shaped in favour of the deal.

Law rewritten for the deal

A law, decree or provisional measure changes the rules for, or just before, the deal.

Spot it: Did a rule change come shortly before the sale or grant? Who asked for it?

Cases: e2-03 (1889) e3-14 (1974) e4-31 (2001) x-21 (2009) e5-15 (2010) e6-06 (2016)

Tagged in 28 of 186 entries. By era: Republic 1 · Dictatorship 3 · 1985–2002 1 · 2003–2016 7 · 2016–2026 7 · Cross-cutting 9.

Rights legalised after the fact

Past occupation or clearing is made legal by an amnesty or regularisation.

Spot it: Does a cut-off date turn earlier illegal occupation into title? Has the date moved?

Cases: e1-17 (1850) x-20 (2009) e5-22 (2012) e6-06 (2016)

Tagged in 11 of 186 entries. By era: Colony 1 · 2003–2016 2 · 2016–2026 1 · Cross-cutting 7.

Regulator absent, late or sidelined

No independent regulator on the day, or oversight arrives later or is overruled.

Spot it: Who regulates this market on the day of sale? Was that body created later?

Cases: e3-23 (1981) e4-05 (1991) x-20 (2009) e5-15 (2010) e6-16 (2021)

Tagged in 24 of 186 entries. By era: Dictatorship 2 · 1985–2002 6 · 2003–2016 6 · 2016–2026 3 · Cross-cutting 7.

Conflict of interest or alleged kickbacks

The valuer or lender had ties to bidders, or prosecutors, courts or plea deals allege bribes. Allegations are not findings.

Spot it: Who valued the asset and who else do they work for? Are there investigations or plea deals?

Cases: e1-13 (1808) e2-09 (1906) x-07 (1975) e3-20 (1980) e4-19 (1997) e5-15 (2010)

Tagged in 17 of 186 entries. By era: Colony 1 · Republic 1 · Dictatorship 1 · 1985–2002 2 · 2003–2016 6 · Cross-cutting 6.

4. Losses go public

Debts and failures are absorbed by the state, before or after the sale.

Bailout

The state absorbs losses or debts when the private venture fails.

Spot it: If it fails, who pays? Is a public bank the main creditor?

Cases: e1-13 (1808) e2-08 (1906) e3-08 (1967) x-10 (1995) e4-17 (1996) e5-20 (2012)

Tagged in 31 of 186 entries. By era: Colony 1 · Republic 3 · Dictatorship 5 · 1985–2002 5 · 2003–2016 6 · 2016–2026 3 · Cross-cutting 8.

Cleanup before sale

The state takes the debts or liabilities first, then sells the cleaned-up asset.

Spot it: Were debts moved to the Treasury or the Union before the auction?

Cases: e4-05 (1991) x-10 (1995) e4-36 (2021)

Tagged in 10 of 186 entries. By era: 1985–2002 6 · 2016–2026 2 · Cross-cutting 2.

How the score works

  1. Each sign tagged on an entry is worth 1 point. The maximum is 13.
  2. The signs were tagged by the researchers who built the data files, from the notes. The fact-check did not test the signs, only the figures.
  3. So the table also shows evidence: how many of the entry's figures are verified or corrected.
  4. The score counts signs in the record. It does not measure the size of the transfer, who is at fault, or whether the deal was a mistake.
  5. A missing sign means "not found in the sources", not "absent". Old cases have thin records and score lower for that reason.
  6. The old ½-point rule is gone. The data no longer grades each sign, so every sign counts the same.

History by era

All 186 entries, oldest first within each era. Click a case to see who got what, on what terms, who paid, what came after, the counter-view and every figure.

Entries keep their era from the research batch they came from. A few concessions that began just before an era's start (Mate Laranjeira 1882, Santos docks 1888) stay with the era they shaped.

1500–1889: Colony and Empire (22 entries)

The Crown leased monopolies, granted land and guaranteed returns to private contractors.

YearsCase (click to open)SignsFigures
1502 to c.1515
e1-01
Brazilwood lease to Fernão de Loronha

In 1502 the Portuguese Crown leased the brazilwood trade of its new lands to a Lisbon merchant group led by Fernão de Loronha. The lessee carried the cost of ships, exploration and a fort, and the Crown took a growing share of the yield. The Crown took the trade back by 1515.

Government
Kingdom of Portugal, King Manuel I
What happened
Exclusive trade in brazilwood from the 'Lands of Vera Cruz' for three years, leased to a Lisbon merchant group. The charter is lost; its contents are known from a 1522 royal letter.
Who got it
Fernão de Loronha's merchant consortium of Lisbon. The note's claims that they were New Christian merchants, and that Indigenous people cut the wood by barter, could not be confirmed. Who financed them is not stated.
Terms
Reconstructed from a letter of 3 Oct 1502 (Rondinelli): Crown share zero in year 1, one-sixth in year 2, one-quarter in year 3. He had to send six ships a year at his own cost, explore 300 leagues of new coast a year and build a fort. A different report (Ca' Masser, 1506/07) says a ten-year charter at 4,000 ducats a year; Vogt thinks that letter is wrong. Wikipedia says the 4,000 ducats may come from a 1505 renegotiation.
Mechanism
Royal charter / lease (arrendamento) of a Crown monopoly.
Who paid
Indigenous peoples and the forest are named as likely cost-bearers, but this is not documented in the sources opened.
What came after
Renewed in 1506 and held to 1512, then passed to the consortium of Jorge Lopes Bixorda. In 1515 the Crown let the lease lapse and took the trade directly. On 14 Jan 1504 the king also gave Loronha the island of São João (Fernando de Noronha) as a hereditary captaincy, making him the first donatary captain. Vogt (1967) argues there may have been no renewal.
Counter-view
This was a risk-bearing exploration contract. The lessee paid up front, armed ships and had to discover coast and build a fort at his own cost, with the Crown share rising over time. The Crown got revenue and coast mapping at no outlay, and re-tendered then retook the trade by 1515. Source: Wikipedia, Fernão de Loronha.
Figures
  • verified Crown share of yield, years 1 / 2 / 3: 0 / one-sixth / one-quarter (1502; Rondinelli letter of 3 Oct 1502, via Wikipedia) source
    Terms are reconstructed because the charter is lost.
  • disputed Ca' Masser report: ten-year charter at 4,000 ducats a year: 4,000 ducats a year (ducats) (1506/07; Ca' Masser; Vogt thinks it is wrong) source
    Conflicts with the Rondinelli three-year terms. Wikipedia suggests 4,000 ducats may come from a 1505 renegotiation.
  • corrected Brazilwood harvested by 1506: 20,000 quintals (quintals) (1506; Wikipedia (single secondary source)) source
    The first notes said there was no citation. Wikipedia does state it. Still one secondary source.
  • corrected Profit over the lump sum and ship costs: about 400-500% (percent) (c.1506; Wikipedia (single secondary source)) source
    The first notes called this unsourced. Wikipedia states it. Still one secondary source.
Sources
  • Wikipedia: Fernão de Loronha
  • Cambridge, The Americas: Fernão de Loronha and the rental of Brazil in 1502
  • USP e-disciplinas resource
  • UNIFESP, Almanack article
Decided by
  • verified Manuel I of Portugal (in office at the time; granted the brazilwood lease (head of Crown))
Exclusive privilege1 verif. 2 corre. 1 dispu.
1532 to 1822
e1-02
Sesmarias (land grants)

For almost 300 years the Crown gave away land in Brazil on the condition that it be farmed. Large grants went to elites and to men who fought Indigenous groups. When grants stopped in 1822, occupation took over until the 1850 land law.

Government
Kingdom of Portugal (colonial Brazil); donatários from 1534; ended under Prince Regent Pedro in 1822
What happened
Free grants of Crown land, conditional on cultivation. The first registered grant was on 10 Oct 1532, from Martim Afonso de Sousa to Pedro de Góis. Donatários also granted them from 1534. The system was suspended in 1822.
Who got it
Settlers and elites. Grants also rewarded military service against Indigenous groups. Examples: 40 leagues in 1674 to men who fought Indigenous groups on the São Francisco; Casa da Torre asked for grants of 40 and 60 leagues in Piauí. These examples could not be confirmed.
Terms
Free land, but the holder had to cultivate it within the set time or lose it, and pay the dízimo to the Order of Christ. A royal letter of 9 Jan 1697 set 3 by 1 league per grant, but the Crown did not hold to it in practice.
Mechanism
Based on the Portuguese Lei das Sesmarias of 1375 (Fernando I). Suspended in 1822 by Resolution no. 76, attributed to José Bonifácio (the notes give 17 July 1822; the day was not seen on the page opened).
Who paid
Indigenous peoples (conflict and dispossession are referenced, but expulsion figures were not found). Vague boundaries fed conflict with other occupants.
What came after
After 1822 occupation (posse) was the main way to get land until Lei 601 of 1850.
Counter-view
Wikipedia notes the cultivation condition was meant to stop idle land, and the system included a forfeiture rule. Source: pt.wikipedia Sesmaria.
Figures
  • verified First registered grant: 10 Oct 1532 (1532; pt.wikipedia) source
    Martim Afonso de Sousa to Pedro de Góis.
  • unverified Standard sesmaria size (royal letter of 9 Jan 1697): 3 by 1 league (leagues) (1697; Periodicos UFAM (via search summary)) source
    The PDF was not opened by the fact-check. The Crown did not hold to this size.
  • unverified Grant to men who fought Indigenous groups on the São Francisco: 40 leagues (leagues) (1674; Periodicos UFAM (via search summary)) source
    Not confirmed by the fact-check.
  • unverified Casa da Torre grant requests in Piauí: 40 and 60 leagues (leagues) (year n/a; Periodicos UFAM (via search summary)) source
    Not confirmed by the fact-check.

  • Canoa do Tempo (UFAM)
Decided by

  • verified John III of Portugal (in office at the time; head of Crown during first Brazilian sesmaria/donatário system)
  • verified Pedro I of Brazil (Prince Regent 1821-22) (in office at the time; as Prince Regent, sesmarias suspended in 1822 (Resolution 76))

1534 to 1770
e1-03
Hereditary captaincies (capitanias hereditárias)

In 1534-1536 the Portuguese Crown handed strips of the Brazilian coast, with legal powers, to private donatários. Most grants failed, and the Crown took the remaining ones back between 1753 and 1770.

Government
Kingdom of Portugal, King João III; Crown reabsorbed them under José I
What happened
The coast of Brazil was split into strips with jurisdiction and given to private donatários. Created 1534-1536. Sizes varied: for example 60 leagues of coast from the São Francisco southward in one grant, and 80 leagues split between two captaincies for Pero Lopes de Sousa.
Who got it
About 12 donatários, mostly nobles and Crown servants. The notes name Duarte Coelho in Pernambuco; the fact-check could not confirm that on the page it opened. Financing is not described.
Terms
Two documents: the Carta de Doação and the Foral. Donatários got jurisdiction, rents and foros on mills and engenhos, part of the dízimos, power to appoint ouvidores and tabeliães, found vilas and distribute sesmarias. The Crown kept brazilwood, dízimos and the quinto. These power details were not re-checked. Monopolies on mills, ovens and salt are mentioned only for Madeira's captaincies.
Mechanism
Royal letters of donation plus a foral; hereditary and indivisible.
Who paid
Indigenous peoples on the land and settlers under donatário jurisdiction. This is not documented in the pages fetched.
What came after
Most failed. Bahia was taken back in 1548-49 when the Governo-Geral was created, which did not end the system. In the 1750s 16 private captaincies remained under José I: 9 in Brazil, 1 Cabo Verde, 1 Príncipe, 3 Madeira, 2 Azores. All were under the Crown by 1770, bought or reincorporated 1753-1770.
Counter-view
Grants were a cheap way to settle a coast the Crown could not afford to occupy, and most captaincies failed, so the Crown retook them. Source: pt.wikipedia, Capitanias hereditárias.
Figures
  • verified Captaincies / lots / beneficiaries: 14 captaincies, 15 lots (quinhões), 12 beneficiaries (count) (1534-1536; pt.wikipedia) source
    These are three different units, not a disagreement between sources.
  • corrected Private captaincies remaining in the 1750s: 16 (9 Brazil, 1 Cabo Verde, 1 Príncipe, 3 Madeira, 2 Azores) (count) (1750s; pt.wikipedia) source
    The first notes implied all remaining captaincies were in Brazil. Not all were.
  • unverified Coast in one grant from the São Francisco southward: 60 leagues (leagues) (1530s; Revista Clio (UFPE)) source
    Not re-opened by the fact-check.
  • unverified Two captaincies for Pero Lopes de Sousa: 80 leagues in total (leagues) (1530s; Redalyc) source
    Not re-opened by the fact-check.

1608 to Empire (end date not found)
e1-04
Tithe (dízimo) tax farming and contratos régios

For the colonial centuries the Crown sold the right to collect the tithe for a fixed sum, and contractors kept what they collected above their bid. The bids give a rough picture of tithe income, but profits and contractor names were not found.

Government
Kingdom of Portugal; the Crown held the dízimos as Grand Master of the Order of Christ under a papal grant (Julius III)
What happened
The right to collect one tenth of output was auctioned in three-year terms for a fixed sum paid to the Treasury. In Minas Gerais the Junta da Real Fazenda ran the auction from 1772. Contractors kept private books outside state archives, so series are scarce.
Who got it
Capitalists who bid before the Provedoria. Their names and financing were not found.
Terms
The bid was the Crown's guaranteed revenue. Contractor profit was collections minus the bid. No margin estimate was found. Where bids were poor the Junta collected directly (Minas 1737-8, 1765-8, 1771-2).
Mechanism
Auction (arrematação) under the Fazenda Real rules, three-year terms. Contract clause details are unverified.
Who paid
Planters and farmers paying the tenth to contractors' collectors. Sugar was about 90% of the Bahia tithe.
What came after
The same contract model was used for entradas, passagens, diamonds and whaling. Treatment in the Empire and the end date of the dízimo were not researched.
Counter-view
Contracts gave the Crown predictable cash in a vast territory, and it could administer directly when bids were poor. Source: Carrara.

    Read once on an opened page in the gaps notes; not independently re-checked.

    Read once on an opened page in the gaps notes; not independently re-checked.

1614 to 1801
e1-05
Whaling monopoly (contrato das baleias)

The Crown owned whales by law and leased the right to hunt them to contractors from 1614. The work depended on enslaved labour. Lease prices were not found.

Government
Kingdom of Portugal; later Crown administration
What happened
Whales were declared royal property (peixe-real) and fishing rights were leased by contract. The first lease of whaling in the Bahia Recôncavo went to Antônio da Costa in 1614 (citing Myriam Ellis). Another source dates monopolies 1747-1764 and 1765-1801; the two periodisations are not resolved.
Who got it
Whaling contractors. Names beyond Antônio da Costa and financing were not found.
Terms
Lease prices were not found.
Mechanism
Asiento/contract leasing of fishing rights. The end date given is the alvará of 24 April 1801, but that date was not confirmed on any opened page.
Who paid
Enslaved labour: 525 enslaved people worked in the Santa Catarina armações in 1801, after the Crown had taken over management.
What came after
The monopoly ended in 1801, together with the salt monopoly.
Figures
  • verified Enslaved people in the Santa Catarina armações: 525 (people) (1801; UFSC SCEH article) source
    Weak confirmation: the PDF text is compressed and only its notes were readable.

1631 to 1801
e1-06
Salt monopoly (estanco do sal)

For 170 years the Crown sold the sole right to ship salt to Brazil. The contractor paid a reported 48 contos a year, and councils complained about prices and neglect.

Government
Kingdom of Portugal
What happened
A Crown monopoly on exporting salt from Portugal to Brazil, auctioned to a contratador.
Who got it
A contratador (contractor). In the 18th century contractors needed a guarantor (fiador). Names and financing were not found.
Terms
According to Azeredo Coutinho, the contractor paid the Fazenda Real 48 contos de réis a year. The date of that figure is not stated.
Mechanism
Crown monopoly leased by contract. Ended by alvará, dated 24 April 1801 in the notes (the date was not seen on an opened page).
Who paid
Consumers. Municipal councils (câmaras) complained of contractors' neglect and excessive prices throughout the 17th century.
What came after
The monopoly ended in 1801 together with the whale monopoly. The main study is Myriam Ellis, O monopólio do sal no Estado do Brasil (1631-1801), 1955.
Counter-view
The contract gave the Crown a fixed income of 48 contos a year without collection cost. Coutinho opposed the monopoly himself but did not want the Treasury to lose that revenue. Source: UFF article metadata and a search result.
Figures
  • verified Annual payment by the salt contractor to the Fazenda Real: 48 contos de réis a year (réis) (not stated; Azeredo Coutinho, via UFF article) source
    Weak confirmation: the PDF was compressed and only metadata and a search snippet were readable.
Sources
  • Revista de História USP A005N004
  • UFF, Tempo article

1674 onward (Junta created 1674)
e1-07
Tobacco monopoly (estanco / contrato do tabaco)

The Crown leased the sole right to buy Brazilian tobacco and sell it in Portugal to Lisbon merchants in three-year contracts. Prices rose from 2.02 to 2.22 million cruzados in the 1750s. Contractor profit and grower losses were not measured.

Government
Kingdom of Portugal, Prince Regent Pedro (decree of 14 July 1674); Pombal reforms 1751
What happened
The exclusive right to buy Brazilian tobacco and sell it in the kingdom and islands, leased in three-year contracts. Earlier origins (1630s) and abolition in 1833 are unverified.
Who got it
The Contratadores Gerais, Lisbon merchants. Their lenders were not found.
Terms
The price came from bidding. Per three-year term, from Pombal's Dedução Compendiosa as reported by Novais: 1750-52 Feliciano Velho Oldemberg, 2,020,000 cruzados; 1753-55 José Machado Pinto, 2,100,000; 1756-58 Duarte Lopes Rosa, 2,220,000; next contract four merchants at 2,210,000. The Crown took a fixed sum and the contractor kept the margin. No estimate of contractor profit was found.
Mechanism
Royal monopoly (estanco) plus auction (arrematação). Junta da Administração do Tabaco in Lisbon (Regimento of 1702, 53 articles); superintendencies in Bahia and Pernambuco (1702), replaced by Mesas de Inspeção in 1751.
Who paid
Brazilian growers selling into a single-buyer system with duties and inspection, Portuguese consumers, and Brazilian planters who carried the 1674 duties. Producer losses were not quantified.
What came after
The Mesa de Inspeção and Pombal's rules came in 1751. The monopoly stayed a pillar of royal revenue. Rosa was awarded his contract without Pombal's approval, was ruined and had his goods sequestered.
Counter-view
The contract gave the Crown cash up front and put the risk of bad years on merchants. Rosa's failure shows contractors could lose, and the Crown seized his goods. Source: Novais thesis (USP). A claim that Bahian tobacco as slave-trade currency favoured Bahian merchants over Lisbon is unverified.

c.1700 to c.1790
e1-08
Gold in Minas Gerais: quinto, foundry houses, capitação, derrama

In the Minas gold rush the Crown kept 20% of the gold but made miners and towns carry the collection risk through a poll tax and a collective charge. Smuggling was the main loss. This case is mostly a tax system, not a sale.

Government
Kingdom of Portugal
What happened
The Crown kept the royalty (the quinto, 20% of gold) but pushed collection and risk onto miners and local elites. Foundry houses from 1719; a per-slave poll tax (capitação); and a collective charge (derrama) if the quinto fell short.
Who got it
Not a transfer of assets. Mining grants (datas minerais) and tax-farm contracts (contratos de entradas) are not covered by the sources.
Terms
Quinto 20%. Capitação from the second half of 1735 to the first half of 1751 (Carrara; Magalhães says 1735 to 1750; the notes' exact days 1 July 1735 and 1 Aug 1751 are not confirmed). Foundry houses were re-established by an order of 3 Dec 1750 with a 100-arroba quota. Derrama: if the quinto fell below 100 arrobas (about 1,500 kg) a year, the shortfall was charged to the population.
Mechanism
Royal tax (quinto), foundry houses, capitação, derrama.
Who paid
Enslaved miners (taxed per head, and the labour itself) and mining towns under the derrama threat. The derrama of 1763 was applied first. The one announced for Feb 1789 was cancelled before collection and tied to the Inconfidência.
What came after
Foundry houses returned in 1750-51 with a quota to fight smuggling.
Counter-view
Here the Crown kept the royalty. The loss was smuggling and evasion: the gap between 557 t shipped and about 73% of estimated output is commonly read as contraband. Foundry houses and the quota were meant to fight it.
Figures
  • verified Quinto rate: 20% of gold (percent) (c.1700-1790; Redalyc 279149151002) source
  • verified Gold that reached Lisbon, 1720-1807: 557 tonnes, about 73% of estimated output (tonnes) (1720-1807; Lima and Sousa working paper (Redalyc)) source
    The gap is not explained in the sources.
  • unverified Peak output c.1730-1755: 18-20 tonnes a year (tonnes) (c.1730-1755; Redalyc 279149151002) source
    The peak figure is hidden in the summary read by the fact-check.
  • verified Derrama trigger: quinto below 100 arrobas (about 1,500 kg) a year (arrobas) (c.1750; Redalyc 384446660010 and search results) source
    Shortfall shared among the four comarcas / charged to the homens-bons.
  • unverified Capitação per enslaved miner: 5$000 réis a year (réis) (1735-1751; Periodicos UFRN (via search summary)) source
    Not found by the fact-check. One study site says 17 grams of gold per slave, also unverified.
Sources

1740 to 1832
e1-09
Diamond contracts and Royal Extraction, Distrito Diamantino

From 1740 the Crown auctioned the right to mine diamonds in a closed district, mostly to two families. In 1771, after smuggling, it took the mines back under a royal monopoly. Enslaved miners did the work.

Government
Kingdom of Portugal: João V and José I; Marquês de Pombal
What happened
The right to mine and sell diamonds in a closed district, leased to contractors who paid the Crown. Six contracts from 1740 to 1771 (some sources start in 1734), each about four years, by public auction. A Crown reserve of 241,405 carats valued over 2,200 contos is mentioned; that is a Crown holding, not contractor output, and was not confirmed.
Who got it
The Fernandes de Oliveira and Caldeira Brant families. The father, with F. Ferreira da Silva, held the first two contracts and the son the last three, so the family took five of six. Felisberto Caldeira Brant held the third (dates vary: 1748-1752, 1749-1753, 1749-1755) and ended in a diamond-theft prosecution. João Fernandes de Oliveira held the sixth, 1762-1771 in one source (Wikipedia pt says he administered the contract 1753-1771). Financing is not stated.
Terms
Sources disagree on payment: proportional to sales revenue vs a yearly fifth. Exact annual sums were not found.
Mechanism
Contract by auction. In 1771 the Crown moved to a royal monopoly (Real Extração), by decree dated 12 Aug 1771 in CartaCapital only. The Regimento Diamantino 1771 imposed licences for residence, trade and movement; unauthorised possession of diamonds was a grave crime (prison, confiscation, exile).
Who paid
Enslaved miners (legal mining only by slave gangs of the Intendência from 1772), and residents under travel and trade bans.
What came after
The privatised contract was reversed by the state in 1771, after smuggling. The Real Extração lasted to 1832 (Intendência abolished 1832; Wikipedia pt also says 1831 for the Real Extração). A UFMG source says officially 1832, in practice 1841. A counter-example of renationalisation.
Counter-view
The contract system was Crown revenue with auctions, and the Crown itself ended it in 1771 because of contraband. Júnia Furtado reads the Regimento Diamantino as a revalidation of earlier laws, not a new regime (UFJF paper, from a search result).
Figures

    Confirmed only from search snippets.
  • verified Contract period: 1740-1771 (some sources 1734-1771); six contracts (years) (1740-1771; pt.wikipedia) source
    The page gives 1740-1771 in the text and 1734-1771 in a heading.
  • disputed Payment terms to the Crown: proportional to sales revenue vs a yearly fifth (year n/a; Conflicting sources in the notes) source
    No source resolved which is correct. Exact annual sums not found.
  • unverified Crown diamond reserve: 241,405 carats, valued over 2,200 contos (carats / réis) (year n/a; Notes (source not identified)) source
    Not found on the page the fact-check opened. A Crown holding, not contractor output.

1755 to 1778
e1-10
Companhia Geral do Grão-Pará e Maranhão

Pombal gave a merchant company a 20-year monopoly on the trade and slave supply of Grão-Pará and Maranhão. It moved 28,083 enslaved Africans before Maria I closed it in 1778.

Government
Kingdom of Portugal: José I and Pombal; closed under Maria I
What happened
A monopoly on foreign trade of Grão-Pará and Maranhão and on the slave supply to those captaincies, planned for 20 years.
Who got it
A joint-stock company of Portuguese merchants with Crown backing.
Terms
Capital about 1.2 million cruzados. No price paid for the monopoly was found.
Mechanism
Royal charter of a joint-stock monopoly company.
Who paid
Enslaved Africans (28,083 transported). Colonists complained of prices. A link to the end of Indigenous enslavement (1755 laws) is noted but not documented.
What came after
Monopolies were revoked and the company shut in 1778 by Maria I after Pombal's fall (the 'viradeira'). An Infopedia entry gives 1775, an outlier. Liquidation took decades.
Counter-view
The company aimed to counter Dutch and English trade and fix labour and credit supply to a poor region. The cost was price complaints and Indigenous and Black enslavement. Not sourced beyond Wikipedia in this pass.

Companhia Geral de Pernambuco e Paraíba

Under Pombal a merchant company got a trade monopoly in Pernambuco and Paraíba from 1759, with the Crown directly involved. The company carried 49,344 enslaved people from Angola in 1761-1786. Capital and liquidation details are missing.

Government
Kingdom of Portugal: José I and Pombal
What happened
A trade monopoly in the northern captaincies of Pernambuco and Paraíba. It also financed slave purchases in Angola (Menz, Afro-Ásia).
Who got it
A merchant company with shareholders and direct Crown financial and managerial involvement.
Terms
Capital was not found.
Mechanism
Royal charter of a joint-stock monopoly company, founded 13 Aug 1759 per Wikipedia (30 July per another source).
Who paid
Enslaved Africans (49,344 carried from Angola to Brazil 1761-1786). Colonial consumers are implied but not documented.
What came after
Privilege suspended at the start of the 1780s. The notes give liquidation 1780-1813, which the fact-check could not confirm.

1759 to 1763 and after
e1-12
Jesuit estates: sequestration and resale

After expelling the Jesuits, the Crown seized their estates and sold many at public auction, often on instalments. Sale totals in Bahia range from about 310 to 548 contos depending on the author. The enslaved people on the estates were sold with them.

Government
Kingdom of Portugal: José I and minister Pombal
What happened
After the expulsion of 1759 the Jesuit estates were seized. Bahia inventory of 26 July 1759: 184 houses, 58 rented plots, 5 engenhos and 698 enslaved people. Rio: Engenho Velho, Engenho Novo, urban houses and Santa Cruz.
Who got it
Public-auction buyers, paying by instalment in two or three fleets. The Misericórdia bought the Cais dos Padres in Bahia. Francisco Carneiro Leão and Antonio Ferreira Malheyros also bought. Gonçalo Marques de Oliveira took a Macaé farm. Financing was not found.
Terms
Carvalho says Rio bids were above appraisals (her view). Chancellor Barreto put the 698 enslaved at 40-48 million réis. Bahia college property was appraised at 190,886,000 réis with rent of 11,451,200.
Mechanism
Sequestration by royal order (Rio sale edict Dec 1760; alvará of 25 Feb 1761 put the goods in the Real Fazenda), then edital and public auction. Unsold estates stayed under Treasury administration.
Who paid
Enslaved and Indigenous people sold as property, Jesuit-run economies, and tenants. Barreto warned that leasing the mills would ruin them.
What came after
Unsold estates were administered at a loss or split up. Santa Cruz stayed with the Crown. A 1799 Santa Cruz sale figure seen in a snippet is unverified.
Counter-view
Carvalho argues the Crown gained on sales. The RBH article stresses instalments and ruinous administration. It is also arguable that the first step went from a private order to the Crown, and only the second to private buyers.

1808 to 1829
e1-13
First Banco do Brasil

The first Banco do Brasil had trading privileges in state-monopoly goods and paid shareholders double-digit dividends. It lent heavily to the Crown and was liquidated in 1829. In 1821 the state took over its liabilities as national debt.

Government
United Kingdom of Portugal, Brazil and the Algarves: Prince Regent João; liquidation under Pedro I
What happened
A privileged bank with exclusive trading in state-monopoly goods (diamonds, brazilwood, ivory, urzela). The notes also listed handling Royal Treasury remittances. Tobacco and a 2% commission were not supported by the sources.
Who got it
Shareholders, mostly in Rio. 1821 holdings: Rio 61.7%, Bahia 15.8%, Minas 8.7%, São Paulo 5.6%, others 8.2%. Directors discounted bills for themselves, absconded and faked bankruptcies (Cardoso).
Terms
Capital 1,200,000$000 in 1,200 shares of 1,000$000; full capital reached only ten years after founding. Dividends 10-19% a year, 18.75% in 1828. The Crown borrowed from the bank: aid to the Real Fazenda of 5-6 million cruzados a year.
Mechanism
Alvará of 12 Oct 1808. Decree of 23 March 1821 turned the bank's liabilities into national debt backed by diamonds and jewels. Liquidation ordered by law of September 1829 (the notes say 23 Sept; the day was not seen).
Who paid
Note holders and, later, the Treasury. Shareholder payout in liquidation was not found. By 1821 paper issued was over three times capital.
What came after
Liquidated in 1829. There was no bank until 1838.
Counter-view
The main cause of the collapse was the Crown's own borrowing: the Royal Exchequer owed the bank 4.8 million (about twice capital), so the court drained the bank, not only shareholders profiting. Source: Cardoso, SciELO. Sampaio blamed internal abuses more than Treasury loans; Cardoso says shareholders had no reason to complain.

1808 to 1844
e1-14
Opening of the ports and the 1810 Treaty of Commerce with Britain

The 1810 treaty set a 15% tariff for British goods, lower than for other nations, and gave British subjects their own judge in Brazil. It ran until 1844. The sources give no figure for the lost revenue.

Government
United Kingdom of Portugal, Brazil and the Algarves: Prince Regent João
What happened
A tariff privilege and a special court for British merchants. Ports opened in 1808; the treaty was signed in Rio on 19 Feb 1810 and lasted to 1844 (original expiry 1825, then renewed). British goods paid 15% on entry vs 25% for other nations (Wikipedia). A juiz conservador da Nação Inglesa (decree of 4 May 1808, consolidated in the 1810 treaty) tried cases of British subjects.
Who got it
British merchants and manufacturers.
Terms
Article 15 set 15% for British goods. In practice monetary instability and valuation disputes often raised the real rate above 15% in the 1820s. Portugal also agreed to limit and consider ending the slave trade.
Mechanism
Treaty of commerce (Strangford Treaty); decree of 4 May 1808 for the juiz conservador.
Who paid
Local handicraft and the Treasury through low tariff revenue. Wikipedia claims Brazilian tobacco and sugar were barred from British markets; a specialist source is still needed. The revenue loss was not quantified.
What came after
The treaty lasted to 1844. The juiz conservador office ended only in 1844 (see the 1827 treaty case).
Counter-view
The treaty was a wartime concession for British naval protection of the exiled court (Strangford), and the preference was matched by high British duties on Brazilian sugar and tobacco. A treasury-loss argument needs revenue figures, which the sources lack. Source: fact-check of Wikipedia.
Figures
  • verified Tariff on British goods vs other nations: 15% vs 25% (percent) (1810; Wikipedia) source
    Wikipedia only for the 25%. The idea that Portuguese goods paid 16% was not found in any source opened.
  • verified Real rate on British goods in the 1820s: often above 15% (percent) (1820s; Pereira, Estudos Econômicos (abstract)) source
    Instability and valuation disputes raised the de facto rate. Confirmed from a search snippet of the abstract.
  • verified Brazilian tobacco and sugar barred from British markets: claimed (1810; Wikipedia) source
    Wikipedia only; check against a specialist source.
  • unverified Juiz conservador, decree of 4 May 1808: to 1844 (1808; Klinghoffer, RSP (ENAP)) source
    Not re-opened by the fact-check.

1827 to 1844
e1-15
Anglo-Brazilian treaty of 1827 (renewal of the 1810 regime)

The 1827 treaty renewed the 1810 deal: a 15% tariff for British goods and a British judge in Brazil. The 15% rate for all nations from 1828 removed the British-only edge, and the treaty lapsed in 1844. Customs were over half of imperial revenue by the mid-1840s.

Government
Empire of Brazil, Pedro I
What happened
The 15% ad valorem tariff on British goods continued to 1843, with Article XIX moving valuation to market prices. The British judge conservador stayed until Brazil provided a 'satisfactory substitute'. Brazil said the 1832 procedure code was one, Britain disagreed, and the post ended on 10 Nov 1844.
Who got it
British merchants and manufacturers, and their own court.
Terms
Canning wrote in 1826 that the treaty was 'more onerous to Brazil'. A 1826 French treaty matched French rates to British, and Brazil's 1828 tariff set 15% for all nations, ending the British-only preference.
Mechanism
Treaty of friendship, navigation and commerce, valid 15 years from ratification; Article VI equality clause.
Who paid
The Treasury, whose main income was customs, and local textile makers (Stein's view, as reported by Pereira).
What came after
The Alves Branco tariff of 1844 raised rates once the treaty lapsed.
Counter-view
Furtado did not blame the treaties for failed industrialisation but saw the cap as limiting autonomy. Pereira finds effective rates in the 1820s were often above 15% because of valuation disputes and currency instability. Revenue lost against a higher tariff was not computed by anyone in the sources.

1830 to 1960/1985
e1-16
St John d'el Rey Mining Company (Morro Velho)

A London company bought the Morro Velho gold mine in 1834 and worked it with Cornish managers and a large enslaved workforce into the 1870s. It is a private purchase, not a state grant. How it ended is reported differently by two sources.

Government
Empire of Brazil: Pedro I and the Regency
What happened
A private purchase of an existing gold mine, Morro Velho, bought in 1834 by a London joint-stock company formed in April 1830. The mine had about 50 years of earlier working. This is a private purchase, not a state grant; it is the template of foreign mining in the era.
Who got it
British joint-stock investors (first chairman John Diston Powles) and Cornish managers, about 350 Cornish miners in the 1860s. Financing came through the London joint-stock company.
Terms
Price not given in the source read. First dividends in 1842.
Mechanism
Private sale and joint-stock company; no state grant.
Who paid
Enslaved labour. In 1845 the company rented 385 enslaved people from the Cata Branca company for 14 years with a promise of emancipation at the end; the promise was ignored after 1859. About 200 people were still enslaved in 1879. Eakin calls it the largest industrial slave complex in Brazil (unconfirmed).
What came after
Formally closed in 1985. Diário do Comércio says it was sold in 1960 to the Moreira Sales group because of Brazilian limits on foreign control. Wikipedia does not mention that sale and says 1957 investors bought control. The buyer is spelled 'Moreira Salles' in other literature.
Figures

    With a promise of emancipation at the end, ignored after 1859.
  • corrected Enslaved people still held in 1879: about 200 (people) (1879; Wikipedia) source
    The first notes quoted a report as 'fully two hundred blacks in Slavery'. Wikipedia says 'about 200 people still enslaved'; the exact quote was not shown.
  • verified Cornish miners in the 1860s: about 350 (people) (1860s; Wikipedia) source
  • disputed When foreign control ended: 1960 sale (Diário do Comércio) vs 1957 control change (Wikipedia) (1957-1960; Conflicting sources) source
    Rests on one press article for 1960. Eakin's title covers 1830-1960; the Duke summary says 1830-1970.

1850 (Lei 601); regulated 1854
e1-17
Lei de Terras (Lei 601)

The 1850 law ended free occupation of public land and made purchase the only way to get it, while confirming existing holdings. Large holders gained, and the poor and Indigenous peoples lost access. The sources do not show how much it changed land concentration.

Government
Empire of Brazil, Pedro II
What happened
The terras devolutas (public lands without valid title). After 17 July 1822 there was no legal grant, so occupation by posse was the only route for 28 years. Lei 601 banned acquiring public land other than by purchase (art. 1; exception: border zone of ten leagues) and defined the devolutas.
Who got it
Existing landholders (squatters and sesmaria holders were legitimised) and buyers with capital.
Terms
Sale at public auction or otherwise (art. 14). Art. 2: squatters who clear or burn land must leave, lose improvements and face prison and a fine; new posse banned. Consolidated posses and sesmarias with effective cultivation were validated. Art. 12: the Government reserves devolutas it judges necessary for Indigenous settlement, towns, roads and shipbuilding. The price schedule was not found.
Mechanism
Lei 601 of 18 Sept 1850, regulated by Decreto 1.318 of 30 Jan 1854.
Who paid
Enslaved and later freed people, the free poor, and Indigenous peoples, whose access to land was closed by the purchase requirement. Some authors argue the law was meant to organise property, not widen access.
What came after
Land inequality predates 1850, so the law confirmed existing holders more than it started concentration. No pre-1850 baseline was found, so the law's own effect cannot be isolated. Frankema: land inequality in Latin America 'did not fundamentally change' across the 19th and 20th centuries.
Counter-view
The law's stated aim was to organise public land, finance immigrant settlement and stop illegal posse. The reading that it was built to keep labour tied to estates is an interpretation (Martins, Costa), not sourced here. Silva (1996) and Motta on the law's limited reach are unverified (search summaries only).

Urban utilities: Rio gas (1851) and City Improvements (1862)

Rio's gas and sewage services went to private companies, and the gas business moved from Mauá to a British firm in 1865. The contract terms are missing, so the case can only be dated.

Government
Empire of Brazil, Pedro II
What happened
Rio's gas lighting by contract with Mauá in 1851, sold in 1865 to the English Rio de Janeiro Gas Company Limited by decree that year. The Rio de Janeiro City Improvements Company Limited, for sewage, was incorporated in England after an Imperial concession; a decree of 1870 regulates its house-cleaning and rainwater sewers.
Who got it
Mauá, then British companies.
Terms
Concession terms, tariff, exclusivity, duration and guarantees are all missing. The sources are not usable beyond the dates.
Mechanism
Imperial concession and contract; decree of 27 April 1865 authorising the gas sale.
Who paid
Not documented.
What came after
Gas passed to British ownership in 1865 after a financial crisis. Dates for the sewage company could not be confirmed.

1852 to 1871 and after
e1-19
Amazon steam navigation privilege to Mauá

In 1852 Mauá received a 30-year exclusive steam-navigation privilege on the Amazon with a yearly subsidy, free land for colonies and a free dock site. The company ran until 1871 and passed to British ownership. The subsidy actually paid and the sale price were not found.

Government
Empire of Brazil, Pedro II
What happened
An exclusive privilege for 30 years for steam navigation on the Amazon, with a subsidy and free land. Also a second line to Nauta (Peru), free land for 60 colonies of foreigners or Indigenous people on the riverbanks, and free state land for a dock in Belém. Operations began in 1853 (Companhia de Navegação e Comércio do Amazonas, 1852-1871).
Who got it
Irineu Evangelista de Sousa (Mauá).
Terms
Subsidy of 160 contos de réis a year for the first 15 years on the Belém-Rio Negro line. The fact-check says this is per round trip under Condition 3; the exact basis is unclear. Obligations: fixed trip schedules, fines for missed trips, minimum speed of 8 miles an hour upriver, free mail and four state passengers per trip.
Mechanism
Decreto 1.037 of 30 Aug 1852. Decree 9.971 of 20 June 1888 later reshaped the British company's capital.
Who paid
The Treasury (subsidy), and riverine and Indigenous lands (colony grants). Context: the state wanted to counter foreign pressure for free navigation of the Amazon.
What came after
The company lasted to 1871. Decree 9.971 of 20 June 1888 cut the British Amazon Steam Navigation Co.'s nominal capital from £1,000,000 to £625,000, reset 50,000 shares from £20 to £12.10, treated 40,419 shares of £15 as fully paid, and kept the clauses of Decree 5020 of 18 July 1872. The line became the British company and later Enasa, whose 1990s privatisation failed because employee labour claims matched the appraised value. The 1871 transfer decree and the 1872/73 sale to a British company are unverified. The subsidy actually paid and the sale price were not found.
Counter-view
The state was trying to secure navigation of the Amazon against foreign claims, and no private operator would run the line without subsidy. Source: UFAM thesis cited in the notes (not opened; its link returned 404).

1852 to 1889
e1-20
Railways: interest guarantees (Decreto 641 of 1852) and the São Paulo Railway (1860)

From 1852 the Empire guaranteed railway investors a fixed return, usually 5%, whatever the traffic, and mostly British capital built the lines. Payments grew over time and were a large part of foreign debt service. The 5% guarantee on the São Paulo Railway came with caps on dividends and a profit-sharing rule.

Government
Empire of Brazil, Pedro II
What happened
The state guaranteed a minimum return (5% typical, up to 7%) on capital spent by railway companies. Four types of concession from 1852 to 1880. About 16 companies on £16.7m of capital covered about 2,900 km of the 9,600 km existing in 1889. São Paulo Railway (Santos-Jundiaí), Decreto 2.601 of 6 June 1860: 5% guaranteed on the first twenty leagues, later extended to the whole line.
Who got it
Mostly British-financed companies, via London. A British engineer-promoter pushed the guarantee idea (Duncan, Cambridge chapter, not read in full).
Terms
São Paulo Railway: 5% a year, paid half-yearly, ceiling of £2,000,000 (at 27 pence per milréis); the Province of São Paulo added 2%; privilege for 90 years; profits above 8% shared with the Government, dividend capped at 12%; the Government could redeem after 30 years; duty-free import of materials (not re-checked). Decree 2450 of 1873: 7%, ceiling 100,000 contos, one company per province. Terms over time (Lanna): 1852 90-year guarantee and zone privilege of 66 km; 1874 zone 60 km; 1878 guarantee 30 years, zone 40 km; 1880 zone 20 km. The 1889 caps (6%, 30 contos per km, decree 10250) are unverified.
Mechanism
Decreto 641 of 26 June 1852 (popularly 'Lei 641' or 'Lei Cochrane'; the first notes called it 'Law 641'), amended by Decreto 2.450 of 24 Sept 1873 and later changes. Decreto 2.124 of 13 Mar 1858 applied 5% to Santos-Jundiaí capital; a later 1859 decree extended it over the whole concession.
Who paid
The Treasury and taxpayers (a contingent liability), exchange losses as sterling was bought in mil-réis, and freight payers.
What came after
The Republic bought the guaranteed lines in 1900 by gold bonds (CIDP). Guarantee payments were 1.7% of public spending in the 1860s and 7.4% in 1890-99. An audited cumulative total in contos to 1889 was not found.
Counter-view
Guarantees were the instrument that attracted British capital to build lines at all. The state also capped the São Paulo dividend at 12%, shared profit above 8% and could redeem after 30 years. Summerhill (Order Against Progress, 2003; EHR 1998) argues railways gave large social savings; his cost estimates and that figure were not opened. Source: fact-check.

Submarine telegraph concessions

The Emperor gave cable concessions to a British promoter in 1873, and British firms laid the Brazilian coast cable. The subsidy, monopoly and term are unknown. The fact-check could not confirm any detail.

Government
Empire of Brazil, Pedro II
What happened
Concessions granted by the Emperor to Sir Charles Tilston Bright, sold to Telcon. The cable was laid in 1873 from Pará to Maranhão, Ceará, Pernambuco, Bahia and Rio by Hooper's Telegraph Works. A Lisbon-Pernambuco cable was laid by the Brazilian Submarine Telegraph Company. Later merged into the Western Telegraph group.
Who got it
Bright, then Telcon, Hooper's and the Brazilian Submarine Telegraph Company (British).
Terms
Subsidy, monopoly and term were not found.
Mechanism
Imperial concession.
Who paid
Not documented.
What came after
Merged into the Western Telegraph group.
Sources
  • Atlantic-Cable: Cable & Wireless, Eastern Telegraph
  • Atlantic-Cable: 1873 Rio-Pará cable

1888 (decree of 12 July)
e1-22
Port of Santos concession

In 1888 the Empire gave a private group a 39-year concession to build and run the Santos quay, with fixed maximum fees and free reversion to the State at the end. No interest guarantee appears in the decree. The company later received long extensions.

Government
Empire of Brazil: Princess Regent, countersigned by Antonio da Silva Prado
What happened
Build and operate the quay at Santos, with usufruct of expropriated land and of reclaimed fill. Some sources date the formal contract and the Companhia Docas de Santos to 1890.
Who got it
Gaffrée, Guinle & Cia., later Companhia Docas de Santos. Named: José Pinto de Oliveira, C. Gaffrée, Eduardo P. Guinle, João Gomes Ribeiro de Avellar, Valdetaro, Benedicto Antonio da Silva, Ribeiro, Barros & Braga.
Terms
39 years from the decree (clause II). Fees fixed in the decree: 1 réis per kg handled, 3 réis per kg for bulky goods, 700 réis per day per metre of quay for steamers, 500 for sailing vessels, 2 réis per kg per month stored. Performance deposit 20:000$000; works to start in 6 months and finish in 3 years; fine of 2:000$ per month of delay. Reversion to the State without compensation at term. No explicit exclusivity, but preference for similar works. No interest guarantee in the text.
Mechanism
Concession under Law 1.746 of 13 Oct 1869 after public tender; Decreto 9.979 of 12 July 1888.
Who paid
Port users (fees) and coastal land.
What came after
The term was later extended to 90 years, the maximum under Law 1.746 of 1869 (the extension was not confirmed on an opened page). The long-run controversy over the Docas de Santos monopoly and its extensions is a later phase not documented here.
Counter-view
The decree set maximum tariffs, a performance deposit, fines for delay and free reversion to the State, so it was a conventional build-operate-transfer. Source: fact-check.
Figures

  • unverified Concession term after extension: 90 years (years) (year n/a; MLaw Review) source
    PDF not opened by the fact-check.
  • verified Tariff ceilings: 1 réis/kg; 3 réis/kg bulky; 700 réis/day/m (steamers); 500 réis/day/m (sail); 2 réis/kg/month storage (réis) (1888; Decreto 9.979, clause V) source
  • verified Performance deposit and delay fine: 20:000$000 deposit; 2:000$ fine per month of delay (réis) (1888; Decreto 9.979) source
Sources

  • Unicamp CMU document
  • MLaw Review

1889–1964: The Republic (20 entries)

Foreign concessions, land strips, railway guarantees and coffee rescues, then state counter-moves from the 1940s.

1882–1943 (republican period 1889–1943)
e2-01
Mate Laranjeira lease, Mato Grosso

A large block of public land on the Paraguay border was leased for mate in 1882 and stayed in private hands into the Republic. About two million hectares were worked. Vargas ended it in 1943.

Government
Empire (1882 decree), then First Republic to Vargas (ended 1943)
What happened
Lease of public (devolved) land on the Paraguay border for yerba mate extraction. About 2,000,000 ha were worked. Larger estimates of 5,000,000 to 5,400,000 ha exist but were not confirmed.
Who got it
Thomaz Laranjeira (1882). In 1892 he partnered with Banco Rio e Mato Grosso (Murtinho family, politically influential). In 1902 it became Larangeira Mendes & Cia. One note says a Buenos Aires firm with foreign capital took over after 1902; the fact-check did not confirm 'Buenos Aires'.
Terms
Royalty and rent terms were not found. Imperial decree n. 8.799 of 9 Dec 1882 legalised mate extraction on devolved land.
Mechanism
Imperial decree of 1882 (concession/lease for exploration). The fact-check says 'monopoly' is not stated; the paper calls it one of the largest land lessees of the First Republic.
Who paid
Workers, mostly Paraguayan, and Indigenous Guarani/Kaiowa lands. Debt peonage and Indigenous impact were NOT verified here.
What came after
Vargas saw the firm as an obstacle to the 'March to the West' and to denationalisation. Decree 5.941 of 1943 created the Colonia Agricola Nacional de Dourados in the new Federal Territory of Ponta Pora. Further details not confirmed.
Figures

    Paper says 'approximately two million hectares'.
  • unverified Total leased area (estimates): 5,000,000 to 5,400,000 (ha) (year n/a; Barros 1996 (via notes)) source
    Not found in the opened paper. Range given by sources: 2,000,000 worked vs 5,000,000-5,400,000 total.

1888–1980
e2-02
Companhia Docas de Santos port concession

Gaffree and Guinle won the Santos port concession in 1888 for 39 years, later extended to the 90-year maximum. It ended in 1980 when the state company Codesp took over. The decree gave customs exemptions but no interest guarantee.

Government
Empire (1888 tender), concession ran through the Republic to 1980
What happened
Right to build and operate Brazil's main coffee port at Santos.
Who got it
Gaffree and Guinle (Eduardo Guinle family) after rival bidders withdrew. Grantees under Decreto 9.979 also included Pinto de Oliveira, Avellar, Valdetaro and others. Financed by the concessionaires; initial partnership capital was 4,000 contos for 4 years.
Terms
Decreto 9.979 of 12 Jul 1888 gave 39 years, with reversion to the state without compensation. A later paper says it was extended to the 90-year maximum. Tariffs were set in the decree. Customs-duty exemption on construction materials and usufruct of reclaimed land. No interest guarantee in the text. The 1869 ports law allowed rate cuts only if net profit exceeded 12%.
Mechanism
Public tender (1888); Decreto 9.979 of 12 Jul 1888; extension up to the 90-year maximum under Decreto 1.746 of 1869 (1890 or 1892, date uncertain). Build-operate-transfer.
Who paid
Port users through tariffs. The state also invested heavily in the port itself (PUC-SP). Profits, dividends, tariff history and buy-out price were not found. An undated claim says tariffs rose 50% when dividends reached 8% (unverified).
What came after
Ended 1980. Codesp (Companhia Docas do Estado de Sao Paulo, controlled by the federal government) was created 1 Oct 1980; Decree 85.309 of 30 Oct 1980 regulated operation. The date 7 Nov 1980 was not verified. Reported repressive toward workers after 1964.
Counter-view
The 1888 decree had no interest guarantee and the concessionaires financed the port. It reverted to the state at the end, so it is a build-operate-transfer concession (fact-check).
Figures

    Old note said 90 or 92 years. The 1888 decree gave 39 years; a later extension reached the 90-year maximum (extension date uncertain).
  • disputed Concession term after extension: up to 90 (some sources say 92) (years) (year n/a; mlawreview paper) source
    90 vs 92 years; 92 is unverified.
  • unverified Initial partnership capital: 4000 contos de reis (1888; PUC-SP research note) source
    Not covered by the fact-check.

1889–1892 (peak 1890–91)
e2-03
Encilhamento: money creation and company boom

In 1890 the new Republic let regional banks print huge amounts of money and cut the capital needed to trade shares. A stock and company bubble followed and burst in 1891–92. Small investors, consumers and the Treasury paid, while the credit may have helped early industry.

Government
Provisional Government under Deodoro da Fonseca; Finance Minister Rui Barbosa (left Jan 1891)
What happened
Not one asset but a licence to create money and companies. The law of 17 Jan 1890 created three regional emission banks (Norte, Centro, Nordeste) allowed to issue up to 450,000 contos, more than double the paper money in circulation. Notes were inconvertible and backed by public-debt bonds. Decrees 164 and 165 cut the paid-in capital needed to trade shares from 20% to 10%.
Who got it
Ex-slaveholders and coffee rentiers (liquidity after abolition), bankers such as Mayrink, and British banks (Rothschilds) per Nassif/Franco/Levy. Financed by the new notes themselves. Banco Nacional do Brasil shares traded at up to a 45% premium (Levy 1980).
Terms
Exchange rate in pence per 1,000 reis: 27 (Nov 1889), 8 (1892), 12 (1902), from a partisan Austrian-school blog (its own '337%' figure is a miscalculation and was not used). Furtado: paper money fell from 216,000 to 197,000 contos in 1880–1889 while foreign trade rose from 411,000 to 477,000 contos, so the starting shortage was real.
Mechanism
Decree-laws of the Provisional Government: banking law 17 Jan 1890; company-formation decrees 164/165; Decreto 1.154 of 7 Dec 1890 merged the banks into the Banco da Republica, allowed to issue three times its reserves (decree seen in search results only).
Who paid
Small investors who lost in the crash; consumers through inflation and devaluation; the Treasury, which funded the rescue with foreign borrowing (Rothschild loans totalled GBP 7.5m from 1894). The Baring crisis of Nov 1890 raised Brazil's risk premium in London.
What came after
The bubble burst in 1891–92. Rui's banks were merged and liquidated. The 1898 funding loan followed.
Counter-view
Stein, Fishlow, Suzigan, Versiani and Lobo argue the credit helped textile and industrial formation and that devaluation protected industry. Fonseca calls Rui a precursor of developmentalism. Critics: Taunay 1923, Furtado, Almeida & Croce 2016 (all via the Analise Economica article).
Figures

    Not covered by the fact-check. 'More than double the paper money in circulation.'
  • unverified Money supply growth 1889 to 1894: 3.5 times (1894; Franco & Lago 2012 (via article)) source
    Not covered by the fact-check.
  • unverified Listed companies: about 90 (1888) to about 450 (1891) (count) (1891; Franco & Lago 2011 (via pt.wikipedia)) source
    Not covered by the fact-check.
  • unverified Note issue 1890–91: 335000 contos de reis (1891; thesis quote) no link
    Source not traced.
  • unverified Rothschild loans from 1894: 7500000 GBP (1894; Cobden Centre blog) source
    Partisan source; not independently checked.

1890–1916
e2-04
Sao Paulo-Rio Grande railway land strip, Lumber company and Contestado

A railway concession gave a private group a wide land strip and a timber company that could log and resell it. Settlers were pushed off and railway workers were laid off, which fed the Contestado War. Estimates of the dead run from 10,000 to 20,000.

Government
Concession 1890 (Decreto 305 of 7 Apr 1890); line commissioned 1908; Hermes da Fonseca (army campaign in the Contestado War)
What happened
The railway concession carried a strip of land along the track. Up to 15 km each side (fact-check: 9 km per km of track up to a maximum of 15 km). The Southern Brazil Lumber & Colonization Co. held rights to extract timber and resell the land. By 1913 it held about 3,248 km2 along the railway, of which about 1,800 km2 at Tres Barras (SC), plus 1,046 km2 at Jaguariaiva (PR).
Who got it
Brazil Railway Co. (Farquhar, North American). The original Teixeira Soares concession was transferred into this group.
Terms
The original concession carried 6% gold interest on 37,000:000$000 of capital for 30 years and 30 km of land each side for 50 years. Decreto 305 of 1890 set capital at 30 contos per km and cut the land zone to 15 km each side. The counter-source says the company built 1,400+ km of line.
Mechanism
Railway concession with a land grant and a guaranteed return; a lumber and colonisation company to log and resell the land.
Who paid
Subsistence farmers (posseiros) were expelled. Construction workers were dismissed when the railway finished; many joined the rebel movement of monk Jose Maria. Contestado War, Oct 1912 to Aug 1916: 10,000 to 20,000 deaths (Wikipedia infobox).
What came after
Land fights. The Lumber company logged the araucaria forest: in its first five years at the Tres Barras mill about 107 million cubic feet (about 249,000 m3) of logs, clearing about 6,011 ha (company report, April 1917).
Counter-view
The land grant was the usual railway-subsidy mechanism of the time (land instead of a cash guarantee), and the company argued it built 1,400+ km of line. The rural-conflict view (settlers already on the land, caboclos without titles) comes from the Contestado literature (Contestado War page).
Figures

    Old note said 15 km each side (about 30 km wide). Corrected to 9 km per km of track up to a maximum of 15 km each side. Decreto 305 of 1890 cut the original 30 km to 15 km.
  • verified Lumber company land held by 1913: 324800 ha (1913; Thome; Gauld (via UVM page)) source
    About 3,248 km2; hectares were 'not found' in the original notes. Includes 180,000 ha at Tres Barras and 104,600 ha (1,046 km2) at Jaguariaiva (PR).
  • unverified Guaranteed interest on original concession capital: 6% gold on 37,000:000$000 for 30 years (reis) (1890; Correa thesis, citing Gremaud 1992) source
    Not covered by the fact-check.
  • disputed Contestado War deaths: 10,000 to 20,000 (count) (1916; Wikipedia infobox) source
    Wide range: rebels 5,000-8,000 dead/wounded/missing; government casualties 800-1,000.
  • verified Logs cut in first five years at Tres Barras: 249000 m3 (1917; Company report April 1917 (via UVM page)) source

1891
e2-05
Transfer of public lands to the states, Constitution of 1891

The 1891 Constitution handed ownership of unclaimed public land to the states. This put land allocation in the hands of state oligarchies. Later land grants and sales to companies followed from it.

Government
First Republic (Constitution of 24 Feb 1891)
What happened
Art. 64 moved ownership of 'terras devolutas' from the Union to the states. The Union kept land needed for frontier defence, fortifications, military works and railways.
Who got it
State oligarchies and land speculators. Later colonisation and railway companies bought or received grants from states (see the Norte do Parana case).
Terms
Not applicable (a constitutional transfer, no price).
Mechanism
Constitutional Art. 64, from the Julio de Castilho amendment.
Who paid
Posseiros and Indigenous peoples. Grilagem (forged titles) through notaries, surveyors and judges is claimed in the literature; this was NOT verified.
What came after
Not covered in the notes.

1899–1979
e2-06
Light: Sao Paulo Tramway, Light and Power and Rio Light

Canadian-led Light held power and tram concessions in Sao Paulo and Rio for most of the century. In 1979 the state bought it back, at a price sources put anywhere from US$380m to US$1.14bn. Light was privatised again in 1996.

Government
First Republic concessions; buy-back under Geisel (Dec 1978 decision, closed 12 Jan 1979)
What happened
Monopoly-type concessions for urban power and trams in the two biggest cities. Duration and tariff terms were not found. In 1978–79 Eletrobras bought Brascan's 83% stake in Light.
Who got it
Canadian capital (with US and European), William Mackenzie and F.S. Pearson. SPTL&P founded 1899 in Toronto; Rio Light founded 1904 and authorised 1905; both under Brazilian Traction from 1912; later Brascan.
Terms
1978–79 buy-back price is disputed: US$380m (or 382m) versus US$1.14bn. A Globe and Mail-based source says US$460m below book value. A private-market alternative backed by ministers Simonsen and Ueki was blocked by Antonio Carlos Magalhaes (Carazza).
Mechanism
Urban concessions; in 1978–79 a share purchase by Eletrobras.
Who paid
Consumers (tariffs, not quantified), and in 1978–79 the Treasury and Eletrobras. A critic (Leite 1997) says the concession expired in 1990 with assets reverting free to the Union, so the state paid for what it would have received.
What came after
Tramways were bought by the Companhia Municipal de Transportes Coletivos in 1946. Eletropaulo was created in 1981. Light passed to the Rio de Janeiro state government and was privatised on 21 May 1996 (Carazza, Valor, 10 Feb 2020).
Counter-view
Light financed and built the first large-scale hydro and tram networks when neither the state nor Brazilian capital would (SPTL&P Wikipedia page). Wikipedia's Brascan page says Brascan was 'forced by the dictatorship'; a purchase below book value argues against overpayment. A fair summary needs a source on consumer tariffs (not found).
Figures

  • unverified Amount said to be below book value: 460000000 USD (1979; Globe and Mail via Wikipedia (Brascan)) source
    Implied book value about US$840m (derived, not stated).

1901–1903
e2-07
Bolivian Syndicate lease of Acre

In 1901 Bolivia leased rubber-rich Acre to a foreign-backed syndicate for 30 years. Brazil bought out the lease in 1903 and took Acre by treaty, promising a railway. The cost fell on the Treasury and on rubber tappers.

Government
Bolivia signed the lease (11 Jun 1901); undone under Rodrigues Alves (Brazil) in 1903
What happened
Bolivia leased the Acre region (rubber territory; about 191,000 km2 later ceded to Brazil) for 30 years, with 'almost total control'.
Who got it
The Bolivian Syndicate, a New York/Jersey City company. Reported shareholders included the King of Belgium and relatives of US President McKinley (Wikipedia: 'very influential shareholders').
Terms
Lease tax, customs and police terms were not found. Brazil ended the lease by paying the Syndicate GBP 110,000 (Wikipedia, Portal Amazonia) or GBP 114,000 (InfoEscola, distrato of 26 Feb 1903).
Mechanism
A foreign-state lease/charter, undone by a negotiated buy-out and the Treaty of Petropolis (17 Nov 1903): GBP 2 million to Bolivia in two instalments, a territory swap, and a promise to build the Madeira-Mamore railway.
Who paid
The Treasury (indemnity, GBP 2m, and the railway) and the rubber tappers in the Acre War.
What came after
Acre became Brazilian. The railway promise created the Madeira-Mamore case.
Counter-view
This was a Bolivian sovereign lease, Bolivia's attempt to assert control over a territory it could not police. Brazil's buy-out ended a foreign-run charter; it was not a giveaway of Brazilian public wealth. Acre was largely settled by Brazilian rubber tappers (Acre War page).
Figures

    Wikipedia does not name the currency (about 35m reis). Unresolved: about 110-114 thousand pounds.
  • verified Payment to Bolivia under Treaty of Petropolis: 2000000 GBP (1903; Treaty of Petropolis page) source
    Two instalments; treaty effective 10 Mar 1904.
  • verified Area of Acre: 191000 km2 (1903; Treaty of Petropolis page) source
    Brazil also gave up more than 3,000 km2 between Abuna and Madeira.

1906–1922
e2-08
Coffee valorization and the Taubate Agreement

From 1906 the state of Sao Paulo, then the Union, borrowed abroad and later printed money to buy surplus coffee for planters. The loans were repaid from a per-bag export levy, and foreign financiers earned large profits. The Vargas government took over Sao Paulo's foreign debts in 1930.

Government
Sao Paulo state (Tibirica); Rodrigues Alves federal role from Decree 1489 of 6 Aug 1906; Union guarantee from 1908; Epitacio Pessoa 1919–22
What happened
Public credit, state loans and later paper-money emissions were used to buy surplus coffee for planters. Taubate Convention signed 26 Feb 1906 by Tibirica, Francisco Sales and Quintino Bocaiuva (Sao Paulo, Minas, Rio). Minimum price 55–65 gold francs per 60 kg bag; Caixa de Conversao. Peak stock reported at 8,474,623 bags. Later rounds in 1917, 1921–22 and the Coffee Institute of 1924.
Who got it
Planters, plus foreign banks and traders. Financiers had 'large profits', planters 'some net profit', Sao Paulo state a net loss (US report). Theodor Wille & Co. bought at 7$000 per arroba and took 200 reis per bag commission. A seven-member committee included Sielcken of Crossman & Sielcken.
Terms
Foreign loans were repaid from a gold-payable export levy of 3 francs per bag (Lei 990), later raised to 5. 1906 crop about 16m bags vs world consumption 16m; supply 29.6m. 1922 terms were harsher than 1908, a creditor committee controlled stock sales, Brazil agreed to no new valorization while the loan ran, and Brazilian Warrant Co. got exclusive rights over valorization operations. No independent valuation of stock vs loan terms found.
Mechanism
State convention, then federal guarantee (Law 1.127 of 25 Aug 1908, seen in search results only); emission decrees (Decreto 3.316 of 16 Aug 1917; Decreto 4.182 of 13 Nov 1920) and a Banco do Brasil rediscount window.
Who paid
Foreign consumers (US consumers paid about US$57m a year for a 6-cent rise, per the US report) and domestic taxpayers through the surtax, the federal guarantee and inflation from the emissions. Other states refused the surtax and Rio state's coffee was hurt.
What came after
The Vargas government assumed Sao Paulo's foreign debts in 1930. Coffee Institute in 1924. Prices stayed artificially high and production kept growing. US report: the scheme ended with the loan repaid and price higher than before 1906 (an interpretation; no net-profit total found).
Counter-view
Purchases were mostly financed by foreign bank loans repaid from the export tax, with coffee as collateral, and prices recovered from 1908 (Brasil Agro). The 1917 round was financed by money issue (MPRA paper). Furtado held that the operation postponed a structural imbalance.
Figures

    Later raised to 5 francs (US report, unverified).

    Not covered by the fact-check.

    Net GBP 919,000. OCR garbled.

1906–1917 (again 1920s)
e2-09
Brazil Railway Company / Farquhar syndicate

Farquhar's Brazil Railway Company gathered nearly half of Brazil's rail network, plus ports, trams and land, in ten years. It leaned on state guarantees and, per weakly sourced claims, bribes. It went bankrupt around 1914 and left the public with the guarantees.

Government
Afonso Pena and following governments; Vargas restricted his activities after 1930
What happened
Control of about 11,000 km of the national network's 23,400 km (about 47%) within ten years. Also Sorocabana, Paulista, Mogiana, Madeira-Mamore, Sao Paulo-Rio Grande and Vitoria-Minas lines, trams in Salvador, Sao Paulo, Belem and Rio Grande, ports, Rio Light interests, telephones, lumber, colonisation, meatpacking and hotels.
Who got it
Percival Farquhar with Belgian, French and British capital. Company created 7 Sept 1906 (founded 9 Nov 1906 per pt.wikipedia).
Terms
Government interest and revenue guarantees, 'often through personal bribery' (Wikipedia on Farquhar; weak, no academic source opened). Port of Para: 6% guarantee on construction capital plus a 2% gold tax on port imports. Authorised US$32m of shares, US$23.5m issued, a GBP 3.6m 50-year 5% bond and 62.5m francs of 60-year 5% bonds.
Mechanism
Concessions with guarantees and land zones; share and bond issues.
Who paid
The treasury (guarantees), investors, and Indigenous peoples and settlers (Wikipedia says 'thousands' of Indigenous deaths, no figures or source).
What came after
Bankrupt by about 1914 as WWI financing was cut (search results; a forced agreement in 1917). Control lasted to about mid-1917. Partial recovery after the war, failed again after 1929; Vargas restricted Farquhar after 1930 and he left Brazil. Madeira-Mamore was handed to the Union in 1931 (price not found).
