1907–1912 (abandoned 1972)
e2-10
Madeira-Mamore Railway

The Madeira-Mamore railway was built by Farquhar's group because Brazil promised it in the 1903 treaty that gave it Acre. Thousands of workers died, with estimates from 3,500 to over 30,000. The rubber boom ended soon after and the line was abandoned in 1972.

Government
Rodrigues Alves / Afonso Pena / Nilo Pecanha era; contract tied to the 1903 treaty (Decreto 6.106 of 7 Aug 1906; 6.755 of 28 Nov 1907; 6.838 of 30 Jan 1908)
What happened
Construction and operation of the rail link around the Madeira rapids. Third attempt; an earlier company (Collins) gave up in Aug 1879 (search only). Construction began 1907; 366 km of track in five years.
Who got it
Percival Farquhar (US financier). Port of Para Co. held 50% of the shares in 1907 (Correa thesis).
Terms
Cost of the project: US$33m (Treaty page). Guarantee terms were not found on any opened page; the claim that Farquhar lived on state guarantees is weak and unconfirmed. An income statement lists a GBP 130,000 profit on issuing GBP 1.6m of 5% bonds and GBP 3,000 guarantee commission (dating unclear). Founders projected about US$70m profit in 10 years.
Mechanism
Contract under a treaty obligation: Treaty of Petropolis (1903) traded Acre for building the line within four years plus GBP 2m.
Who paid
Workers. Death toll is uncertain: 3,500–7,000 (Brown Univ.), 6,000 (Brazilian government), 7,000–10,000 (Uys), over 30,000 (Picoli); pt.wikipedia says about 6,000 deaths among about 30,000 workers.
What came after
The rubber boom collapsed (Asian plantations) and the line became redundant. Handed to the Union in 1931. Deactivated by Decreto 58.501 of 25 May 1966; last train 1972, after BR-364.
Counter-view
The line was the price of Acre, a state treaty obligation to Bolivia (free transit), not purely a concession to a private investor (fact-check).

Itabira Iron Ore Co. (Farquhar) and its end in Vale do Rio Doce

Farquhar tried to get the Itabira iron ore and a guaranteed-return railway in the 1910s–30s. The state answered by creating Vale in 1942. Vale was itself privatised in 1997.

Government
Epitacio Pessoa (contract signed for the government); Vargas (Vale created 1942)
What happened
Sought: Itabira ore deposits, a railway to a port near Vitoria, and export rights. Farquhar bought the Brazilian Hematite Syndicate in 1911 and renamed it Itabira Iron Ore Co. (the Farquhar Wikipedia page does not mention Itabira). He worked on the project 1919–1941.
Who got it
Percival Farquhar's Itabira Iron Ore Co. The company was 'Brazilianized' in the 1930s into Companhia Brasileira de Mineracao e Siderurgia.
Terms
Railway construction was guaranteed a 6% return in gold on invested capital, up to Cr$30,000 per km (Rogers 1959). Compensation to Itabira holders was not found.
Mechanism
Contract with the government signed by Epitacio Pessoa with Transport Minister J. Pires do Rio (the year 1920 is not on the opened page).
Who paid
Not stated; the project was largely not carried out as planned.
What came after
Opposition came from Minas's state Secretary of Agriculture and Industry, Clodimiro de Oliveira, under President Bernardes (the old note called it a 'Bernardes veto'). Vitoria-Minas line linked 1936; ore first exported 1940 (about 5,740 t to Great Britain on the Modesta). Decree-law 4,352 (1 Jun 1942) created CVRD, capitalised Cr$200,000,000. CVRD was privatised in May 1997 (41.73% sold).

State of Parana land sales (Brazil Plantations Syndicate organised 1924; CTNP organised 24 Sept 1925)

Land in northern Parana. About 515,000 alqueires paulistas were planned for colonisation between the Paranapanema, Ivai and Tibagi rivers (one source says over 500,000; hectares not computed). The company bought the Sao Paulo-Parana railway project in 1928.

British Parana Plantations Ltd / Brazil Plantations Syndicate (Lord Lovat named in a search result only), organised by Arthur Thomas and Antonio Moraes Barros. Founded Londrina.

State land sales; colonisation company.

Costs to existing posseiros and Indigenous (Kaingang) were not found.

The British sold in 1944 to Sao Paulo businessmen. Renamed Companhia Melhoramentos Norte do Parana in 1951.

The company sold planned plots to small farmers and founded Londrina, so large areas were settled and not left idle (search only).

Light's Billings project: Pinheiros reversal and Cubatao

Light got the right to reverse the Pinheiros river and expropriate land for the Borden plant. A 1929 flood killed 38 people and only 10% of seized land went back to its owners. The company was never formally indicted.

Government
1927 state/federal contract (Washington Luis era)
What happened
Right to divert the Tiete's surplus flow and reverse the Pinheiros river to feed the Henry Borden plant at Cubatao, plus the right to expropriate wetlands, with buy-back priority for former owners. Work began 1927; first phase 1935–37; underground plant 1956 (880 MW).
Who got it
Sao Paulo Tramway, Light and Power Company (Canadian capital).
Terms
Terms not stated in the notes.
Mechanism
A 1927 contract granting water-diversion and expropriation rights.
Who paid
The Feb 1929 flooding caused 38 deaths (the date 'Feb' is not stated on the page). Through side agreements only 10% of expropriated properties were returned to the original owners. Pollution of the reversed river.
What came after
The Billings reservoir became a metropolitan water source but is polluted. The reversal was restricted by a 1992 clause of the Sao Paulo state constitution (5 Oct 1992) to exceptional cases such as flood control, so it was not fully stopped. Water-rights questions persist.

Ford received a very large Para concession with tax exemption in 1927. The rubber plantation failed and he sold it in 1945 for US$244,200. Ford lost the money, so this case is weak evidence of a public-to-private transfer.

Government
State of Para (Governor Dionisio Bentes; approval 1927, exact day unconfirmed); sale to the federal government in Dec 1945
What happened
A concession to Henry Ford of about 10,100 km2 (about 1m ha; a municipal source cites 14,568 km2).
Who got it
Henry Ford. Export-tax exemption; Ford to pay 7% of profits to the government and 2% to municipalities. 'Granted free' was not confirmed.
Terms

A state concession with tax exemption.
Who paid
Workers recruited from the Northeast. Ford bore the financial loss after plantation failure (blight). Indigenous land impact not sourced.
What came after
Sold to the federal government in 1945.
Counter-view
This was a foreign private investment where the private party lost, and the Brazilian state recovered the land cheaply, so it is a poor example of a public-to-private transfer (fact-check).

Coffee purchase and destruction

Under Vargas the state bought surplus coffee from planters and burned it between 1931 and 1944. Estimates of the amount destroyed run from 72 to 80 million bags. Duties and loans paid for it; the price paid per bag was not found.

Government
Vargas; Conselho Nacional do Cafe (1931); Departamento Nacional do Cafe by Decreto 22.452 of 10 Feb 1933; mandate extended to 30 Jun 1944
What happened
The government bought surplus coffee from planters and destroyed it. Totals disagree: 78.2m bags (Daily Coffee News), about 72m (Santos municipal PDF, snippet) or 80m (CINDES PDF, snippet). The 1937 peak burned 70% of the annual stock.
Who got it
Planters and the coffee trade received purchase payments, financed by raised customs duties plus foreign loans. Coffee was over 50% of export value around 1929; a bag fell from 200,000 reis to about 20,000 in 1929.
Terms
No purchase price per bag or total outlay was found on an opened page.
Mechanism
Decrees creating the CNC and DNC; a funding tax on exported coffee (details unverified).
Who paid
Taxpayers and consumers through duties and loans; non-coffee sectors.
What came after
The programme ended in 1944.
Counter-view
Defenders see it as Keynesian-style demand support before Keynes (Furtado's income-maintenance argument, cited generally and not checked). No opened source quantified it.

The public sector.

Not covered.

e2-17
Banco de Credito da Borracha and the Washington Accords

In 1942 the state and the US created a bank with the sole right to buy and sell Amazon rubber at a US-fixed price. About 55,000 to 60,000 workers were recruited, and an estimated 30,000 died. The bank itself did well financially.

Government
Vargas; US side Rubber Reserve Company / Rubber Development Corporation
What happened
Decreto-lei 4.451 of 9 Jul 1942 created the bank with capital of 50,000 contos: at least 55% Treasury, 40% Rubber Reserve Company, the rest Brazilians only. It held the exclusive right of final purchase and sale of all rubber (Art. 8). Capital rose to Cr$150m by Decreto-lei 5.651 of 5 Jul 1943: 87,500 shares Treasury, 60,000 RDC, 2,500 private Brazilians.
Who got it
The US bought rubber for the war. Contract ran 3 Mar 1942 to 31 Dec 1946, with financing via a Reconstruction Finance Corporation letter of credit. Rubber barons (aviadores) lost the retail monopoly to the bank.
Terms
Fixed price of 39 cents per pound for Upriver Acre Fine f.o.b. Belem, plus a 2.5 cent premium on 5,000–10,000 tons a year and a US$5,000,000 RRC fund. No independent estimate of whether 39 cents was below market was found.
Mechanism
Washington Accords of 3 Mar 1942 plus Decreto-lei 4.451/1942; SEMTA (recruitment).
Who paid
The migrants. Projections of 100,000 tons a year were unrealistic. 'Half never returned' is an estimate of about 30,000 deaths (Portal Amazonia); the real count is not documented. Of those returning in the first half of 1946, 248 were judged unfit, mostly from malaria and avitaminosis. Full return transport guarantees not honoured (claim not verified).
What came after
Law 13.831/2019 put the rubber soldiers in the Livro dos Herois. ADCT art. 54 (1988) grants a pension of 2 minimum wages; EC 78/2014 added R$25,000; about 6,500 pensioners remained in Nov 2025 (search result).
Counter-view
The bank is described as financially successful: the value fund equalled capital within 3 years, helped by US premiums (Martinello). The death figure is only an estimate.

Production ended 1997 (SGB) or 1998 (HCS-Manguinhos). Tailings were removed in 1998.

Hanna Mining and the Minas iron-ore fight

A 1961 decree let Hanna mine 156 ha in Minas, on land its British subsidiary already held. Critics saw a first step to larger iron-ore reserves. Quadros annulled it, and Hanna later joined MBR after the 1964 coup.

Government
Juscelino Kubitschek (Decree 49.889, 12 Jan 1961 per the Senate text; its signature line says 1960, likely a typo); Janio Quadros annulled it 21 Aug 1961; Goulart tried to revoke again
What happened
Decree 49.889 authorised Mineracao Hanna do Brasil Ltda. to mine iron ore at Fazenda do Tamanduá, Nova Lima: 156 hectares, land belonging to St John del Rey Mining. Critics say it was the first step to the Paraopeba reserves.
Who got it
M.A. Hanna Co. (Cleveland); George Humphrey (director; the pt article calls him chairman), ex-US Treasury Secretary. In 1957 Hanna bought British St John del Rey Mining shares for US$6 million.
Terms
Taxes were payable and the authorisation could be declared null if obligations were not met.
Mechanism
Presidential decree under the Mining Code.
Who paid
Not covered.
What came after
Quadros annulled the decree on 21 Aug 1961, returned the deposits to the national reserve and resigned on 25 Aug. After the 1964 coup, MBR was formed in 1965 by CAEMI (Antunes group) with Hanna; it became the second biggest Brazilian producer in 1971. Vale bought Caemi; Caemi merged into Vale in Dec 2006. Claims that Hanna fed the coup are in pt Wikipedia only and are contested.
Counter-view
The decree covers only one 156 ha property already owned by the British company and was a routine Mining Code authorisation that required payment of taxes (Senate decree). The 'unconstitutional' reading and the link to the 1964 coup (pt Wikipedia) are contested.

    The Caemi page gives no Hanna percentage.

1959–1964
e2-20
Brizola's takeovers and the 1964 Eletrobras buy-out of Amforp

Brizola seized Bond and Share's CEERG in 1959 and ITT's telephone company in 1962. In 1964 Eletrobras bought Amforp's ten Brazilian subsidiaries, at a price sources put between US$135m and US$470m. Critics call the buy-out too generous; the buyers called it fair.

Government
Brizola (RS governor, 1959; 1962 telephone decree); Goulart (negotiation interrupted); Castello Branco (Nov 1964 contract)
What happened
Counter-move and buy-out. 13 May 1959: Rio Grande do Sul governor Brizola took over Bond and Share's CEERG. Feb 1962: decree 13.186 cancelled ITT's Companhia Telefonica Nacional concession; assets were expropriated. Nov 1964: AMFORP sold its ten Brazilian subsidiaries plus CAEEB to Eletrobras under Law 4.428 of 14 Oct 1964.
Who got it
Eletrobras (public) bought Amforp/Bond & Share assets and credits.
Terms
Per a thesis (Bastos, quoting Saes & Sasse 2012): US$135m for the assets, plus US$10m for delay and US$7.7m for interest and dividends, paid as a loan over 45 years at 6.5% a year. The April 1963 agreement already stood at US$135m, calculated on historical cost under the water code and considered fair for all Amforp assets. Brizola's 1959 'encampacao' of CEERG used a symbolic Cr$1 offer; the company claimed no less than Cr$2.1bn.
Mechanism
Law 4.428/1964; Treasury guarantee; Eximbank loans (search results). CEERG case never got a first-instance judgment; the thesis infers the indemnity was settled within the 1964 deal.
Who paid
Treasury and Eletrobras borrowers. The thesis says the purchase was meant to 'clear the slate' (limpar a barra) with the US after the 1963 delays.
What came after
The US government and AMFORP argued compensation was inadequate; the dispute continued until 1964. Brizola's position was that the company had an expired concession and was not investing. As federal deputy on 30 May 1963 Brizola called the purchase a 'crime de lesa-patria' and blamed San Tiago Dantas. Lacerda's position: not found.
Counter-view
Brizola argued the concession had expired and the company was not investing (Sul21 opinion piece, search only). The US/Amforp side said compensation was inadequate.
Figures
  • unverified Price for Amforp assets: 135000000 USD (1964; Bastos thesis, quoting Saes & Sasse 2012) no link
    Thesis URL path not re-verified; fact-check could not confirm.
  • disputed Amforp compensation (alternative figure): 470000000 USD (year n/a; pt.wikipedia (via search)) source
    Range US$135m vs US$470m. Fact-check: the US$470m refers to post-1964 settlements, not 1959; the Extraclasse page returned 403.
  • unverified CEERG valuation: Cr$1.35bn reduced to Cr$70m (Cr$) (1959; Extraclasse (one account)) source
    Uncorroborated.
  • unverified Company's claim for CEERG: not less than 2,100,000,000 (Cr$) (1959; Bastos thesis) no link
    Gross investment Cr$1,630,457,000, net Cr$1,362,623,000 in 1959; historical investment Cr$3,098,143,000 corrected to 1963.

1950s–1990
e3-01
Public land in Mato Grosso, Pará and Maranhão sold to colonisers and companies

State land bodies in Mato Grosso collected and sold millions of hectares of public land to colonisers and companies. Titles above the legal limit were arranged through nominee buyers. Hectare data for Pará are missing.

Government
State of Mato Grosso; federal INCRA and Sudam (Maranhão: state company COMARCO)
What happened
Millions of hectares of public land in Mato Grosso passed through state land bodies to colonisers and companies. In Maranhão, COMARCO (Dec 1971) took in 2.1 million ha of public land at once. No hectare series for Pará.
Who got it
Private colonisers SINOP, INDECO and CONTRIGUAÇU, and nominee buyers ('laranjas'). Who financed the buyers: Sudam tax incentives or their own resale. 1970s per-hectare prices were not found.
Terms
1950-64: colonisers paid Cr$7-10 per ha and resold at Cr$100-300 per ha, with average holdings of 200,000 ha.
Mechanism
Titles above the 3,000 ha constitutional limit were arranged through powers of attorney to nominee buyers. Decreto-Lei 1.164/1971 put about 60% of Mato Grosso under federal control until 1978. State companies CODEMAT and INTERMAT, and INCRA, then collected and sold land.
Who paid
The public domain, and the Indigenous and posseiro occupants. Settlers paid high resale prices.
What came after
The state land department (DTC) was closed in 1966 after repeated fraud. Programmes named 'Terra Pública' or direct INCRA sales to companies were not found in any opened source.
Counter-view
The sales were also how the state settled the north. The authors' main complaint is the lack of control, fraud and speculation, not the settlement itself (Moreno 1999 via Lilian da Rosa 2017).
Figures
  • verified Resale gain for 1950-64 colonisers: bought at Cr$7-10 per ha, resold at Cr$100-300 per ha; average 200,000 ha each (BRL (cruzeiros)) (1950-1964; Moreno 1999 via Lilian da Rosa 2017) source
    Secondary summary of Moreno 1999. Holdings were above the 100,000 ha limit that needed Senate approval.
  • verified Share of Mato Grosso under federal control (DL 1.164/1971): about 60%, until 1978 (1971-1978; Moreno 1999 via Lilian da Rosa 2017) source
  • verified CODEMAT public land collected and sold, 1978-90: more than 6 million ha collected; more than 5 million ha sold in the north (1978-1990; Moreno 1999 via Lilian da Rosa 2017) source
    Aripuanã, Juruena, Alta Floresta, Juína and others.
  • verified INTERMAT and INCRA land collected: INTERMAT about 6.4 million ha; INCRA more than 7 million ha collected and about 3.6 million ha titled along federal highways (1978-1990; Moreno 1999 via Lilian da Rosa 2017) source
  • verified COMARCO (Maranhão) public land taken in, Dec 1971: 2.1 million ha (1971; entropia.slg.br article) source
    Side note on the Sarney land law.

1955–1984
e3-02
Cubatão industrial pole (São Paulo)

Cubatão was a state-led industrial pole whose pollution fell on residents. The Vila Socó fire of 1984 killed 93 officially, and perhaps far more. It is a weak fit for the study and kept as a short note.

Government
Military governments (industrial pole from the 1950s)
What happened
A state-led industrial pole (Petrobras refinery 1955, Cosipa steel, petrochemical plants) where pollution costs fell on residents. Weak fit for 'public assets to private': it is a case of private firms pushing environmental cost onto others under a regime with no environmental law and no press freedom. Keep as a short note.
Who got it
Not applicable.
Terms
Not applicable.
Mechanism
No environmental regulation (per the note).
Who paid
Residents. 37 stillbirths of 1,800 births (Oct 1981-Apr 1982) came from a mayor's opinion piece. At Vila Socó a gasoline leak of 700,000 litres from a Petrobras pipeline caused the fire of 24 Feb 1984.
What came after
Vila Socó fire 24 Feb 1984; 'Vale da Morte' label in the early 1980s.
Counter-view
Petrobras's then-president Sigeaki Ueki says the company never admitted 500 dead and 'there is no proof' (Agência Brasil).
Figures
  • disputed Vila Socó fire deaths: 93 (official count); believed up to 508 (MP/commission); residents say 500 or more (1984; Agência Brasil; Toda Matéria) source
    The earlier note's 'one source says 11' is wrong: 11 is the P-36 platform toll (2001), so it was dropped.
  • unverified Stillbirths in Cubatão: 37 stillbirths of 1,800 births, Oct 1981 - Apr 1982 (1981-1982; Mayor of Cubatão (PT), opinion piece) source
    Weak source. A study by R. Monteleone Neto found 10,218 live births and 160 stillbirths for Jun 1982 - Dec 1985, a different period.

Codeara got the largest Sudam tax incentive among 13 listed projects in the Mato Grosso Araguaia. Owners and price are not confirmed. Posseiros bore part of the cost.

Government
Sudam approvals 1961-70; INCRA actions under Figueiredo and Sarney
What happened
One of the largest Sudam-approved farm projects in the Mato Grosso Araguaia, with the largest incentive of 13 listed projects.
Who got it
Owners not confirmed. A snippet says Banco de Crédito Nacional (BCN) created it in 1966 (unverified).

Price and terms not found.

Sudam tax incentives.

What came after
Sudam projects covered more than 2 million ha by 1970. Under Figueiredo INCRA expropriated 34,000 ha of the neighbour Agropasa; in 1989 under Sarney it took two more farms (15,654 ha).

1962–1967
e3-04
Hanna / MBR iron ore and the 1967 Mining Code (Minas Gerais)

In 1962 the Goulart-era government voided Hanna's iron-ore registrations in Minas Gerais. After 1964 the dictatorship changed the rules to let foreign capital in, and Hanna and Caemi formed MBR in 1965. The sources show the new legal framework and the merger, but not the price or how the 1962 order was undone.

Government
Quadros and Goulart (cancellation); Castelo Branco and Costa e Silva (new rules and MBR)
What happened
Iron, manganese and bauxite deposit rights in the Quadrilátero Ferrífero held by Hanna's Novalimense (Águas Claras, Capão do Xavier, Pico do Itabirito and others). A 1962 order by minister Gabriel Passos voided the registrations. Tonnage and hectares are not given in the sources.
Who got it
Caemi (Augusto Antunes) and M. A. Hanna, through MBR, formed in 1965. Who financed them: not found.
Terms
No price or compensation figure found. The terms of the 1967 settlement and who got which deposit are unverified.
Mechanism
On 23 Dec 1964 Castelo Branco signed a decree letting private and foreign capital into subsoil exploration (oil, coal, nuclear minerals and hydraulic reserves excluded). Decreto-Lei 227/1967 (Mining Code, 28 Feb 1967) followed; its full text on who may hold concessions was not confirmed. MBR was the merger solution. No source shows a formal annulment of the 1962 order, so 'restored by the dictatorship' is unconfirmed.
Who paid
The national mineral patrimony. Not quantified.
What came after
Hanna and the Antunes group sued in Aug 1962; the Supreme Court sent the question back to the government, and it was settled under Costa e Silva in 1967. Vale bought out Caemi in 2001-2006 and took 100% of MBR in 2007.
Counter-view
The companies argued the 1938 registrations were lawful and vested, and that the 1962 order was a ministerial despacho, not a decree. US ambassador Lincoln Gordon protested, and Novalimense president Lucas Lopes called the order illegal (niepmarx). ICOMI director Glycon de Paiva argued that more state action would make foreign buyers stop dealing with Brazil (Unesp).
Figures
  • verified Vale buyout of Caemi, 2001-2006 (total): about 3.2 billion (USD) (2001-2006; Wikipedia (Caemi)) source
    16.82% in 2001 for US$278.7 mn; Mitsui stake 2003 for US$426.4 mn; remaining 39.8% in Mar 2006 by share swap, US$2.5 bn.
  • verified Vale takes 100% of MBR, 2007: 231 million for 6.25% of EBM, plus a 30-year lease of 13.75% (US$60.5 mn down plus US$48.1 mn a year) (USD) (2007; Wikipedia (Caemi)) source
  • unverified Hanna share of MBR's operating entity (US Bureau of Mines, 1968): 34% (1968; US Bureau of Mines) source
    Page text did not render. A search snippet says one entity holds 50%, Hanna 34%, State of Minas Gerais the rest; the entity is not named and may be the Caemi holding, not MBR. Do not quote as '34% of MBR'.

1962–2015
e3-05
Fazenda Suiá-Missu and the Xavante of Marãiwatsédé, Mato Grosso

A huge estate in Mato Grosso, helped by Sudam incentives, was sold on to an Italian group and later to Agip. The Xavante were flown out in 1966 and about 80 died in an epidemic. The land was returned in law in 1998 but in practice only from 2015.

Government
Castelo Branco onward; Cardoso (1998 homologation)
What happened
The Suiá-Missu estate, founded by Ariosto da Riva. The Xavante were removed in 1966. Estate area is disputed (see figures).
Who got it
The Ometto family bought the area in 1962. In the 1970s most went to Liquigás (Italian Ursini group), renamed Liquifarm Agropecuária Suiá-Missú. After Ursini failed in 1978, Agip do Brasil (state-owned ENI/Agip Petroli) absorbed Liquigás and Liquifarm in 1979-81. Price paid by Liquigás: not found. Part (250,000 ha) went to the Brazilian Garavelo group in 1989.
Terms
Price not found. Sudam incentives of Cr$7,878,000 went to the Ometto-owned company.
Mechanism
Sudam tax incentives are cited by academic sources (the Pública article does not mention them). The Campo-Território text describes fraud in the 1960 registration; no court finding is cited. The Xavante were flown out by FAB aircraft in 1966.
Who paid
The Xavante: about 300 flown out in 1966; a flu and measles epidemic then killed about 80 (about 30% of the group). The Treasury paid the incentives.
What came after
In 1992 Funai delimited a 200,000 ha Marãiwatsédé land (168,000 ha inside the farm). At Rio-92 Agip/ENI announced the return of about 165,000 ha; this did not happen because the Brazilian subsidiary's shareholders disagreed. Posseiros then invaded. Homologated 1998; Xavante possession only from 2015; about 80% later deforested.
Counter-view
The sources say the 1970s sale chain was private-to-private; the public transfer was the incentive and the title (Campo-Território).

    Sudam 500,000; Ianni 1979 670,000; Sudam table 695,843; about 800,000 after Ariosto da Riva joined the Ometto group; Pública 800,000. Search results also gave 560,000 and 1.7 million (unverified).

    One search result says 250,000 ha; unresolved.

    Described as the most deforested Indigenous land in Brazil.

e3-06
SUDAM fiscal incentives (Operação Amazônia)

SUDAM waived tax for firms investing in the Amazon, mainly ranches and agribusiness. By 1985 it had approved incentives for 959 firms. No total hectare figure for the Amazon was found.

Government
Castelo Branco (SUDAM created 1966) through Figueiredo
What happened
The state waived income tax for firms investing in the Amazon, with up to 100% exemption for varying periods on income or import tax. Firms could invest as shareholders in third-party projects (Art. 17) or via branches (Art. 18).
Who got it
Mostly agribusiness and cattle ventures, many from the South and Southeast (VW, Ometto group, banks).
Terms
By end-1985 SUDAM had approved incentives for 959 firms. Land book value equalled 92% of the projects' own resources, and many firms did not meet job targets.
Mechanism
Tax-credit funds under Decreto-Lei 756/1969 (revoked 2001; the Planalto page was not opened, so this is unconfirmed).
Who paid
The Treasury (waived tax), the forest, peasants and posseiros (possession turned into private property in Conceição do Araguaia), and workers.
What came after
Per the paper, approvals fell by the 1990s and ended in fraud scandals; SUDAM closed in 2001 (not verified).
Counter-view
No defence of the incentives (regional development, security goals) was found in the opened sources.
Figures
  • verified Incentives approved by end-1985: US$ 3.928 milhões as printed (likely US$3.9 billion); 959 firms (USD) (1966-1985; Costa 2012 via Rielo (ABPHE 2023)) source
    Confirmed only as printed in the Rielo paper. The unit is not explained; Costa 2012 itself was not opened.
  • verified Land book value as share of projects' own resources: 92% (1985; Costa 2012 via Rielo) source

    Corrected scope: the original note said 'installed by the regime'. The paper says these are in the Conceição do Araguaia region, not all of the Amazon.

1967–1982 (debt outcome 2000)
e3-08
Jari Project (Daniel K. Ludwig), Pará and Amapá

Ludwig bought a huge Amazon holding in 1967. When the project failed in 1981-82, the government pushed a Brazilian consortium to take over. Accounts differ on who ended up with the debt: Em Tempo says the state, English Wikipedia says the new owners.

Government
Castelo Branco to Figueiredo
What happened
An enormous private landholding in the Jari valley, plus state-backed finance, and in the end the debt. Size sources disagree (see figures).
Who got it
Ludwig bought the firm Empresa de Comércio e Navegação Jari Ltda in 1967. Brazilian law did not limit project area as long as Brazilians own it. In 1981-82 a consortium of 23 Brazilian groups took over; the government pushed businessmen to join as a 'patriotic duty'.
Terms
English Wikipedia: 1.6 million acres (6,475 km2) for US$3 mn (the price is unsourced there). Ludwig invested US$845 mn by 1982.
Mechanism
Ludwig bought privately. For the exit, per Em Tempo (opposition weekly, partisan): he refused a US$20 mn instalment on a US$200 mn foreign debt guaranteed by the BNDE; the government assumed US$180 mn in exchange for shares without voting rights; BNDE lent Antunes US$35 mn to buy Ludwig's MBR and St John del Rey shares and was released from the guarantee.
Who paid
Per Em Tempo, the treasury and BNDE guarantee. English Wikipedia and CSMonitor say Ludwig got no money and lost US$845 mn, and that the debt passed to the new owners. Caboclo and extractivist communities are also named in the notes (not sourced).
What came after
The group later passed through other owners. The 2000 sale to Sergio Amoroso's group was for R$1 with about US$400 mn of debt.
Counter-view
English Wikipedia and CSMonitor say Ludwig received nothing and lost US$845 mn. Em Tempo says he walked away 'without spending a penny' and kept a rice farm (about US$100 mn), a bauxite deposit (about US$600 mn) and securities (about US$480 mn). Resolving this needs BNDES records, not found.

    Confirmed as what Em Tempo printed (partisan source). English Wikipedia says the debt passed to the new owners and does not mention BNDE.

1967–1985
e3-11
Estatização of external debt (Res. 63 to the 1983-84 project deposits)

From the mid-1970s the state took over more and more of Brazil's external debt. After 1982 the Central Bank became the borrower and guarantor through deposit schemes. No source gives the total of private debt absorbed.

Government
Costa e Silva; Geisel; Figueiredo
What happened
External debt concentrated in the public sector. Part of the debt first contracted by private firms was moved to the Central Bank, mainly through foreign-currency deposit schemes.
Who got it
Private borrowers (industrial groups and banks) whose dollar obligations moved to the Central Bank. Total US$ of private debt absorbed in 1979-85: not found in any opened source.
Terms
Not a price. Res. 63 loans grew from about 7% of external debt (1968) to about 20% (1974) and 18.4% of the stock in 1980.
Mechanism
Two different instruments. Resolução 63 (21 Aug 1967) let banks and BNDE borrow abroad and on-lend; it is not a transfer to the state. Circular 230 (1974) and Resolução 432 (23 Jun 1977) allowed registered foreign-currency deposits, moving exchange and interest risk to the Central Bank. In 1983-84 'project deposits' made the Central Bank borrower and guarantor of global debt, private and public.
Who paid
The Central Bank balance sheet, then the Treasury, financed by monetary expansion and domestic debt (IPEA); in the CPI da Dívida reading, taxpayers via the Brady transfer.
What came after
The 1990s Brady operation (about US$50 bn) transferred US$28 bn of Central Bank liabilities to the Treasury.
Counter-view
Meira and Cruz present the rise of public debt mainly as a result of state firms' borrowing for the II PND and of the creditors' cartel and IMF conditions after 1982, not only a rescue of private debtors. Carneiro (2002) calls state firms' borrowing the 'traditional' channel. The Auditoria Cidadã chapter is advocacy and says 'estatização' does not appear in its own text.

    Advocacy body.

    Resolved from 'at least 52.1% of something' in the first note.
  • verified Central Bank as borrower: CGA-1983 and DFA-1983: US$4.4 bn and US$4.3 bn (USD) (1983; Auditoria Cidadã) source
  • verified 1985 and 1986 amortisations deposited at the Central Bank: US$6.8 bn (1985) and US$8.9 bn (1986) (USD) (1985-1986; IPEA, Cavalcanti 1988) source

Federal-highway land strips (DL 1.164/1971) and Transamazônica colonisation

A 1971 decree made a 100 km strip along Amazon highways federal land. Settlement fell far short of the plan (8,000 families against 100,000). The link to private ranches is the author's inference, not shown in the sources.

Government
Médici
What happened
The decree declared the public lands in a 100 km strip on each side of listed federal highways in the Amazon indispensable to security and development, i.e. federal property. The Transamazônica was listed.
Who got it
The note's link to ranches and companies is an inference (cases on SUDAM, VW and Suiá-Missu). No source gives the volume of strip land sold.
Terms
Not applicable. Art. 3 had INCRA recognise legitimate possession; Indigenous rights were reserved.
Mechanism
Decreto-Lei 1.164 of 1 Apr 1971 (terras devolutas in the Legal Amazon). Revoked by DL 2.375 of 24 Nov 1987, which removed the 'indispensable' status except in the border strip. 'Returned to the states' is not verified.
Who paid
Indigenous peoples: a 2013 report says the road affected 29 groups, 11 of them isolated. Settlers: the plan was for about 100,000 families but no more than 8,000 were settled in the three Pará poles (Marabá, Altamira, Itaituba).
What came after
Integrated Colonisation Programs closed in late 1978 after land-title conflicts.

Itaipu: contracts and beneficiaries

Itaipu was financed mostly by public creditors, and its debt cost goes to consumers through the tariff. The sources do not give contract prices or contractor margins, so the private-gain side is undocumented.

Government
Médici (treaty 1973), Geisel, Figueiredo
What happened
The binational dam. Fit with 'public to private' is weak: the sources document cost and debt, not contractor margins.
Who got it
Civil works went to the Brazilian consortium Unicon (five firms) and the Paraguayan Conempa (six), 1975 contract. Unicon members per Itaipu's transparency page (Cetenco, CBPO, Camargo Corrêa, Andrade Gutierrez, Mendes Júnior) are unverified. Financed by Eletrobras (main creditor), BNDES, Banco do Brasil, and originally about 70 financiers with Treasury guarantees.
Terms
Contract prices not found.
Mechanism
Tariff 'pelo passivo': the tariff covers operating costs and debt service, so debt costs go directly to consumers.
Who paid
Brazilian and Paraguayan consumers through the tariff. Utilities' arrears were about US$4 bn in the early 1990s, with a Paraguayan dispute over about US$4 bn of the debt.
What came after
Debt paid off in Feb 2023. The 2009 deal raised Paraguay's compensation by 200% (Brazil's payments from about US$120 mn to US$360 mn a year by 2011).
Counter-view
Itaipu is a working, amortised asset (record 98,630 GWh in 2013, CPDOC). The controversy is the debt's dollar charge and the contractors' margins, which could not be documented.

e3-14
Tucuruí dam and subsidised power for Albras, Alunorte and Alumar

The state built Tucuruí and took over its cost so that aluminium smelters could buy cheap power. The size of the subsidy is only a journalist's estimate (US$2 bn to over US$3 bn). Eletronorte, other electricity consumers and riverside people bore the cost.

Government
Geisel and Figueiredo (setup); Lula (2004 renewal)
What happened
Subsidised electricity from a state dam for Japanese-owned (Albras and Alunorte with CVRD) and Alcoa/Billiton-owned (Alumar) aluminium smelters. More than half of Tucuruí's energy goes to electro-intensive mineral industry; 64.3% of Pará's 2003 generation fed them.
Who got it
Albras and Alunorte (NAAC: 32 private firms 60% plus the Japanese government 40%; CVRD 51% in the original project; agreements 20 Jun 1978) and Alumar. Contractor Camargo Corrêa. Vale sold its Albras stake to Hydro (2011).
Terms
Original price: a 1976 protocol set a price tied to aluminium with a minimum of 8 mills/kWh; the tariff approved in Aug 1979 was 10.5 mills/kWh (blog source, no primary document). By 2004 Albras paid about R$34 (US$11-12) per MWh and Alumar almost double. After 2004 Albras won an auction at the R$53/MWh ceiling; Alumar about R$60/MWh.
Mechanism
A 1976 protocol and a 1979 tariff, with the state taking over the cost of the hydro plant (Pinto: 'o governo federal decidiu assumir completamente o custo da usina', meaning Tucuruí, not the smelter). The state energy monopoly was bent to let the Japanese hold up to a third of Eletronorte shares; they never joined the works.
Who paid
Treasury and Eletronorte, electricity consumers (the difference falls on non-favoured consumers, mainly households), and riverside populations: 1,100 islands formed with 6,500 people on them, and compensation is still litigated.
What came after
Contract renewed 1 May 2004 for 20 years (US$3.4 bn, US$170 mn a year), with profit-sharing when aluminium exceeds US$1,450/t. Eletronorte wanted US$20-22/MWh and Albras offered about US$15.
Counter-view
The design tied price to the aluminium price with a floor and later a profit-share clause, and the contracts anchored demand for a dam Eletronorte could not otherwise sell. Eletrobras filings describe the 2004 price as a floor at Tucuruí's break-even tariff plus an aluminium premium (SEC filing, page not opened, unverified). The government and Eletronorte argument that cheap power was the condition for export earnings was not found in an opened source.

1974–1986
e3-15
Fazenda Vale do Rio Cristalino (Volkswagen), Santana do Araguaia, Pará

Volkswagen ran a 139,000 ha ranch in Pará from 1974 to 1986, backed by SUDAM incentives and cheap loans. Prosecutors say workers were held in forced labour. Courts have ordered R$165 mn in collective damages, and VW denies responsibility and has appealed.

Government
Médici, Geisel and Figueiredo
What happened
A ranch of about 139,000 ha run by VW's subsidiary Companhia Vale do Rio Cristalino, acquired in 1974, with SUDAM tax incentives and low-interest loans.
Who got it
Volkswagen, through its subsidiary. Repórter Brasil and prosecutors say it was acquired 'in a consortium with the military government'; Pública does not say 'consortium' and says it was financed by SUDAM and Banco da Amazônia (Basa). Sold in 1986 to the Matsubara group, which inherited the debts.
Terms
No original SUDAM amount found.
Mechanism
SUDAM incentives and low-interest loans.
Who paid
Workers (forced-labour allegations 1974-86), the Treasury and the forest. About 300 officially employed; clearing was done by informal workers recruited by 'gatos', some under 18. The investigation rests on at least 42 victims and 11 witnesses.
What came after
The labour prosecutor (MPT) filed a civil action in Dec 2024 seeking R$165 mn. The Redenção labour court ordered R$165 mn in collective moral damages, upheld by TRT-8. Four former workers won R$2 mn each in individual suits (12 Jun 2026). The judge rejected the time-bar argument and held VW responsible as the main shareholder. The two outcomes are separate, not conflicting.
Counter-view
Volkswagen denies responsibility for the Pará ranch, does not comment on ongoing proceedings, and has appealed (Repórter Brasil).
Figures
  • verified Ranch size: about 139,000 ha (1974-1986; Pública) source

1975 Brazil-Germany nuclear deal and Nuclebrás

Brazil signed a 1975 nuclear deal with West Germany worth US$4-10 bn on the sources' estimates. Costs ballooned and the programme was scaled back from 1978. Contract prices and Nuclebrás debt were not found.

Government
Geisel (project run by Paulo Nogueira Batista at Nuclebrás)
What happened
Two 1,300 MW reactors by 1985 with an option for six more by 1990; enrichment (jet nozzle), fuel fabrication and pilot reprocessing; up to 20% of Brazilian uranium ore to Germany. Nuclebrás was created Dec 1974; agreement signed in Bonn 27 Jun 1975. Fit with 'public to private' is weak.
Who got it
Kraftwerk Union/Siemens (reactors), German banks (loans) and Nuclep (heavy equipment, created 1975 with Germans). Contract-level terms and prices are unverified.
Terms
Value is a range of US$4-10 bn (see figures).
Mechanism
An intergovernmental agreement and state company Nuclebrás.
Who paid
The Treasury and Eletrobras/Nuclebrás (state financing). Costs 'ballooned with little demonstrable result' (Wilson Center). Nuclebrás' total debt: not found.
What came after
Scaled back from 1978. Angra 2 (planned 1985) operated only in 2000/2001. Angra 3, under construction since 1986, has consumed more than R$20 bn (DW/Forte, 2025). Of eight planned plants, one runs and one is unfinished. The jet-nozzle company was liquidated in 1993. A parliamentary inquiry (CPI) about 1978 is cited but was not opened (unverified).
Counter-view
The aim was energy security after the 1973 oil shock and the US cancelling enriched uranium for Angra 1. It became a parallel autonomous Navy enrichment programme from 1979 (Atlas FGV). Jet-nozzle enrichment was unproven (Wilson Center).

Government
Geisel and Figueiredo
What happened
Subsidised credit to mills and distillery builders, price parity with sugar for ethanol, an obligation on Petrobras to buy all alcohol, and levies on gasoline, diesel and lubricants to cover costs.

Mill and distillery owners (Ferro: 'usineiros inadimplentes' sustained by the public purse). Named beneficiaries and loan-level data: not found.

Petrobras (Conta Álcool), Banco do Brasil and the financial system, and gasoline consumers through the levies (per Ferro and biodieselbr).

Not applicable (public programme).

Coroa-Brastel (1983)

The Central Bank and the Caixa propped up the Coroa-Brastel group before its 1983 collapse. Letter holders lost most, and the Treasury later owed a judgement of about R$400 mn. Ministers were acquitted. The Caixa loan amount was not found.

Government
Figueiredo; ministers Delfim Netto (Planning) and Ernane Galvêas (Finance); Central Bank president Carlos Langoni
What happened
Liquidity support and a Caixa Econômica Federal loan (1981) to Assis Paim Cunha's Coroa/Brastel group. The loan amount was not found. The Central Bank made 'several large liquidity injections'; Paim asked for a Cr$30 bn credit line, which forced an inspection.
Who got it
Paim's financial and brokerage group (Coroa, Brastel, and the Laureano brokerage, linked by DCM to a Golbery family connection; not a finding).
Terms
Not found.
Mechanism
Central Bank assistance lines and a Caixa loan; regulators suspended inspections. On 30 May 1983 Delfim told Langoni that Paim had liquidity problems; the Bank intervened in June 1983 and liquidated the group.
Who paid
Letter holders lost most, since Coroa letters had no public guarantee. Later the Treasury: in March 2014 the STF's 1st panel (3-0) held the Central Bank's rescission action time-barred, leaving a judgement for brokerage PEBB of about R$400 mn to be paid by the Treasury.
What came after
Paim confessed to the fake issues and got 8 years 3 months, appealing free. Delfim and Galvêas were accused of diverting funds via the Caixa loan and acquitted by the STF (pt.wikipedia says charges were filed in 1985).

The DCM author says it cannot be proved that Delfim directly favoured Paim, and found no wrongdoing by Langoni.

Delfin (BNH) debt swap, 1982-83

The BNH accepted two plots of land at Cr$60.8 bn to settle a Delfin debt of about Cr$70 bn. Its own technicians valued the land at about one-sixth of that. Courts later accepted the swap on a 'potential value' basis.

Government
Figueiredo; Minister Mario Andreazza (Interior, in charge of BNH)
What happened
Delfin (Ronald Levinsohn) owed the Banco Nacional da Habitação about Cr$70 bn (about US$250 mn), or Cr$77 bn at intervention. It offered two plots (Barra da Tijuca in Rio and Cotia in São Paulo) at Cr$60.8 bn.
Who got it
The Delfin group, which had about 3.5 million savings depositors. Approved with the backing of Andreazza, with Delfim Netto and Galvêas also involved (a claim of the DCM source).
Terms
BNH technicians valued the plots at about Cr$6.3 bn, roughly one-sixth of the price accepted; a BNH director resigned. Another account has the land at Cr$9.6 bn (unverified).
Mechanism
BNH settled a debt in kind. The swap came out in Folha de S.Paulo on 30 Dec 1982; depositors ran on 3 Jan 1983; the Central Bank intervened and moved accounts to Caixa. O Globo said 'irregular operations diverted Cr$6 bn' of depositors' funds.
Who paid
BNH (a body fed by FGTS) bore the difference between debt and land value. The sources do not say how losses were finally allocated.
What came after
In 1991 Levinsohn agreed to pay the rest in 13 years and, per DCM, no instalment was paid. In March 2006 the STJ accepted payment with the two plots on a 'potential value' basis (some sources say STF, unverified).
Counter-view
The defence's potential-value valuation, which the STJ accepted, treats the land as worth more once built on.

Sulbrasileiro, Comind, Auxiliar and Maisonnave bank failures (1985)

In 1985 the state took over Sulbrasileiro through a new bank, Meridional, which received thousands of land and beach plots. Three other banks were liquidated. No total public cost was found.

Government
Figueiredo to Sarney
What happened
The Central Bank intervened in Sulbrasileiro on 7 Feb 1985. In May 1985 the federal government created Banco Meridional do Brasil and expropriated Sulbrasileiro's shares by decree-law. On 19 Nov 1985 Maisonnave, Comind and Auxiliar were liquidated the same day by decree-law.
Who got it
Banco Meridional received about 15,000 items: 5,000 beach plots on ten beaches and 80,000-90,000 ha of rural property. The Maisonnave group got US$20 mn from the Central Bank in a rediscount line.
Terms
Not applicable.
Mechanism
Decree-law expropriation of shares (the decree-law number 7315/1985 printed in English Wikipedia looks odd, unverified). Liquidation by decree-law is presented as the only time Sarney used one to revoke bank charters.
Who paid
For Sulbrasileiro, taxpayers through a federally created successor (one headline says shareholders would not be compensated; unclear). For the three Nov 1985 banks, creditors and clients; the sources give no Treasury cost.
What came after
A Maisonnave debt of R$406 mn was still on the books in a CMN record of 27 Nov 1997. No verified total public cost for 1983-85 bank rescues was found.
Counter-view
The Meridional solution was pushed by Rio Grande do Sul politicians, a political rescue of a regional bank rather than of owners. Comind, Auxiliar and Maisonnave were liquidated rather than rescued, so this is less a transfer than a failed rescue.

1985–1990
e3-26
Calha Norte (1985)

Calha Norte was a secret military plan for the northern border strip, handed to the first civilian government. The sources do not show any land or mining right given to a named company. It is a thin case.

Government
Sarney (the first civilian government; the plan was prepared by the dictatorship's National Security Council)
What happened
A military and settlement programme on a 160 km strip along the northern borders, 6,500 km long, 1.2 million km2 (about a quarter of the Legal Amazon), 1.6 million people. Thin case: no source shows a concession of land or mining rights to a named company.
Who got it
No named beneficiary. The authors of the source say the strip holds large gold, diamond and manganese deposits and that a government survey says 40% of the region is exploited by foreign companies; this is their interpretation.
Terms
Planned budget 10,787,165 OTNs through 1990; the total spent was unknown at the time.
Mechanism
Drafted in secret in military offices, coordinated by Gen. Rubens Bayama Denys, head of the Casa Militar.
Who paid
Cimi said the plan would affect 50,000 Indigenous people of 33 nations.
What came after
A Brasil de Fato piece says the budget jumped from R$1.2 mn to R$24 mn the following year (snippet, unverified).
Counter-view
The programme's stated aims were border protection, settlement, bilateral policy and Indigenous policy (pt.wikipedia, snippet, unverified).

    Snippet only.

1985–2002: Privatization (32 entries)

The National Privatization Programme, state-bank rescues and the big federal and state sales.

YearsCase (click to open)SignsFigures
1985–1989
e4-01
Sarney-era reprivatizations (BNDESPar, Mafersa, Radiobras)

In the late 1980s BNDESPar sold off firms it had taken over for debts. BNDES counts 13 firms (1987-89) in one paper and 38 in the decade, for about US$780 million. Buyers and per-firm prices are mostly unknown.

Government
Sarney (programme began under Figueiredo)
What happened
Under a Nov 1985 decree (Decreto 91.991), BNDESPar re-sold firms it had taken over for debts. BNDESPar counts 13 companies from June 1987 to Dec 1989. BNDES's own history counts 38 firms in the 1980s. The list of the 38 was not obtained. Radiobras stations were also transferred or closed from 1988.
Who got it
Buyers and prices per firm were not found. Mafersa (rail equipment) was sold on 11 Nov 1991 to Refer. Refer sold 65% of it for R$1,000 in 1995. How Refer was financed was not found.
Terms
Mafersa sold at Cr$143.50 per share against a minimum of Cr$54.95 (161% above). No overall valuation of the 1980s sales was found.
Mechanism
Decreto 91.991/1985, then Decreto 95.886 of 29 Mar 1988 (Programa Federal de Desestatizacao). The 1988 decree revoked Decretos 91.991/1985 and 93.606/1986. Lei 8.031/1990 replaced it. The 1988 decree is known only from a search summary.
Who paid
Most of the liabilities moved to buyers were BNDES credits, so the bank kept the exposure.
What came after
Mafersa ended in bankruptcy. In broadcasting, 23 of 37 Radiobras stations were transferred or closed, and 1,028 radio and TV licences were granted in the period.
Counter-view
BNDES describes these sales as an orderly sale of firms acquired through rescue (BNDESPar paper). The 1988 decree gave two aims: shift activity to the private sector and cut the public deficit. The older note claim that the aim was 'not to raise money' is not supported by the decree summary.
Figures

    Researcher opened source; not re-checked.
  • unverified Liabilities moved with those 13 firms (mostly BNDES credits): 500 USD million (1989; BNDES (BNDESPar paper)) source
    'Almost US$500 million'. Researcher opened source; not re-checked.
  • verified 1980s sales, 38 firms: 780 USD million (1989; BNDES) source
    Fact-check confirmed '38 empresas reprivatizadas ... cerca de US$ 780 milhoes'. The gap between 13 and 38 firms is scope (BNDESPar 1987-89 vs whole decade); the 38-firm list was not obtained.
  • unverified Mafersa face value: 48.4 USD million (1991; Capital Aberto) source
    Researcher opened source; not re-checked.
  • unverified Mafersa premium over minimum price: 161 percent (1991; Capital Aberto) source
    Cr$143.50 vs Cr$54.95 per share. Researcher opened source; not re-checked.

1990–1997
e4-02
National Privatization Programme (Lei 8.031/1990) and the 'moedas podres'

The 1990 programme let buyers pay with old federal debt securities at face value. Cash was a small part of early deals (about 3% in Siderbras). Cash grew to about 75% of payments by 1996.

Government
Collor; expanded under Itamar Franco and Cardoso (Lei 9.491/1997)
What happened
Legal framework for selling or conceding federal firms, run by BNDES. Bidders could pay with 'moedas de privatizacao': federal debt securities accepted at face value in auctions.
Who got it
Bidders in the federal sales. Biondi (critical) says BNDES itself sold the 'moedas' to bidders, up to 12 years to pay, at privileged interest. IPEA also records BNDES selling securitized credits over 12 years at full monetary correction plus 6% a year.
Terms
IPEA to mid-1993: about US$17 bn was expected; US$5.36 bn was raised at face value. Average premium (agio) 13.7%. Paid in: privatization certificates 24.2%; securitized Union debt 29.6% (83.4% of that was overdue Siderbras debts); Siderbras debentures 17.5%; FND 11.5%; TDA 8.3%; CEF letters 5.3%. Siderbras sales brought US$6.33 bn in 1991-93 against US$7 bn expected, 65% from steel; cash was about 3% of the Siderbras sales.
Mechanism
Lei 8.031 (April 1990, 12 Apr by URL pattern, not opened); Lei 9.491 (9 Sep 1997 per a search result) set up the Conselho Nacional de Desestatizacao.
Who paid
The Treasury (discount on securities) and BNDES (credit to buyers). Steel workers paid in jobs (see the Siderbras case).
What came after
Cash grew over time: BCB 1996 shows cash rising from 36.4% of payments earlier to about 75% in 1996. BNDES says 'moedas' were heavily used in 1990-92, with more cash per deal in 1993-94 but 'not less important'. Sector agencies came later: Anatel was created by Lei 9.472 of 16 Jul 1997. ANEEL, ANP, ANTT and ANTAQ dates were not checked.
Counter-view
BNDES presents 'moedas' as part of fiscal adjustment, cutting federal debt. The BCB 1996 report shows cash rising to about 75% of payments. Biondi's own table lists 'moedas' per company (Cosipa 99.6%, CSN 96%, Usiminas and others 100%), which conflicts with Garcia/Schmidt's Usiminas cash share of 2.6%. One search result says the 'moedas' traded at under half of face value; another says they were taken at face value (unreconciled).
Figures

    Expected about US$17 bn. IPEA economic tally of 5,357.5 + 3,613.6 + 172.1 + 680.5 = 9,823.7 US$ million; labels of the middle terms were not confirmed.
  • unverified Average agio to mid-1993: 13.7 percent (1993; IPEA) source
    23.1% in 1992, 14.1% in 1991, 0 in 1993.
  • unverified Securitized debts outstanding mid-1993: 46000 USD million (1993; IPEA) source
    About US$46 bn.
  • verified Siderbras sales 1991-93 (65% steel): 6330 USD million (1993; Garcia (Unicamp)) source
    Expected about US$7 bn. Fact-check confirmed p.111-112.
  • verified Cash share of Siderbras sales: 3 percent (1992; Passanezzi Filho 1992, cited by Garcia) source
    Confirmed: 'algo em torno de 3%'.

    About 45% of sale value; BNDES loan column 'nd'. No independent BNDES/TCU document confirms the 12-year financing of the 'moedas' themselves.

    Up from 36.4% earlier. Fact-check opened the BCB report.

1990–2002
e4-03
PND totals: proceeds against debts transferred

Official totals show tens of billions of dollars raised and billions of debt moved to buyers. Totals differ by source, currency and scope, so ranges are shown. The net cost to the public is not computed in any source.

Government
Collor, Itamar Franco, Cardoso
What happened
Overall tally of the federal and state sales: money raised and debt that moved to the buyers. Sources disagree on currency and scope.
Who got it
Not applicable (aggregate).
Terms
BNDES federal PND 1990-2015: 99 operations, sale revenue US$54.5 bn, debt transferred US$9.2 bn (excludes hydro concessions and transmission lines). FIPE by period: Collor 1990-92 US$4.0 bn plus US$1.3 bn debt; Itamar US$4.6 bn plus US$1.9 bn; Cardoso 1995-2002 US$78.9 bn plus US$14.9 bn (federal US$51.0 bn, debt US$8.1 bn; state US$27.9 bn, debt US$6.8 bn). Wikipedia lists R$78.6 bn for the Cardoso years; the currency mismatch with FIPE is unresolved.
Mechanism
PND auctions under Lei 8.031/1990 and Lei 9.491/1997.
Who paid
The net fiscal effect depends on the value of securities accepted at face value and on state debts. No opened source nets it. Castelar estimates state distributors cost the Treasury up to US$26 bn (Congresso em Foco).
What came after
Public debt grew over the period (see figures). A claim of a 'US$85 bn PND total' was not found.
Counter-view
Officially, proceeds plus debt relief count as a gain. BCB 1996: 1996 sales were about US$4.1 bn, about 30% of all proceeds since the programme began. A Camara presentation says privatizations cut the rise of net debt by 3.4 points of GDP in 1996-98. Critics point to the paper used as currency and the BNDES credit.

1991
e4-04
Usiminas (24 Oct 1991)

Usiminas was the first PND sale, in October 1991. Sources disagree on the price (US$1.2 bn or US$1.49 bn). Very little was paid in cash, according to Garcia.

Government
Collor
What happened
Control of the Siderbras steel mill at Ipatinga (MG). First sale under the PND. A consortium bought 51% control.
Who got it
A consortium including Bozano Simonsen, steel distributors, employees and Nippon Usiminas (Japanese mills). Employees hold about 10% of capital (search summary). Biondi's table lists Usiminas as 100% paid in 'moedas'.
Terms
Price is disputed: US$1.49 bn (Garcia, citing Schmidt 1998) against US$1.2 bn, 14% over the minimum (Christian Science Monitor, 1991). Garcia says only US$39 million (2.6%) was cash.
Mechanism
PND auction under Lei 8.031/1990, financed with BNDES loans plus 'moedas' (see the PND case).
Who paid
The Treasury, through BNDES loans and discounted securities; workers through job cuts (13,838 in 1989 to 8,448 in 2000, minus 39%).
What came after
Usiminas control later moved among Nippon, Votorantim and Ternium (not detailed here). Garcia argues many job cuts came from financial policy and pre-sale restructuring, not only technology.
Counter-view
The sale was 14% over the minimum price (CSM). Garcia notes Usiminas was already lean under state management, so the 'inefficient state firm' claim does not fit it. The two critical sources disagree on the cash share (Garcia 2.6%, Biondi 100% in 'moedas').
Figures
  • disputed Usiminas price (Garcia/Schmidt): 1490 USD million (1991; Schmidt 1998, cited by Garcia) source
    Contemporaneous CSM says US$1.2 bn, 14% over minimum. No third source. Show both; do not state a single price.
  • disputed Usiminas price (CSM): 1200 USD million (1991; Christian Science Monitor, 29 Oct 1991) source
    14% above the minimum price. The 27 Sep 1991 CSM article cited earlier reported the auction CALLED OFF (minimum about US$1.5 bn nominal for 75% of voting shares), so it is not a source for the sale.
  • verified Cash paid: 39 USD million (1991; Schmidt 1998, cited by Garcia) source
    About 2.6%. Confirmed as cited in Garcia.
  • verified Jobs 1989 to 2000: 8448 jobs (2000; Garcia (Table 2)) source
    From 13,838 in 1989 (minus 39%).

1991–1997
e4-05
Siderbras steel: Cosipa, Acesita, CSN (1993), Acominas

The Siderbras steel mills were sold in 1991-93, mostly in federal debt securities and BNDES credit. Critics say the sale price was below the mills' own capital by US$2.7 bn or more. Steel jobs fell about 62% from 1989 to 2000.

Government
Collor (Acesita 1992); Itamar Franco (CSN, Cosipa 1993)
What happened
Sale of the state steel group Siderbras. CSN: 60.1% control block auctioned 2 Apr 1993 at the Rio exchange (another source says 91% of CSN shares were sold across auctions). BNDES total for 8 steel firms: US$5.56 bn revenue plus US$2.63 bn debt transferred. Acominas: sold 1993; Gerdau took control by 2002.
Who got it
CSN: Grupo Vicunha (Steinbruch), Bamerindus, Docenave (then a Vale subsidiary), plus pension funds such as Previ (search summary). Acominas 1993 consortium: CEA 20%, Mendes Junior, Econômico, BCN, BEMGE/Credireal, CVRD, Aços Villares. Gerdau entered with NatSteel in 1997, held a minority in 1997, about 37% in 1999 and 87% in 2002.
Terms
CSN was sold for about US$1.05 bn. Biondi (critical) says R$1.01 bn of it was paid in 'moedas' and only R$38 million (3.6%) in cash; BNDES sold the 'moedas' over up to 12 years. Garcia says cash was about 3% of all Siderbras sales. Garcia: the sum of own capital of the state steelmakers exceeded their sale value by more than US$2.7 bn, and building mills of CSN's size would cost over US$10 bn against US$5.56 bn BNDES revenue for all steel firms. The Acominas price was not found. For comparison, Piratini (1992) sold at US$105 million against a US$42 million minimum.
Mechanism
PND auctions with 'moedas' and BNDES loans; debts moved to the Treasury before sale (Garcia: CSN and Cosipa cuts came from 'saneamento previo').
Who paid
Treasury through discounted securities and BNDES credit; workers: CSN jobs 23,208 (1989) to 9,302 (2000), minus 59.9%; Cosipa 21,505 to 5,769, minus 73.1%; whole steel sector 134,046 to 50,365, minus 62.4% (flat-steel plants minus 59.8%).
What came after
Original Acominas partners were replaced by Gerdau. CSN later became a buyer in Vale and Light (see those cases). Biondi says CSN also received a R$1.1 bn BNDES expansion loan.
Counter-view
Seller's case: debt relief and an end to subsidies. CSN's minimum price was set from a Bradesco/Merrill Lynch valuation (search summary). No defence primary document was opened.

    Corrected scope: 'more than US$2.7 bn' is the SUM for the state steelmakers, not Usiminas alone.

    'Acima de dez bilhoes' against US$5.56 bn BNDES revenue.

1991–2003
e4-06
BNDES loans to privatization buyers

BNDES lent to the buyers it was selling to. The TCU found the 50%-of-minimum-price limit and an asset-exposure limit were exceeded. When buyers such as AES defaulted, BNDES took shares and renegotiated.

Government
Collor to Cardoso; audit in Lula's first year
What happened
BNDES was seller, adviser and lender in the sales. It financed bidders, mainly in electricity. The TCU audit found limits broken. A single all-sector total of buyer financing was not found.
Who got it
Electricity buyers. AES owed BNDES US$1.2 bn. 12 distributors were financed by BNDES; 8 had not settled their debts by 2003. Early phase: BNDES sold securitized credits over 12 years at full monetary correction plus 6% a year (IPEA).
Terms
Distributors yielded R$27 bn in sales but consumed R$22 bn of BNDES money; 14 of 22 firms got R$7 bn (TCU audit as reported). 20 distributors and 4 generators were sold for US$30 bn in 1995-2003.
Mechanism
Rules: financing up to 50% of the minimum price and an exposure limit of 30% of total assets. The audit reports both were exceeded.
Who paid
Taxpayers through the Treasury that funds BNDES. BNDES net worth fell from R$13 bn to R$10 bn between 2002 and mid-2003, but the cause is not isolated to these loans.
What came after
The 2003 AES deal gave BNDES 50% minus one share of Brasiliana and cut the debt to US$510 million. A R$3 bn capitalization line found no taker. TCU also audited the matter in a journal discussion.
Counter-view
Defenders argue the credit was the only way to make buyers appear in a thin domestic market; no opened source states this explicitly. The Congresso em Foco piece frames BNDES lending as a policy choice to attract capital: BNDES allocated R$22 bn to the sector since 1995, R$7 bn of it for privatization financing.
Figures
  • unverified BNDES money used by electricity distributors: 22000 BRL million (2003; TCU audit, via Congresso em Foco) source
    Against R$27 bn raised in the sales.
  • unverified BNDES financing to 14 of 22 firms: 7000 BRL million (2003; TCU audit, via Congresso em Foco) source
  • unverified AES debt to BNDES before 2003 deal: 1200 USD million (2003; Congresso em Foco) source
    Check 1 notes the loan was US$1.2 bn with US$400 million guarantee; JB 2007 says US$1.3 bn. Debt cut to US$510 million.
  • verified Electricity sales 1995-2003 (20 distributors, 4 generators): 30000 USD million (2003; Congresso em Foco) source
    Fact-check confirmed in Congresso em Foco; distribution 1995-2002 about US$16.4 bn, generation US$1.86 bn per Eixos citing BNDES.
  • verified Post-sale BNDES credit lines, 8 projects (Dec 1998): 864.6 BRL million (1998; BNDES Informe v.11 n.123) source
    Opened by researcher. Includes CPFL 187.5, Escelsa 131, Cemat 133.3, Celpa 110, Energipe 22.45 (R$ million).
  • unverified BNDES net worth fall 2002 to mid-2003: 3000 BRL million (2003; Congresso em Foco) source
    R$13 bn to R$10 bn; cause not isolated to privatization loans.

1992–2002
e4-07
Petrochemical and fertiliser firms (pole by pole)

Petrochemical firms were sold pole by pole in 1992-96, with Petroquisa often staying as a minority partner. Buyer financing and fair-value checks are not documented. Copene ended with Odebrecht in 2001-02.

Government
Collor, Itamar Franco, Cardoso (BNDES as manager)
What happened
27 petrochemical operations (Copesul, Politeno, Oxiteno, PQU, Copene and others) and 5 fertiliser firms. Sales were pole by pole. Petroquisa (Petrobras) kept minority stakes and sold some later. Copene control moved in 2001-02 and became Braskem.
Who got it
Copesul (15 May 1992): a group including Ipiranga 17.81%, OPP 9.91%, OPP Polietilenos 9.91%; Petroquisa kept 14.99%. Petroquisa kept 17.48% of PQU. Copene: the private group already held control; a 1995 Petroquisa share auction left Norquisa with full control. Odebrecht and Mariani bought control in July 2001; Braskem was approved 16 Aug 2002. BNDES financing of buyers was not found. Biondi's table lists petrochemicals as 100% paid in 'moedas'.
Terms
BNDES: 27 operations, US$2.70 bn plus US$1.00 bn debt transferred; fertilisers US$418 million plus US$75 million. BNDES 50 anos: 27 companies, US$3.7 bn including about US$1 bn of debt. Press expected US$1-1.5 bn before the Dec 2000 Copene auction. Odebrecht bought Conepar for BRL 785 million (Encyclopedia.com). No independent valuation was found.
Mechanism
PND auctions under Lei 8.031/1990 and, from 1997, Lei 9.491/1997.
Who paid
Not quantified in any opened source. Buyers who used BNDES credit for Petroflex lost about 27% in real terms (IPEA), which is a buyer loss, not a public one.
What came after
Braskem became the Odebrecht-led consolidator. A search did not support a 'Copene sold in 1996' event; only the 1995 share auction and the 2001 control sale appear.
Counter-view
BNDES presents the sales as restructuring that kept Petroquisa as a minority partner (BNDES 50 anos).

1994–2019
e4-09
Embraer (7 Dec 1994)

Embraer was sold in December 1994 to a group of a bank, two pension funds and others, with a Union veto share. Sources differ on the price (US$171-182 million). It later became an exporter, which defenders cite as success.

Government
Itamar Franco (sale); Cardoso (restructuring)
What happened
Control of the state aircraft maker: 55.4% of voting shares. The sale rules created a golden share held only by the Union (veto on name change, military programmes, parts supply, transfer of control). It was never used, not even in the 2018-19 Boeing deal, which government approved.
Who got it
A Bozano Simonsen-led group with pension funds Previ and Sistel. Voting shares after the sale: Previ 24%, Bozano 20%, Sistel 20%, 'Grupo Europeu' 20%, Union 1%. BNDESPar held 13.9% of total capital (DIEESE, Moraes 2013). Bozano Simonsen tried to exit by 1999. Biondi lists Embraer as 100% paid in 'moedas'; DIEESE says US$130 million of the price was paid in 'moedas'.
Terms
Bid R$154 million after six postponements; Aviation Week says US$182.4 million; Flightglobal says about US$171 million. R$154 million at about R$0.85 per US$ is about US$182 million, so no real conflict between the first two.
Mechanism
Auction under the PND (edital PND-A-05/94) with a golden share.
Who paid
Workers: 1,700 of 5,550 jobs cut in 1995 (Flightglobal). The public side: buyers used discounted public paper (DIEESE).
What came after
Embraer listed on the NYSE in 2000-01, raising US$544 million; free float rose from 18.6% to 59.0%. BNDES financing to Embraer was R$8.2 bn in 2010-16 (DIEESE).
Counter-view
Embraer later became a global exporter. This is the usual defence of the sale and is not sourced from an opened page.
Figures

    Fact-check opened. Flightglobal (snippet) gives about US$171 million; range US$171-182.4 million.

    Bozano Simonsen, Previ and Sistel; auction postponed six times.
  • disputed Price per Flightglobal: 171 USD million (1994; Flightglobal) source
    Range US$171-182.4 million across sources.
  • unverified Part of price paid in 'moedas': 130 USD million (1994; DIEESE) source
    Biondi's table says 100% 'moedas'; the two critical sources differ.
  • corrected Stakes quoted by earlier note (Previ 12.2%, Sistel 5%, Bozano 9.9%, BNDESPar 13.9%): 13.9 percent of total capital (2013; DIEESE citing Moraes 2013) source
    These are shares of TOTAL capital after privatization, not the auction result. Capital is 34% ordinary, 66% preferred.
  • unverified Jobs cut 1995: 1700 jobs (1995; Flightglobal) source
    Of 5,550.
  • unverified BNDES financing 2010-16: 8200 BRL million (2016; DIEESE) source
    Outside the sale; shows continued BNDES support.
  • unverified Golden share size: 0.3 percent of capital (1994; Earlier note) source

Escelsa (11 Jul 1995)

Escelsa was the first federal distributor sold under Cardoso, in July 1995. Banks and pension-fund foundations bought it. Only the headline price is known, from one source.

Government
Cardoso (first federal electricity distributor sale)
What happened
Control of the Espirito Santo distributor, the first federal electricity sale of Cardoso's term. Already in the PND since Decreto 572 of 22 Jun 1992.
Who got it
Iven S.A. (banks Opportunity, Pactual, Nacional, Icatu, Citibank, Bozano Simonsen) and GTD (11 pension-fund foundations). After the sale: Iven 45.1%, GTD 25%, Eletrobras 14.7%, employees 7.7%. The name 'Parcel consortium' was not found in the BNDES paper. BNDES lent R$131 million after the sale (Dec 1998 Informe); a figure of R$225.5 million was also seen but not confirmed.
Terms
R$357.92 million (Wikipedia citing Folha; no second source). Agio and fairness: not found.
Mechanism
PND auction under Lei 8.031/1990. Concession laws: Lei 8.987 (13 Feb 1995) and Lei 9.074 (7 Jul 1995). EC 6/1995 was not opened.
Who paid
Not documented. Later effects fall under the BNDES-financing and tariff-recomposition cases.
What came after
Not documented.
Counter-view
The BNDES regulatory paper says bidder interest did not reflect earlier expected demand; its focus is that indemnity rules acted as a risk shield for buyers. No price-fairness dispute found.

e4-11
First federal highway concessions

The first federal toll roads were granted in 1995-97 to the lowest toll bidder, with no payment to the state. Real tolls rose 36-55% above inflation on the five roads by 2005-06. IPEA ties the rises to contract balance rules.

Government
Itamar Franco (preparation); Cardoso
What happened
Federal toll-road concessions from 1995. The first stage covered 858.6 km (Dutra BR-116 Rio-SP 402 km; Ponte Rio-Niteroi 13.2 km). IPEA lists five works to 1997: Rio-Niteroi 13.2 km, Juiz de Fora-Rio 179.7, Rio-SP 406.8, Rio-Teresopolis-Alem Paraiba 144.4, Osorio-Porto Alegre 112.3. The Osorio contract is dated 4 Mar 1997, so not all of the first stage is 1995.
Who got it
Concessionaires won by offering the lowest toll. Names were not collected.
Terms
Lowest-toll bid with no payment (outorga) to the government. BNDES: highways revenue US$0, 21 operations.
Mechanism
Lei 8.987/1995 and Lei 9.074/1995. Initial regulator DNER (extinct 2001); ANTT from 2001.
Who paid
Road users, through real toll rises. IPEA explains the rises as coming from contract rules that guarantee economic-financial balance, not from abuse.
What came after
Tolls rose faster than inflation on all five roads (see figures). The concessionaires' side (ABCR) was not opened.
Counter-view
IPEA's own study is critical of the model but neutral in tone; rises came from the contract-balance rules.

End of the Petrobras monopoly (EC 9/1995, Lei 9.478/1997, ANP rounds)

A 1995 constitutional amendment and a 1997 law opened oil exploration to private firms and created the regulator ANP. The first bidding rounds raised about R$790 million in signature bonuses. Petrobras itself stayed state-controlled.

Government
Cardoso
What happened
EC 9 of 9 Nov 1995 let the Union contract private firms to explore and produce oil. Lei 9.478 of 6 Aug 1997 created ANP and CNPE and set the concession model. The in-situ resource stays the Union's; the contractee gets ownership of the oil produced. EC 9 ended Petrobras's exclusivity, not the Union monopoly in law (a doctrinal dispute; ADI 3273 challenged parts of Lei 9.478).
Who got it
Round 1 (1999): 11 winning firms including Petrobras (one source: only one Brazilian winner among 38 qualified firms).
Terms
Round 1 (23 Sep 1999) signature bonuses R$321.7 million; round 2 (7 Jun 2000) R$468.3 million. R$789.9 million over two years (321.7 + 468.3 = 790.0).
Mechanism
Constitutional amendment plus the Lei do Petroleo; auctions by ANP.
Who paid
Not assessed in the files.
What came after
Not assessed. Royalties, 'round zero' and pre-salt consequences are gaps.

1995–2019
e4-13
PROER: credit for buyers of failing private banks

Proer lent about R$20.4 bn (R$31.7 bn with reserve overdrafts) so that other banks would take over failing ones. Taxpayers took losses: about R$28 bn is still owed by two failed banks. The government says it avoided a bank run.

Government
Cardoso (MP 1.179/1995, Nov 1995)
What happened
Central Bank credit line to buyers of failing private banks (Nacional, Economico, Bamerindus, others). Proer credits at historical prices were R$20,359 million. R$5,038 million of that went to Caixa to buy the mortgage books of Economico, Bamerindus and Banorte. With unsecured overdrafts on bank reserves at the liquidation dates, the total was R$31.7 bn.
Who got it
Bamerindus went to HSBC (later Bradesco). Nacional's assets went to Unibanco while its liabilities stayed with the Central Bank. Economico's assets went to Excel, then BBV, then Bradesco (2003).
Terms
Per bank at historical values (CPI do Proer): Nacional R$5,898 million, Economico R$5,226 million, Bamerindus R$2,945.5 million, Mercantil R$530 million, Banorte R$476 million, Pontual R$125 million, Crefisul R$120 million.
Mechanism
MP 1.179/1995 and Central Bank credit lines.
Who paid
Taxpayers. The Central Bank booked provisions of R$6.06 bn (1998) and R$9.49 bn (1999) for credits on liquidated banks. Its 1999 loss of R$13 bn was covered by the Treasury in Jan 2001 with federal bonds. Outstanding balances today: Nacional R$20.659 bn, Economico R$7.35 bn (after R$12.732 bn was amortised in 2013), Crefisul R$26 million; total about R$28 bn (BC reply 2019). Bamerindus has none outstanding.
What came after
A CPI do Proer was held in the Chamber. Gazeta do Povo counts the R$28 bn outstanding as part of at least R$71 bn passed on.
Counter-view
The Central Bank and Cardoso's government argued Proer avoided a systemic bank run, and that the money came from compulsory deposits, not the budget ('sem dotacao orcamentaria'). The same CPI chapter concedes the 1999 Central Bank loss was covered by the Treasury.
Figures
  • verified Proer credit lines released (historical): 20359 BRL million (1997; CPI do Proer) source
    R$20,359,046 thousand. Fact-check read the CPI report.
  • verified Proer plus unsecured reserve overdrafts: 31700 BRL million (1997; CPI do Proer) source
    Proer 20.36 + reserves 11.38 bn. May be the origin of the 'about R$30 bn' figure attributed to Cardoso, which could not be confirmed.
  • unverified Cost as share of GDP (Maia 2003): 2.7 percent of GDP (1997; Maia 2003, via PUC paper) source
    Average GDP 1995-97. The PUC PDF returned 403 in the fact-check. Cardoso's own '~2.5% of GDP' is also unconfirmed.
  • corrected Nacional, Proer credit: 5898 BRL million (1997; CPI do Proer) source
    Earlier note had R$5.8 bn from a Congresso em Foco item that actually reports outstanding balances.
  • corrected Economico, Proer credit: 5226 BRL million (1997; CPI do Proer) source
    Earlier note had R$5.2 bn (misattributed source).
  • corrected Bamerindus, Proer credit: 2945.5 BRL million (1997; CPI do Proer) source
    Earlier note had R$3.2 bn. R$2.5 bn at 31 Mar 1997 plus R$445.5 million.
  • verified Caixa, mortgage books of Economico, Bamerindus, Banorte: 5038 BRL million (1997; CPI do Proer) source

  • verified Still owed: Nacional: 20659 BRL million (2019; Central Bank reply, via Congresso em Foco) source

Light (21 May 1996)

Light was sold in May 1996 for about US$2.3 bn to foreign utilities and CSN, with BNDESPar and Eletrobras keeping stakes. The company was split first, freeing it of a US$1.24 bn debt. Price sources vary between US$1.7 bn and US$2.4 bn.

Government
Cardoso
What happened
Control of the Rio de Janeiro distributor. In Jan 1996 the company was split (LightRio vs LightPar for Sao Paulo), which freed it from a US$1.24 bn debt owed by Eletropaulo (Wikipedia only).
Who got it
EDF, Houston Industries and AES (about 11.4% each), CSN 7.3%, BNDESPar 9.1%, Eletrobras about 29-30%, employees 10% (offer not yet completed). In 2000 BNDESPar sold 9.23% to EDF for R$506.3 million; in 2001 CSN sold its stake to EDF and AES for US$362 million (Wikipedia citing Folha). After the 1998 blackout, BNDES lent Light R$730 million (Biondi).
Terms
About US$2.3 bn (BCB 1996: Light was 57.4% of the year's US$4.1 bn proceeds; US$2.4 bn with later employee offers). Wikipedia/Folha: US$2.26 bn. Congresso em Foco: 'over US$2 bn'. English Wikipedia on Light says US$1.7 bn (outlier, unsourced).
Mechanism
PND auction; Lei 8.987/1995 and Lei 9.074/1995 (concessions).
Who paid
The debt split moved the Eletropaulo debt off the company; tariff history after sale was not researched.
What came after
Not researched beyond the stake changes.
Counter-view
The BNDES paper says the minimum price for 100% of Light exceeded the book indemnity value, meaning buyers worried about political risk. USP case notes say investors criticised the minimum price as too high. A Senate speech of 16 May 1996 says the government cut the final price by accepting 30% in 'moedas' (opposition claim; snippet).

e4-15
Railways: RFFSA concessions and FEPASA

The railways were leased for 30 years in 1996-98. The numbers often quoted are minimum prices set by the state, not final prices. The TCU noted that Centro-Leste bidders agreed on a single consortium, so no one bid above the minimum.

Government
Itamar Franco (RFFSA on PND from 1992); Cardoso (sales 1996-98)
What happened
30-year leases of the RFFSA networks (split into Sul, Oeste, Leste/Centro-Leste, Nordeste, Sudeste plus Tereza Cristina) and the Paulista (FEPASA) network. RFFSA debt in 1994 was R$3 bn plus R$1 bn of labour liabilities. BNDES counts 7 rail operations.
Who got it
Centro-Leste: a Vale-led consortium; Sudeste: MRS. Pension funds Previ and Funcef appear in the Ferroban (FEPASA) owner group; CSN/CVRD appear in FCA/CFN/MRS. A TCU minister's note says bidders for Centro-Leste agreed beforehand to form a single consortium, which prevented bids above the minimum.
Terms
The figures quoted in the earlier notes are the TCU's minimum prices, not necessarily the winning bids. These are leases, so 'price' means an up-front payment plus instalments.
Mechanism
PND concessions (leases) under Lei 8.987/1995 and Lei 9.074/1995.
Who paid
Not researched. Concession payment terms and TCU audits are gaps.
What came after
Passenger service was almost all dropped; CPTM took over Sao Paulo urban passenger (Wikipedia only, not checked).
Counter-view
The BNDES paper argues a minimum concession value tied to expected cash flow was the best way to revive a sector whose losses the state had to cover.
