PROES and the sale of state banks

The Union issued R$61.4 bn of bonds to clean state banks before they were sold for about R$11.4 bn in total. The central bank says the states were legally bound to cover the losses and the banks were already insolvent. Critics see taxpayers paying for the clean-up.

Government
Cardoso (MP 1.514/1996; Lei 9.496/1997)
What happened
The Union took over state banks' debts and turned them into state debts to the Union over 30 years. It issued R$61.448 bn of bonds to sanitize state banks: SP R$36.1265 bn (23/24 Dec 1997), PR R$5.19763 bn, MG R$4.69719 bn, RJ R$3.87968 bn, RS R$2.55615 bn, BA R$1.711 bn, PE R$1.2444 bn, CE R$984.72 million. By 2002: 10 state banks privatised, 10 extinguished, 16 turned into development agencies, 5 stayed state-owned (counts from the ANPUH paper, not BNDES). State banks' share of financial-system assets fell from 17.6% (1996) to under 1.5%.
Who got it
Itau and Bradesco were the most frequent buyers: Banerj (Itau, 26 Jun 1997), Credireal (BCN, 7 Aug 1997), Bemge (Itau, 14 Sep 1998), Bandepe (ABN Amro, 17 Nov 1998), Baneb (Bradesco, 22 Jun 1999), Paraiban (Real ABN Amro, 8 Nov 2001), BEG (Itau, 4 Dec 2001), BEA (Bradesco, 24 Jan 2002). Meridional (Bozano Simonsen, Dec 1997) was a federal-controlled bank, not a state bank in the PROES sense. Banco do Maranhao went to Bradesco in Feb 2004. Banespa and Banestado have their own cases.
Terms
BCB table prices (R$ million): Banerj 311.10; Credireal 134.20; Bemge 603.06; Bandepe 182.90; Baneb 267.80; Banestado 1,799.26; Banespa 7,160.92; Paraiban 79.14; BEG 680.84; BEA 192.54; total R$11.41 bn including subsidiaries, employee sales and leftovers.
Mechanism
MP 1.514/1996 and Lei 9.496/1997. Incentives: Banerj allowed part payment in privatization certificates; buyers could count the agio and Bemge's fixed assets toward the fixed-asset limit for five years; tax credits were the 'most controversial' incentive.
Who paid
Taxpayers. The Union's net debt is affected only by the interest differential. ANPUH puts the total PROES cost above R$73 bn, 'almost four times PROER', with about R$53 bn spent cleaning banks that were later privatised. Sul21 (opinion) puts debt assumption plus PROES at about R$500 bn in Dec-2010 prices, 90% to SP, RJ, MG and RS; the two numbers measure different things.
What came after
49 administrative processes were opened and 10 denuncias sent to the Ministerio Publico (BCB book). BEM (2004) and BEC (2005) were sold later.
Counter-view
Official BCB view: privatization was optional, but covering the uncovered liability was a legal obligation of the states, so comparing the federal loan with sale proceeds is 'simplistic'. The banks were already insolvent.

    Another source says R$260 million. Prefer BCB.

CC5 accounts and the Banestado CPI

CC5 accounts moved large sums abroad in 1996-2002. Estimates range from US$24 bn to US$124 bn, and the CPMI ended without a voted report. This case is linked to the Banestado privatization only through the same bank.

Government
Cardoso (flows); Lula (CPMI, installed 18 Jun 2003, ended 27 Dec 2004)
What happened
Money sent abroad through non-resident CC5 accounts, mainly through banks in Foz do Iguacu, 1996-2002. Estimates differ widely.
Who got it
90+ 'laranja' accounts in 1996-97 (O Povo); about 100 convicted (count unverified).
Terms
Estimates: US$30 bn 1996-2002 (Senate, Operation Macuco); US$124 bn in ten years (a Federal Police delegate, single source); US$24 bn and over US$28 bn (Gazeta do Povo); CPMI report: evasion up to R$150 bn with 91 indictments proposed.
Mechanism
CC5 non-resident accounts (Carta-Circular 5, text not opened). A 1996 central bank decision for Foz do Iguacu banks led to a proposal to indict the then central bank president Gustavo Franco.
Who paid
Treasury (evasion); the state bank Banestado, privatized to Itau in 2000.
What came after
Two competing CPMI reports; it ended unvoted on 27 Dec 2004. Tax assessments came to R$8.376 bn; US$8.2 million was seized.
Counter-view
Franco's indictment was a political outcome of one report; the other report did not follow it. Search summaries did not support a Janot link to Banestado.

    'Evasion', not directly comparable with sums moved. Not yet voted.

    O Povo's R$ figures conflict with Gazeta's US$ figures.

e4-19
Companhia Vale do Rio Doce (6 May 1997)

Vale was sold in 1997 for about US$3.0 bn at a 19.99% premium. Critics say its ore reserves were left out of the valuation and that the lead valuer had a conflict of interest. Courts left the sale in place; in 2024 the STJ closed the many suits, citing earlier TCU approval.

Government
Cardoso
What happened
41.73% of voting shares of the world's top iron-ore company, with Carajas and large mineral rights (also described as 27% of total capital). The government kept 35.19% of ordinary shares (not confirmed).
Who got it
Consorcio Brasil via Valepar (created 9 Apr 1997): CSN 16.30% (R$1.3 bn), Litel (Previ, Petros, Funcef, Fundacao Cesp) 10.43% (R$834.5 million), Eletron (Opportunity) 10% (R$800 million), Sweet River (NationsBank) 5% (R$400 million). One source says NationsBank put in R$1.2 bn, conflicting with R$400 million. Critics and one secondary article say BNDES gave subsidised financing; no official figure found.
Terms
R$3.338 bn (about US$3.0 bn), a 19.99% premium over the R$26.67 minimum (R$32.00 per share). The company was valued at US$9.3 bn (R$10.4 bn) at the time (Merrill Lynch-led). Critics' ranges go to R$100 bn. Coppe-UFRJ: ore reserves reported to the US SEC in 1995 were Carajas 4.970 bn t and Sistema Sul 7.918 bn t, but the sale notice used 1.8 bn t and 1.4 bn t (gap 9.688 bn t); ore was valued in situ, not at the mine gate; excluded reserves valued at R$1.094 bn to R$87.579 bn depending on method; 104 deposits valued at zero were worth US$114.5 million. Titanium (92.5 Mt) and niobium (69.1 Mt) were not valued (DNPM document).
Mechanism
PND auction (Lei 8.031) at the Rio stock exchange. Mining stayed under DNPM; no sector regulator.
Who paid
Brazil lost control of a strategic asset, say critics. Pension funds of state firms put in R$834.5 million (Litel). Six valuers were paid R$63.7 million.
What came after
Dozens of popular-action suits from 1997; in Oct 2005 TRF-1 sent 69 suits back to Belem for expert review; 107 suits counted in 2007 (Estadao via Wikipedia); in 2010 STF Justice Gilmar Mendes suspended annulment cases. A STJ ruling reported on 2 Sep 2024 (rapporteur Mauro Campbell, IAC 7) held that res judicata in one popular action binds all (erga omnes), applied the fait accompli doctrine and noted prior TCU approval; reported as ending 70+ suits. No re-nationalisation. Vale's market value was R$84.4 bn by March 2006 (market quote, not a valuation of what was sold).
Counter-view
Roger Agnelli, then Vale's president: it was an open, public auction. The 2006 value is a later quote. The STJ found no damage and relied on TCU approval. The sale notice used two outside valuations plus a third review (BNDES pamphlet 'O Estado no lugar certo'). Unvalued mineral rights belong to the Union, not the company (defence line; not sourced in opened pages). A TCU document itself was not retrieved.

    Folha de Londrina headline says 19.98% (page 403). A Senate speech claims 77% (opposition rhetoric, snippet).

    R$10.4 bn. CUT reports R$12.5 bn at the auction share price and says some estimated up to R$100 bn.
  • verified Excluded reserves (Coppe-UFRJ range, low): 1094 BRL million (2006; Coppe-UFRJ) source
    High end R$87.579 bn depending on method.

CEEE (RS): 1997 split of distribution into AES Sul and RGE

In 1997 Rio Grande do Sul split CEEE's distribution area and sold two parts. The state kept the weaker remainder and its debts. The price is known only from a snippet.

Rio Grande do Sul state government (Governor Britto)
What happened
CEEE's distribution area was cut in two and sold as AES Sul and RGE. CEEE kept generation, transmission and the rest of distribution (later CEEE-D).
Who got it
AES (AES Sul) and the RGE consortium. Per-lot prices not confirmed.

Total R$3.14 bn for the two concessions (snippet only, unverified).
Mechanism
State sale of two distribution concessions. BNDES role not established.

A former Fundacao CEEE manager says CEEE 'lost 50% of revenue and inherited 88% of expense' (claim by an interested party).
What came after

Cemig (MG): 1997 stake sale and the shareholders' agreement fight

In 1997 a group including AES bought about a third of Cemig's voting shares with BNDES financing, as the only bidder. The deal gave the buyer vetoes and led to years of fights with the state. BNDES ended up with the debt, finally settled around 2009.

Government
Minas Gerais state government (Itamar Franco as governor from Jan 1999)
What happened
Auction on 28 May 1997 on the Rio stock exchange of about 33% of voting shares. Southern Electric Brasil (Southern Co., AES, Opportunity) was the only bidder of five pre-qualified.
Who got it
Southern Electric Brasil (SEB). The deal gave the buyer a veto over investments above US$1 million.
Terms
US$1.056 bn for 33% of voting shares, a 14.4% economic interest (Southern release). A local source says R$1.1 bn paid in installments over ten years, financed by BNDES (that article wrongly dates the sale to 1995). Minimum R$1.13 bn with half financed by BNDES at 3.35% a year (snippet, unverified).
Mechanism
Share auction with a shareholders' agreement giving veto rights.
Who paid
BNDES held the buyer's debt: R$2.115 bn contracted in 1997, R$3.19 bn at the end of 2008. AES later defaulted on BNDES.
What came after
In Jan 1999 Governor Itamar Franco, whose state held 51% of ordinary shares, ordered a review of the agreement; a state inquiry in Sep 1999 judged it 'unsound'. In 2007 SEB offered US$1.2 bn cash, which BNDES would accept. The Ministerio Publico said this meant a loss and asked a court to veto it. Andrade Gutierrez assumed the debt, with only about R$300 million of discount in court costs. The closing year is probably 2009 but not stated. Court details (STJ agravo 164.822-9; MP civil action dismissed Sep 1998; minority holders got 4 of 11 board seats) are from snippets.
Counter-view
The buyers' side was that they paid for control rights and the state later changed the rules.

State electricity distributors: Coelba, CPFL, Enersul, Coelce, Celpe, Cemar

Several states sold distributors in 1997-2000 mostly to Iberdrola, Enel/Endesa, Previ and others. Prices are known mainly from snippets. Cemar's buyer asked to leave within two years after drought, rationing and a refused tariff review.

Government
State governments (Bahia, Sao Paulo, Mato Grosso do Sul, Ceara, Pernambuco, Maranhao)
What happened
Sales of state distributors in 1997-2000, with BNDES running lending to buyers. Federalised distributors (Ceal, Cepisa, Eletroacre, Ceron, Ceam) were taken into Eletrobras in 1997-99 and only privatised in 2018. Eletrobras also ran Enersul, Cemat, Saelpa, Cosern, Cemar and Celpa until their sales 1997-2000 (not checked).
Who got it
Coelba (31 Jul 1997): Iberdrola 39%, Previ and Banco do Brasil 61%. CPFL (5 Nov 1997): VBC 46% and Previ 38%. Enersul (19 Nov 1997): Iven 52%. Coelce (2 Apr 1998): a Cerj/Endesa/Enersis consortium. Celpe (17 Feb 2000): Guaraniana (Iberdrola, Previ, Banco do Brasil). Cemar (15 Jun 2000): PPL.
Terms
Coelba R$1,730.88 million; CPFL R$3,014 million (CVM Deliberacao 301: R$3.015 bn paid, agio R$2.694 bn); Coelce R$987 million (about US$880 million per IFC); Celpe about R$1.7 bn but a minimum of R$1.78 bn appeared in another snippet (a sale below the minimum is not plausible, so one figure is wrong); Cemar R$552.79 million. Enersul price not found. Most prices are snippet-only.
Mechanism
State PND-style auctions. BNDES approved post-sale credit lines. Pernambuco and Ceara got federal PROES bonds for their state banks.
Who paid
Consumers and BNDES. Cemar: on 22 Jul 2002 PPL proposed selling its 90% to Franklin Park for a 'nominal price'. Aneel had denied the extraordinary tariff review in June 2002, and PPL said it had 'no choice, short of filing for bankruptcy'. It cited drought, rationing and a non-functioning wholesale market.
What came after
Coelce: an ex-president says service declined in the early private years, then improved after ANEEL and ARCE acted. Enel Ceara ranks 25th of 29 in the ANEEL continuity ranking; April 2022 tariff increase 24.85%. Cemar's foreign buyer left within about two years, which shows the risk the 1997-2000 premiums carried.
Counter-view
Enel (Coelce article): DEC down 28.2%, FEC down 21.8%, R$2 bn invested. Tariff histories after sale were not found for Coelba, CPFL, Celpe, Enersul or Cemar. CERJ, Coelba and CPFL prices were 'not verified' in the fact-check; do not use names from memory.

Eletropaulo (15 Apr 1998)

Eletropaulo was sold in April 1998 at the minimum price to buyers who put in no capital: BNDES and banks lent the money. The TCU found BNDES exceeded its lending limit. When AES defaulted, BNDES took shares in the holding company.

Government
Cardoso (BNDES ran the sale; Sao Paulo state under Covas owned the asset)
What happened
The main Sao Paulo distributor, bought through Lightgas (a vehicle created by Light's controllers) with AES, EDF, Houston/Reliant and CSN.
Who got it
Lightgas shares: AES 11.46%, Houston 11.46%, EDF 11.46%, CSN 7.32%. The buyers put in no capital of their own: BNDES lent 50% of the minimum price, and a bank syndicate lent the rest through a Cayman vehicle (LIREnergy Ltd).
Terms
Sold AT the minimum price, about 2.026 bn (pt-Wikipedia; currency unstated, probably R$). The 'several hundred million above minimum' line in Latin News was a pre-auction expectation.
Mechanism
BNDES auction; BNDES advances for debentures and shares.
Who paid
TCU found BNDES exceeded its 50% limit by advancing money for debentures and shares, and a 30%-of-assets exposure limit. Taxpayers took the AES defaults.
What came after
AES Elpa defaulted on about US$420 million in 2003 (the earlier note said 2002). End-2003: BNDES renegotiated more than US$1 bn (loan US$1.2 bn, US$400 million guarantee) and took shares in the Brasiliana holding as partial payment (JB: of a US$1.3 bn debt); it held about 50% minus one share of Brasiliana and sold part from 2007. Debt was cut to US$510 million. BNDES held a stake in the holding, not 'the assets'.
Counter-view
AES and EDF inherited a split-up, indebted utility and invested. The Congresso em Foco piece frames BNDES lending as a policy choice to attract capital. Allegation of collusion: the Financial Times reported an AES-Enron agreement (April 1998) that Enron would not bid in exchange for gas contracts; AES denied it.

e4-24
Telebras breakup (29 Jul 1998)

Telebras was sold in July 1998 in 12 pieces for R$22.06 bn, 63.74% above the minimum, mostly to foreign telecoms. Critics say it was worth more; supporters point to the premium and to phone lines growing afterward. The regulator Anatel was set up before the sale.

Government
Cardoso
What happened
12 holdings auctioned in one day at the Rio stock exchange: 3 fixed-line, 1 long-distance (Embratel), 8 mobile (Banda A). Legal basis: EC 8/1995 (end of the telecom monopoly), Lei 9.295/1996 and Lei Geral de Telecomunicacoes 9.472 of 16 Jul 1997, which created Anatel before the sale.
Who got it
Telesp: Telefonica Internacional, RBS, Portugal Telecom, Iberdrola, BBV. Tele Centro Sul: Telecom Italia, Algar, Splice, Opportunity. Tele Norte Leste: AG Telecom and Inepar-led Telemar. Embratel: MCI. Telesp Celular: Portugal Telecom. 'With La Fonte' was not confirmed.
Terms
R$22.057 bn total, 63.74% over the government's combined minimum (about R$13.47 bn by arithmetic). BNDES's own page says 53.74%, which looks like a typo. Per company (R$ and agio): Telesp 5.783 bn (64.28%); Tele Centro Sul 2.070 bn (6.15%); Tele Norte Leste 3.434 bn (about 1%); Embratel 2.650 bn (47.22%); Telesp Celular 3.588 bn (226.18%); Tele Sudeste Celular 1.360 bn (138.59%); Telemig 756 million (228.69%); Tele Celular Sul 700 million (204.34%); Tele Nordeste 660 million (193.33%); Tele Centro-Oeste 440 million (91.3%); Tele Leste 428 million (242.40%); Tele Norte Celular 188 million (108%).
Mechanism
Auctions at the Rio stock exchange after the 1997 telecom law.
Who paid
BNDES reports US$2.125 bn of debt transferred with the fixed-line and long-distance companies (missing from the earlier note). Its US$ table shows US$29.05 bn total auction revenue.
What came after
Telephone access expanded (supporters credit privatization; critics credit technology). Oi/Telemar went into judicial recovery in 2016 (outside this era; not sourced).
Counter-view
Supporters: the 63.74% premium; the highest premiums were in the mobile units (up to 242%); teledensity rose (12.1 lines per 100 inhabitants in 1998, 14.9 in 1999; 14.7 million access lines in 1997, teledensity 9.1). A UFRJ working paper (Resende) judged the new model as showing 'encouraging results' in network expansion with universal access, quality and competition still open. Cardoso argued on 29 Jul 1998 that the sale helped public finances and that creating Anatel first was an innovation. Critics (FPA, Brasil de Fato) say assets were worth more, but the FPA page gives no valuation estimate or BNDES-loan figure; do not quote 'R$19 bn sold / R$11 bn BNDES loans'.

    Per-company prices sum to the total; Wikipedia 22.058 bn.
  • verified Premium over combined minimum: 63.74 percent (1998; Teletime) source
    BNDES page says 53.74% (probable typo; it would imply a R$14.35 bn minimum). Implied minimum about R$13.47 bn is derived.

    Reported by the fact-check from the BNDES page; not in the earlier note.

    The earlier note said Brasilcom/Arthur D. Little won one contract. They won two separate services: B (valuation and sale execution, Brasilcom) and A (second valuation, Arthur D. Little/Coopers & Lybrand, R$8.274 million).
  • verified Tele Norte Leste agio: 1 percent (1998; Teletime) source
    'Pouco mais de 1%'.

Federal generation sales: Gerasul, Paranapanema, Elektro

Three federal generation and distribution firms were sold in 1998-99 to Tractebel, Duke and Enron. Prices agree between sources when currency is accounted for. Buyers' financing was not researched.

Government
Cardoso
What happened
Gerasul (Eletrosul generation) sold 15 Sep 1998 to Tractebel (Franco-Belgian). Paranapanema sold in 1999 to Duke Energy. Elektro sold to Enron (Eron International).
Who got it
Tractebel (Gerasul); Duke Energy (Paranapanema); Enron (Elektro).
Terms
Gerasul R$947 million (Wikipedia/CPDOC), US$800.4 million (BNDES; paid entirely in cash). The two agree at about R$1.18 per US$. Congresso em Foco says US$760 million. Paranapanema R$1.239 bn (agio 90.2%). Elektro US$215.86 million (agio 98.9%); BNDES dates it 1999, the earlier note said 1998/99.
Mechanism
Federal electricity auctions.
Who paid
Not researched.
What came after
Federalised distributors Ceal, Cepisa, Eletroacre, Ceron and Ceam were taken into Eletrobras in 1997-99 and only privatised in 2018. Sector: distribution 1995-2002 about US$16.4 bn, generation US$1.86 bn (Eixos citing BNDES).

1998–1999
e4-26
The 'grampo do BNDES' and the Tele Norte Leste/Telemar case

The Telemar group that won Tele Norte Leste borrowed R$686.8 million (20% of the price) from BNDESPar. The TCU found BNDES never tested the borrowers' finances. Tapes published in November 1998 led to resignations, but the courts rejected the improbity case in 2010.

Government
Cardoso
What happened
Tele Norte Leste went to the Telemar consortium for R$3.434 bn (TCU: R$3,434,000,108) in the 29 Jul 1998 auction. Recordings of officials discussing the consortium were revealed by Elio Gaspari in Folha de S.Paulo and O Globo on 8 Nov 1998.
Who got it
Telemar (AG Telecom/Inepar, Andrade Gutierrez, Macal and others). The MPF alleged first-instalment funds came from BNDES, Banco do Brasil insurers and pension-fund-controlled firms, forming the consortium with 'illegal loans'. The defence says Previ was in the Opportunity consortium, not Telemar; the MPF argued Previ had a relevant role in Tele Norte Leste (disputed).
Terms
BNDES help was R$686.8 million, 20% of the control price (TCU paragraph 266). The first instalment of R$1,373.6 million was paid with a R$400 million advance split between Andrade Gutierrez (133 million), Macal (133 million) and Inepar (134 million), then two further R$143.4 million tranches. A news site's 'almost half a billion reais' refers to the R$400 million first advance, not a conflict.
Mechanism
BNDESPar financing; auction at the Rio exchange.
Who paid
TCU: BNDES made no studies proving the borrowers' (or guarantors') economic-financial capacity (paragraph 267). Dec 1998 determinations to BNDESPar: publicise financing in future sales, analyse borrowers' finances, and use a special auction when selling Telemar shares; three people were summoned to a hearing.
What came after
Luiz Carlos Mendonca de Barros testified in the Senate on 19 Nov 1998; he and Andre Lara Resende told Cardoso on 22 Nov 1998 they were leaving (Poder360). Wikipedia says four officials resigned (Mendonca de Barros, Lara Resende, Pio Borges, Jose Roberto Mendonca de Barros); only the first two are independently confirmed. The Federal Police declined to investigate (tapes illegally obtained) and the ruling parties blocked a CPI in May 1999 (Wikipedia only). In April 2010 the 3rd Turma of TRF-1, with Desembargador Tourinho Neto writing, rejected the MPF's improbity appeal; first instance (Judge Moacir Ferreira Ramos, 17a Vara DF) had already dismissed it.
Counter-view
Defence outcome: TRF-1 relied on a TCU report that found no irregularity; the court said it is not bound by the TCU but a ruling aligned with it is not unreasoned, that annulment was 'not in the public interest', and that improbity needs bad faith. Defendants: Mendonca de Barros (ex-Communications Minister), Lara Resende (ex-BNDES president), Pio Borges (ex-interim BNDES president) and the former Anatel president. The FPA page says the tapes showed officials favouring Opportunity's bid, with no quotes; no confirmed transcript exists in the sources.
Figures
  • verified Tele Norte Leste control price: 3434 BRL million (1998; TCU) source
    R$3,434,000,108.
  • verified BNDESPar financing of the Telemar buyers: 686.8 BRL million (1998; TCU) source
    20% of the control price; first-instalment advance R$400 million.
  • verified First-instalment advance split among three firms: 400 BRL million (1998; TCU) source
    133 + 133 + 134 million. The earlier 'R$490 million' was a different figure.

Sao Paulo state highway concessions

Sao Paulo granted 12 highway lots in 1998, mostly to the highest outorga bid. Contracts were later extended by about five years on average. The regulator ARTESP came in 2002. Cartel and bribery claims are unverified.

Government
Sao Paulo state government (Covas, 1995-2001)
What happened
12 lots (more than 3,500 km) granted in 1998. The first stage ran 20 years, but contracts were extended on average by about 5 years, up to 28 years, after concessionaires' rebalancing claims. Second stage (2007-11) added 2,700 km, chosen by lowest toll, with 30-year terms. As of Feb 2018 there were 22 concessionaires, 149 toll plazas and 8,292 km of 22,095 km (37.5%) of state highways.
Who got it
Concessionaires won by highest outorga in 11 of 12 tenders. Names not collected. Snippets (403) say Ecovias admitted cartel and bribery in all 12 contracts from 1998 to 2015 and will pay R$650 million to the MP-SP.
Terms
Outorga totals and 1998 toll values were not found.
Mechanism
Concession contracts; ARTESP was created only in 2002. Tamoios PPP began 2015.
Who paid
Road users, through tolls (paper's reading: highest-outorga rule pushed value to the state up front and into tolls later).
What came after
A 2025 TCE-SP note says 21 monitored concessions total R$148.33 bn (snippet).
Counter-view
Concessionaires' standard defence: extensions were rebalancing after traffic and cost changes.

2000
e4-28
Petrobras share sales and the FGTS Fundo Mutuo (Aug 2000)

In 2000 workers could use FGTS savings to buy Petrobras shares, while the Union kept control. Results depend on the end date: the fund lost to FGTS by 2016 and beat it by 2022.

Government
Cardoso
What happened
Workers could use FGTS savings to buy Petrobras shares at a discount of up to 20%. The fund held about 7.4% of ordinary shares (4.3% of capital); by 2010 that had fallen to 3.7% of ordinary (2.1% of capital). The Union kept control. The 'up to half of the FGTS balance' limit was not confirmed in opened pages.
Who got it
Workers (individuals using FGTS).
Terms
BNDES lists the Petrobras share sale above the Union's controlling stake: 1 operation, US$4.84 bn revenue.
Mechanism
Share offer with an FGTS investment window, under the privatization rules.
Who paid
Workers bore the market risk of their forced-saving money.
What came after
Returns depend on method and dates. To Jan 2016: FGTS beat Petrobras funds (4.78% vs 4.32% a year; cumulative from 17 Aug 2000 FGTS 110.68% vs 91.48%; in real terms FGTS minus 23.08%, funds minus 30.09%). To May 2022 (Genial via Folhapress): Petrobras shares +1,153% vs FGTS +185% (IPCA +289%); another outlet gives +1,236.2% vs +152.7%.
Counter-view
Workers chose to use the option. Over 2000-2022 the Petrobras fund beat FGTS by far; over 2000-2016 it lost to FGTS. Both belong in the case.

2000
e4-29
Banestado (Parana, 17 Oct 2000)

Banestado was sold to Itau in October 2000 for R$1.625 bn in cash, after Parana spent billions cleaning the bank. Staff and branches were cut sharply. A later fight over Copel shares ended in a R$1.7 bn settlement still pending in 2023.

Government
Cardoso; Parana Governor Jaime Lerner
What happened
State bank of Parana sold to Itau on the stock exchange. The date is 17 Oct 2000 (Brasil de Fato); one STF notice says 16 Oct. A search result gives 88.04% of capital and about 303% agio (not verified).
Who got it
Itau. The Itau executive said the price was paid in cash with no BNDES or FCVS money, and noted Bradesco had valued Banestado at about R$700 million.
Terms
R$1.625 bn, in cash (Itau executive, Isto E Dinheiro, Nov 2000). The union source says R$1.652 bn (looks like a transposition); R$1.45 bn was not found in any opened page. The BCB table gives R$1,799.26 million on a different basis. Parana PROES bonds: R$5.19763 bn.
Mechanism
State bank sale under PROES.
Who paid
The union claims Parana spent about R$5.1 bn on cleanup and owed the Union R$5.6 bn from a 1997 deal (refinanced to 2048). Workers: about 15,000 staff before and 8,000 in 2000 after two voluntary-redundancy plans (CUT); Brasil de Fato says about 10,000 at the sale and just over 500 ex-staff left at Itau; Tribuna says about 8,000 lost jobs; Itau received 346 branches and 552,000 account holders and closed 76% of former branches by Sep 2002 (CUT).
What came after
Dispute over a Copel-share guarantee (pledged in 1998 for an operation involving 'precatorios podres'; debt about R$700 million at the start). Forbes, 11 Apr 2023: Min. Lewandowski homologated a conciliation under which Parana pays Itau R$1.7 bn in three instalments; Fux, Gilmar, Toffoli and Moraes followed, but Min. Mendonca asked for vista, so approval was not final at publication. A separate R$1.7 bn is in Tribuna (2004): tax credits Itau used, which Parana sought to recover. Do not conflate the two. The final STF outcome was not checked. The CC5 scheme at Banestado is a separate case.
Counter-view
Buyer side: Itau paid cash and no BNDES or FCVS money; Bradesco had valued the bank at about R$700 million. This is the main counter to 'sold too cheap'. Staff figures differ by source and the union figures are advocacy.

e4-30
Banespa (Sao Paulo, 20 Nov 2000)

Banespa was sold in seven minutes in November 2000 for R$7.05 bn, 281% above the minimum. Before the sale the Union had issued R$36.1 bn of bonds for the bank's state. Defenders cite the premium; critics say the minimum price was too low.

Government
Cardoso; Sao Paulo state (federal takeover Nov 1996)
What happened
State bank of Sao Paulo. The federal takeover came in Nov 1996 (Wikipedia gives 27 Nov 1996; 51% to the Union, unverified). Sold to Santander Central Hispano.
Who got it
Santander Central Hispano. Rivals: Unibanco bid R$2.1 bn and Bradesco R$1.8 bn. Itau and Safra did not bid. The sale took seven minutes. Rival bankers called the bid a 'descalabro' and 'incrivelmente afoita'.
Terms
R$7.05 bn against a R$1.8 bn minimum, agio 281% (fits a R$1.85 bn minimum). BCB table: R$7,160.92 million (different basis). Sao Paulo received R$36.1265 bn in federal bonds (23/24 Dec 1997), the biggest of any state; Santander paid about a fifth of that. Snippets (unverified): Dieese and Unicamp said the minimum should have been double; R$4.2 bn of tax credits; SP debt R$45 bn.
Mechanism
State bank sale under PROES, preceded by the federal takeover.
Who paid
Taxpayers via the bond issue. The cost of the Banespa cleanup to the Union was not found.
What came after
Tax litigation: the agio was about R$4 bn; the Union's shares fetched R$7 bn, or R$9 bn including minorities and employees. CARF held the agio legitimate (not simulated) on 30 Sep 2011 while the lawfulness of the tax planning was still open. Receita sought a 150% fine; the CVM found no simulation. A later CARF reversal of a R$3.95 bn fine is unverified.
Counter-view
The high agio is the strongest argument that the sale was good value. Against it: unions, Dieese and Unicamp economists said the minimum should have been about double; a prosecutor contested the price. No source opened gives the government's own defence.
Figures
  • verified Price paid by Santander: 7050 BRL million (2000; Istoe Dinheiro) source

  • verified Minimum price: 1800 BRL million (2000; Istoe Dinheiro) source
    Agio 281% fits R$1.85 bn: 7.05/1.85 = 3.81.
  • verified Federal bonds issued for Sao Paulo: 36126.5 BRL million (1997; Banco Central do Brasil) source
    The price paid was about a fifth of this.
  • unverified Agio (tax litigation): 4000 BRL million (2011; Conjur on CARF) source
    'About R$4 bn'. Union shares R$7 bn, R$9 bn with minorities.

2001–2002
e4-31
Electricity rationing and the tariff recomposition (RTE)

The 2001 rationing cut sales for distributors, many newly privatised. A 2002 law let them recover the loss through higher tariffs and BNDES loans. Consumers and BNDES carried the cost; the causes are still argued.

Government
Cardoso (Camara de Gestao da Crise); settlement under Lula
What happened
Compulsory rationing from about Jun/Jul 2001 to Feb 2002 (one search result: 1 Jul 2001 to 19 Feb 2002). Targets: 20% for residential users above 100 kWh a month, 20% commercial, 20-25% industrial, with a surcharge for overshoot and a bonus for savers. The 2001 General Agreement (MP 14 of 21 Dec 2001, Lei 10.438 of 26 Apr 2002) set an Extraordinary Tariff Recomposition (RTE).
Who got it
Distributors and generators, which lost revenue when use fell. Concessionaires' loss is put at R$8 bn by Pinguelli Rosa (one author; no official total in an opened page).
Terms
RTE of 2.9% a year for residential (rural, public lighting) and 7.9% a year for others, none for low-income users; a news summary says it ran 72 months (snippet). The law also describes a one-time recomposition applied for 12 months. BNDES lent the firms the amount to be recomposed: about R$7 bn for RTE financing and R$8 bn for plants (TCU/BNDES reporting via Congresso em Foco).
Mechanism
Contract rebalancing (reequilibrio economico-financeiro) by law, with BNDES credit.
Who paid
Consumers through the RTE; taxpayers through BNDES loans. In 1993 Lei 8.631 had already settled sector accounts at about US$26 bn, paid by the Treasury. A news item attributes to a TCU audit losses of R$45.2 bn 'mostly paid by consumers', but this was not found in an opened page; do not use it. An uncited blog saying about 60% was passed to consumers is unconfirmed.
What came after
Eight of 12 financed distributors had not settled their debts (Congresso em Foco). Many distributors had been privatised; they were barred from raising prices while sales fell, which created the liquidity crisis that the agreement moved to consumers and BNDES.
Counter-view
Causes are disputed. The government and sector analysts blame a severe drought plus delays in generation works and missing long-term contracting rules. Critics blame low investment and a ban on Eletrobras investing because of privatization plans (FPA, a critical source). Castelar and Lessa argue rationing, not privatization, was the problem. The BNDES paper itself is the official view, not neutral.
Figures

    Earlier note omitted the 100 kWh threshold. Industry 20-25%.
  • verified Lei 8.631 sector account settlement, 1993: 26000 USD million (1993; BNDES TD-97) source
    Paid by the Treasury.
  • verified RTE cap, residential: 2.9 percent per year (2002; BNDES TD-97) source
    Industry/other 7.9% a year.
  • unverified BNDES financing of RTE: 7000 BRL million (2002; TCU/BNDES via Congresso em Foco) source
    BNDES also put about R$8 bn into emergency plants.
  • unverified Concessionaires' rationing loss (Pinguelli Rosa): 8000 BRL million (2001; Pinguelli Rosa via Congresso em Foco) source
    One author's estimate.

e4-32
Seguro-apagao (emergency capacity charge, CBEE)

After the rationing, consumers paid a per-kWh charge from 2002 to fund emergency power plants contracted by a state company. A court briefly suspended it in November 2002. The total collected was not found.

Government
Cardoso, then Lula
What happened
A surcharge on consumers to pay for emergency thermal capacity contracted by the state company CBEE. Charged from Feb 2002 through distributors under an emergency program (MP and Lei 10.438/2002). It ended in Dec 2005 or Feb 2006 (sources differ).
Who got it
CBEE and the contracted plants. CBEE collected about R$300 million in fines (CanalEnergia).
Terms
R$0.0057 per kWh in 2002 with exemption under 80 kWh; R$0.0067 per kWh in Feb 2005. A search summary gave R$0.0035 and annual revenue of about R$1 bn (unverified). Cumulative total not found. Cost of capacity versus use not found.
Mechanism
Emergency program by law; collected on electricity bills. A 17a Vara Civel Federal injunction suspended collection on 20 Nov 2002. PIS/Cofins rose from 3.65% to 9.25% and the charge was cut 22% (CanalEnergia).
Who paid
All grid consumers except low-income (search summary only, unverified).
What came after
Charge ended early after CBEE was capitalised (unverified).
Counter-view
Defenders held that the plants were insurance against another shortfall. No opened source states this.

2003–2015
e5-01
Oil and gas concession rounds 5 to 13 (ANP)

Between 2003 and 2015 the state sold oil and gas exploration rights in nine bidding rounds. Early signing bonuses were small, from R$ 27 million to R$ 1.1 billion, and the blocks were not independently valued. After the pre-salt discoveries the government moved to other models.

Government
Lula 1 and 2, Dilma 1 and 2
What happened
Exploration and production rights over offshore and onshore blocks of Union-owned subsoil were sold by concession in rounds 5 to 13. Signing bonuses ran from R$ 27 million (round 5) to R$ 2.48 billion (round 11).
Who got it
Petrobras, foreign majors and, from round 9 on, many small Brazilian firms. Winners are named only for round 7 (for example Petrobras, Petrogal, Devon, ENI, Shell, Koch, Repsol YPF, Statoil). Financing is not documented in the sources.
Terms
The signing bonus was the only up-front price. No source values the blocks. ANP reports only the bonus, the minimum exploration programme and local-content offers.
Mechanism
Concession model of Lei 9.478/1997. From round 5 the bonus, exploration programme and local-content offer were scored together. Minimum local content in round 5: 30% deep water, 50% and 60% shallow water, 70% onshore. Round 12 weights: 40% bonus, 40% exploration programme, 20% local content.
Who paid
The Union gave up subsoil rights in exchange for bonuses. Round 8 was stopped by a federal-court injunction after 38 blocks were sold. No rounds were held in 2009–2012.
What came after
After the 2007 pre-salt discoveries the government stopped concession rounds in the pre-salt area and moved to production sharing (see cessão onerosa and Libra). Local-content waivers per round and winner lists for most rounds were not found.
Counter-view
ANP's stated aim of scoring exploration programme and local content in the bid was to raise exploration and local supply (ANP yearbook 2004). Low early bonuses may reflect frontier risk before the pre-salt was known (this is an interpretation, unverified).

2003–2015
e5-02
BNDES export-service loans to Brazilian contractors abroad (Odebrecht, Mariel, Angola)

BNDES financed US$ 10.5 billion of services that Brazilian contractors sold to foreign governments. Almost all went to five firms, led by Odebrecht. Most of the money was repaid, but arrears and non-repayable transfers to Cuba drew criticism.

Government
Lula 1 and 2, Dilma 1 and 2
What happened
BNDES disbursed US$ 10.5 billion to finance engineering services exported by Brazilian contractors. Five contractors took 98% of it and Odebrecht took 76%.
Who got it
Odebrecht 76%, Andrade Gutierrez 14%, Queiroz Galvão 4%, Camargo Corrêa 2%, OAS 2%. Foreign states such as Cuba (Mariel port) and Angola were the borrowers. Odebrecht was also the third-largest recipient of all BNDES disbursements in 2003–2018 (R$ 51.3 billion, domestic and export).
Terms
Loans to foreign states, to be repaid. For Mariel, MDIC confirmed some Treasury transfers without return. Sources disagree on the size of the Angola exposure.
Mechanism
BNDES export financing, with repayment risk on foreign states. A Treasury-backed export guarantee fund is mentioned in the notes (unverified).
Who paid
BNDES and the Treasury carry the default risk. From 2018 Venezuela, Mozambique and Cuba stopped paying (arrears US$ 554 million by June 2019).
What came after
Secrecy fight over BNDES files, CGU and TCU probes, and Odebrecht plea deals in Lava Jato.
Counter-view
Aos Fatos: these were loans to be repaid, not donations. BNDES had received US$ 10.3 billion of the US$ 10.5 billion disbursed, so the loss was small. Only the Mariel Proex transfers were confirmed as non-repayable (Aos Fatos, https://www.aosfatos.org/noticias/e-falso-que-pt-doou-r-14-bilhoes-do-bndes-para-governo-de-angola/).

about 2004–2014 (revealed 2014; leniency deals 2015–2019)
e5-03
Petrobras contractor cartel and kickbacks (Lava Jato) and the leniency deals

Prosecutors and plea-bargainers say a cartel of contractors inflated Petrobras contracts and paid kickbacks to political parties. Estimates of the loss range from 3% to 20% of contract values. The leniency deals agreed about R$ 8 billion, but only about R$ 1 billion had been paid by mid-2022.

Government
Lula 1 and 2, Dilma 1
What happened
Contractors inflated Petrobras contracts and paid 1-3% kickbacks to parties, according to plea testimony. Petrobras recognised a R$ 6.19 billion corruption loss in 2014. Later leniency deals with the main contractors agreed about R$ 8 billion, of which about R$ 1 billion was paid by mid-2022.
Who got it
Odebrecht and Andrade Gutierrez led the cartel, per the Federal Police and prosecutors. Ex-director Paulo Roberto Costa said PP, PT and PMDB split Petrobras directorships to collect 1-3% on big contracts. Youssef said 60% of the bribe fed political agents.
Terms
Costa said the 3% was embedded in contractor margins and denied overpricing at some works. The Federal Police estimated losses of up to 20% of contract values, while plea-bargainers admitted 3%. TCU found about R$ 4.2 billion of overpricing at three works alone (Rnest, Repar, Angra 3).
Mechanism
Cartel in Petrobras tenders plus political division of directorships. Afterwards the Anticorruption Law (Lei 12.846/2013) allowed leniency agreements: first MPF agreements, then CGU/AGU agreements that credit the earlier ones, with Selic indexation. Firms may keep selling to the public sector.
Who paid
Petrobras (minority shareholders and the Treasury), Eletrobras and taxpayers. The notes also say workers lost jobs afterwards (not sourced).
What came after
Plea deals and leniency agreements followed. In 2022 the firms were trying to rewrite the agreements for longer terms or lower amounts.
Counter-view
Costa said the 3% was embedded in contractor margins and denied overpricing at some works (Gazeta do Povo). Firms argue the sums cannot be paid while they are barred from contracts and that restructuring preserves jobs (Congresso em Foco, 13 Jun 2022).

e5-04
PPP law and the first PPP, São Paulo Metro Line 4

The 2004 PPP law let the state guarantee payments to private partners. Line 4 of the São Paulo Metro was the first such deal. Critics call it capitalism without risk, while supporters point to faster delivery.

Government
Lula 1 (federal law); São Paulo state (Line 4 contract)
What happened
Lei 11.079/2004 created public-private partnerships with state payment guarantees. Line 4 of the São Paulo Metro (ViaQuatro) was the first metro PPP: private operation for 30 years.
Who got it
The ViaQuatro consortium, which buys trains and systems and operates the line.
Terms
No audited cost figure was found. A union publication says the government pays 80% of civil works, the rest is financed by BNDES over 30 years with the state as guarantor, and the state pays the shortfall if demand is lower.
Mechanism
Sponsored and administrative concessions under Lei 11.079 of 30 Dec 2004. The state guarantees the payments. The public side builds tunnels and stations.
Who paid
The São Paulo state treasury carries demand and guarantee risk, according to the union text.
What came after
ViaQuatro later sought about R$ 500 million from the state for works delays (search result only), which shows risk also hit the private side. Total investment is given in the press as about US$ 2 billion (not verified).
Counter-view
Pro-PPP view: private operation brought driverless trains and quicker works. The critical text is a union advocacy publication (metroviarios.org.br).

Outcome and community impacts were not researched.

The law is defended as a way to fight illegal logging while keeping the land public (Brasil61). It is a weak 'handover' case.

e5-06
Madeira River dams: Santo Antonio and Jirau (Rondônia)

Two big dams on the Madeira River were won at low tariffs and built with R$ 13 billion of BNDES loans. State firms held large stakes. Residents and workers bore much of the social cost, and courts and prosecutors are still dealing with floods and alleged bribes.

Government
Lula 1 and 2, Dilma 1
What happened
Two large hydropower concessions on the Madeira River, with BNDES loans of R$ 6.1 billion (Santo Antonio) and R$ 7.2 billion (Jirau). Total investment was estimated at about R$ 28 billion.
Who got it
Santo Antonio: Furnas 39%, a Banif/Santander fund 20%, Odebrecht Investimentos 17.6%, Andrade Gutierrez 12.4%, Cemig 10%, CNO 1% (public share 49% with Cemig). Jirau: GDF Suez, Camargo Corrêa, Eletrosul, Chesf, with Funcef and Petros in Camargo's stake.
Terms
Santo Antonio won the 10 Dec 2007 auction at R$ 78.87/MWh (Exame: 78.90), 35% below an ANEEL ceiling of R$ 122 and 16.1% below the runner-up. No independent valuation was found.
Mechanism
ANEEL auctions in 2007–2008 and BNDES project-finance loans.
Who paid
Displaced riverside residents and workers. The Union through Furnas' stake and BNDES financing (BNDES amounts for this point not opened). Workers rioted in March 2011 over conditions; BNDES kept disbursing.
What came after
MPF, public defenders and OAB-RO sued on 6 Mar 2014 after a flood. A court ordered help for about 10,500 displaced people and new impact studies within 90 days, under a R$ 100,000/day fine. The final outcome was not found. In July 2025 MPF sued Jirau for flooding beyond its licensed quota into Mapinguari National Park. Plea testimony alleges about R$ 80 million in bribes tied to Santo Antonio; the accused dispute it.
Counter-view
The low auction tariff gave consumers cheaper energy. Later cost overruns suggest the bid may have been unrealistic (unverified). The bribery claims are allegations, not findings.

2007–2013 (TCU audits 2015–2018, ruling 2024)
e5-07
BNDES 'national champion' equity in JBS and Bertin

BNDES put billions into JBS and Bertin so Brazilian meatpackers could buy abroad. TCU auditors estimated losses between R$ 711 million and R$ 5.08 billion. In 2024 TCU found no debit in the special accounts, and BNDES says it made a profit.

Government
Lula 2, Dilma 1
What happened
BNDESPar put equity and debenture money into JBS to buy foreign meatpackers. A police and TCU table sums R$ 8.11 billion across the JBS group. BNDESPar rose to 33.40% of JBS.
Who got it
JBS/Friboi (Batista family). BNDES also bought 26.92% of Bertin in 2008 for R$ 2.5 billion.
Terms
Disputed. TCU technical staff estimated losses between R$ 711 million and R$ 5.08 billion. BNDES says the operations gave a R$ 2.8 billion positive result. In April 2024 TCU judged the special accounts regular and found no debit.
Mechanism
Discretionary BNDESPar equity purchases and debentures under the 'national champions' industrial policy.
Who paid
BNDES and the Treasury, which funds BNDES (see the BNDES/Treasury funding case).
What came after
The 2017 JBS plea deal (Joesley Batista) and police and TCU probes followed. JBS became the world's largest meat processor.
Counter-view
BNDES says the operations gave a R$ 2.8 billion positive result (O Antagonista). TCU Acórdão 628/2024-Plenário found 'inexistência dos débitos' and rejected both alleged losses (https://portal.tcu.gov.br/imprensa/noticias/compra-de-acoes-da-empresa-jbs-pela-bndes-participacoes-nao-gerou-debitos.htm).

e5-08
Eike Batista's EBX group (OGX, MMX, LLX/Prumo, OSX, MPX)

BNDES and the shipping fund backed Eike Batista's companies with billions in loans. The R$ 10.4 billion figure is what was approved, not what was paid out. OGX filed Latin America's largest judicial recovery in 2013, and no independent estimate of BNDES's loss was found.

Government
Lula 2, Dilma 1
What happened
BNDES and the Merchant Marine Fund (FMM) lent to Eike Batista's companies. About R$ 10.4 billion was approved, and about R$ 6 billion was contracted according to BNDES's president.
Who got it
Eike Batista's companies.
Terms
Eike told the CPI that BNDES had 'zero loss'. No independent loss estimate was found.
Mechanism
BNDES/BNDESPar credit and FMM financing.
Who paid
BNDES and so the Treasury. Part of Eike's personal assets was pledged to R$ 2.3 billion of BNDES loans.
What came after
OGX filed the largest judicial recovery in Latin America on 30 Oct 2013 (R$ 11.2 billion owed). OSX also filed. The OGX recovery closed on 2 Aug 2017.
Counter-view
Eike told the CPI do BNDES (17 Nov 2015) that BNDES money of about R$ 10 billion was only part of R$ 150 billion of total investment, and that BNDES had no loss (Congresso em Foco). BNDES president Coutinho said contracted loans were about R$ 6 billion, not R$ 10.4 billion.

    Not opened.

e5-09
Oi / Brasil Telecom merger ('supertele') and public-bank exposure

A 2008 decree changed the telecom plan so Oi could buy Brasil Telecom, and BNDES lent heavily to Oi. Oi collapsed in 2016 with R$ 65 billion of debt, then the largest judicial recovery in Brazil. State banks were among its biggest creditors.

Government
Lula 2 (merger), Dilma and Temer (collapse and recovery)
What happened
Decree 6.654 of 20 Nov 2008 changed the telecom concession plan, which allowed Oi (Telemar) to buy Brasil Telecom. BNDES lent R$ 2.569 billion to restructure Telemar's control. In 2004–2018 BNDES lent Oi R$ 14.129 billion in total.
Who got it
Telemar/Oi controllers (Andrade Gutierrez, La Fonte/Jereissati, funds), then Portugal Telecom in 2010–2014.
Terms
BNDES owned 16.89% of the Telemar holding (about 2013). Banco do Brasil reportedly financed R$ 4.3 billion of the Brasil Telecom purchase and private banks R$ 5.6 billion in notes (unverified).
Mechanism
Decree 6.654/2008 (new Plano Geral de Outorgas) plus BNDES credit. Sector sources say the plan change enabled the merger, but the exact article that removed the cross-ownership barrier was not confirmed.
Who paid
BNDES, Banco do Brasil and Caixa as creditors, and so their shareholder, the Union. Effects on consumers are not sourced.
What came after
Oi filed for judicial recovery on 20 Jun 2016 with R$ 65.38 billion of debt, then the largest in Brazil. The recovery closed on 14 Dec 2022, with about R$ 35 billion still owed. BNDES held over 30% of Oi in 2010 and 5.73% at end-2017, and as the only creditor in its class voted for the plan on 20 Dec 2017.
Counter-view
A law firm (BKBG) argued that the plan did not need to change for the merger (Baguete, https://www.baguete.com.br/public/noticias/fusao-oibrt-pgo-nao-precisaria-ser-alterado); not opened by the fact-check. The government line was that a national champion would bring scale and investment (not sourced).

    Cited page returned 403.

    Purpose was network expansion and school broadband, not the Brasil Telecom purchase.

e5-10
Votorantim Celulose (VCP) buys Aracruz and becomes Fibria

BNDES backed Votorantim's purchase of Aracruz with up to R$ 2.4 billion, and the price was set before Aracruz's US$ 2.1 billion derivative loss became public. Years later BNDES sold into the Suzano merger and received about R$ 8.5 billion in cash.

Government
Lula 2
What happened
BNDES agreed to put up to R$ 2.4 billion into the new VCP to enable the Aracruz purchase. VCP agreed to pay R$ 2.7 billion for the Lorentzen family's 28% of voting shares.
Who got it
The Votorantim group. The notes say Fibria ended with BNDESPar 34.9% and Votorantim 29.3%.
Terms
The price was kept as before Aracruz's derivative losses were disclosed, to avoid a fine of about R$ 1 billion under the shareholder agreement. Aracruz lost US$ 2.1 billion on dollar-linked derivatives. Preferred shareholders got about 17.8% below the prior price.
Mechanism
BNDES equity and credit support for a private merger.
Who paid
BNDES, as co-investor in the new company.
What came after
Fibria later merged with Suzano. At the March 2018 announcement BNDESPar would receive about R$ 8.5 billion in cash plus shares in the new company, and kept a minority stake.
Counter-view
BNDES president Coutinho defended the deal as preventing the companies from falling apart (Exame). The 2018 cash exit shows BNDES was a long-term shareholder who sold, which weakens the 'transfer' framing. Critics, including BMO Capital Markets, objected to BNDES's role.

    Announcement date 15 Mar 2018, not completion.

2008–2017
e5-11
Angra 3 nuclear plant contracts

Angra 3 is a long-delayed state nuclear plant whose assembly tender drew only two bidders from the same group of contractors. TCU found possible overpricing of R$ 96 million to R$ 314 million. Works stopped in 2015, and prosecutors allege kickbacks.

Government
Lula 2, Dilma 1 and 2, Temer
What happened
Works resumed in 2008 on the Eletronuclear (Eletrobras) plant, started in 1984. The original estimate was R$ 8.3 billion in 2008. Eletronuclear later estimated over R$ 25 billion including sunk costs.
Who got it
Electromechanical assembly tender GAC.T/CN-003/13 had only two bidders for two packages. The winning consortium included Camargo Corrêa, UTC, Andrade Gutierrez, Odebrecht, EBE and Queiroz Galvão. Financing came from BNDES loans (amount not found).
Terms
TCU found indications of overpricing of R$ 314 million (10.5%) in the tender, reduced after Eletronuclear's reply to R$ 96 million (3.2% of R$ 2.98 billion). The tender allowed bids up to 5% above budget.
Mechanism
Public tender under Lei 8.666/1993 by a state subsidiary. TCU imposed a ban of up to five years on cartel firms in the same ruling.
Who paid
Eletrobras and electricity consumers through the tariff.
What came after
Works halted in Oct 2015 and Eletronuclear sought partners. MPF said Eletronuclear's president Othon Luiz Pinheiro da Silva received R$ 4.5 million from consortium firms; he denied it.
Counter-view
TCU downgraded its finding from 'serious, halt' to 'serious, may continue' after Eletronuclear's reply (TCU ruling).

    Not re-checked: read from the cited page in the gaps research.

2008–2015
e5-12
Treasury funding of BNDES and PSI subsidised credit ('bolsa-empresário')

From 2008 the Treasury borrowed at market rates and lent to BNDES at cheaper rates, with R$ 441-455 billion going in by 2014. Economists disagree sharply about the cost, from R$ 44.5 billion to over R$ 200 billion depending on method. Defenders say the programme paid for itself.

Government
Lula 2, Dilma 1 and 2
What happened
The Treasury borrowed at market rates and lent to BNDES at the lower TJLP rate. Treasury injections into BNDES were R$ 441-455 billion in 2008–2014. Estimates of the subsidy cost differ by orders of magnitude.
Who got it
Mostly large firms (67.9% of disbursements in 2012 went to large firms, per Márcio Garcia), including the firms in the JBS, Oi, EBX and Votorantim cases. Named beneficiaries of PSI were not extracted.
Terms
Cost depends on method: R$ 11.6-15.9 billion in 2008–2010 (Mansueto Almeida), R$ 44.5 billion versus R$ 180.7 billion over four decades (Coutinho), R$ 205.6 billion in 2008–2022 (IBRE). PSI 2011 cost was R$ 11.8 billion (SPE) or R$ 19.2 billion (Treasury method).
Mechanism
Treasury bond issues on-lent to BNDES at TJLP, and PSI interest equalisation paid by the Treasury (PSI ended 31 Dec 2015).
Who paid
Taxpayers through public debt. R$ 27.2 billion of equalisation was owed to BNDES by mid-2015; the government paid R$ 15.1 billion in Dec 2015. TCU classed the deferred equalisation as a fiscal 'pedalada'.
What came after
PSI ended in 2015. No TCU ruling quantifying total PSI cost was found.
Counter-view
Luciano Coutinho (BNDES president) argues the cost is R$ 44.5 billion with BNDES's margin included, against R$ 180.7 billion gross, and claims a net fiscal benefit of +R$ 16.6 billion to +R$ 33 billion in two scenarios (https://pt.org.br/luciano-coutinho-o-bndes-e-o-tesouro-nacional/, advocacy site; figures via search summary). IBRE authors say the subsidy may have generated GDP, jobs and tax revenue that offset the cost, but give no estimate.
Figures
  • unverified Subsidy on Treasury transfers to BNDES, 2008–2010: R$ 11.6 billion to R$ 15.9 billion on R$ 236 billion transferred (BRL) (2010; Mansueto Almeida (Ipea economist) via Exame) source
    Exame page not opened. It is an Ipea economist's calculation, not an institutional Ipea study. Adding R$ 5 bn of PSI gives R$ 16.6-20.8 bn.
  • corrected Treasury transfers to BNDES since 2008: R$ 414 billion (the BNDES part of a total near 10% of GDP to public banks) (BRL) (2014; Márcio Garcia (PUC-Rio), Valor column) source
    Notes said R$ 414 bn went to public banks. It is the BNDES part.
  • verified 'Bolsa-empresário' cost: more than 0.6% of GDP (2014; Márcio Garcia) source
    Opinion column.

2009 onward
e5-13
Terra Legal: land regularisation in the Amazon (MP 458/2009, Lei 11.952/2009)

Terra Legal gave titles to people who occupied federal land in the Amazon, with small plots free and larger ones sold at the minimum table price. About 2 million hectares were titled by 2017. Audits found many beneficiaries who did not qualify, and critics called it the legalisation of land grabbing.

Government
Lula 2
What happened
Federal public land in the Amazon was titled to occupants, up to 15 fiscal modules and a maximum of 1,500 ha. TCU data cited by MPF show 28,331 titles covering 2,057,119.95 ha by 31 Dec 2017.
Who got it
Occupants of federal public land who were there before 1 Dec 2004 (article 5 IV).
Terms
Free up to one fiscal module. Above that, paid titles priced from the minimum value in the Incra reference table, adjusted for time, region and size. Resale is restricted for 10 years, and over 4 modules can be transferred after 3 years.
Mechanism
MP 458/2009 converted into Lei 11.952/2009. Later the cut-off date moved to 22 July 2008 (Lei 13.465/2017, from a search summary), and the 2,500 ha ceiling was added by a congressional amendment in that conversion bill, not in MP 759.
Who paid
The public land stock. A TCU audit found poor functioning and incentive to land grabbing.
What came after
In Nov 2015 the Chamber asked TCU for an audit. TCU preliminary: 712 beneficiaries (9%) did not meet requirements and 3,075 (38.87%) showed signs of not qualifying. Carta Capital cites TCU that about one third of the area donated in Rondônia (about 21,000 ha, about R$ 1 billion) is occupied irregularly (article of Dec 2021).
Counter-view
The notes found no government source. The ruralist view (Frente Parlamentar da Agropecuária) is that regularisation brings legal certainty and cuts deforestation (not sourced for this case). Free titles up to one module were the programme's stated social aim. The critics are the CPT, which called MP 458 a 'legalisation of land grabbing' (https://www.congressoemfoco.com.br/noticia/78037/pastoral-da-terra-publica-nota-de-repudio-a-mp-da-amazonia), TCU and MPF.
Figures
  • verified Titles issued to 31 Dec 2017: 28,331 titles, 2,057,119.95 ha (ha) (2017; TCU via MPF/PFDC nota técnica 8/2020) source
    The numbers come from the MPF note quoting TCU. Another source says almost 40,000 titles in 2012–2017 (not found).
  • unverified Titles per other source: almost 40,000 titles, 2012–2017 (2017; Notes) source
    Not found in any opened source; counting methods differ.
  • corrected Maximum title size: 1,500 ha (15 fiscal modules); later raised to 2,500 ha in Lei 13.465/2017 by congressional amendment (ha) (2009–2017; Lei 11.952 text; Pública) source
    Notes put the 2,500 ha ceiling in MP 759/2016. It came from an amendment (Dep. Nilson Leitão) in the conversion bill. Pública counts 2,376 properties and 6.3 m ha overlapping.
  • corrected Share of donated area occupied irregularly (Rondônia audit): about one third; about 21,000 ha, about R$ 1 billion (ha) (2021; TCU via Carta Capital) source
    Notes said 33% of the area, date unknown. It is the Rondônia audit only; article of Dec 2021.
  • verified Public land involved, per CPT: 67.4 million ha (ha) (2009; Comissão Pastoral da Terra) source
    Advocacy source.
  • verified TCU preliminary audit of beneficiaries (2015): 712 beneficiaries (9%) not meeting requirements; 3,075 (38.87%) with signs of not qualifying (2015; TCU via Agência Câmara) source

e5-14
Caixa buys a stake in Banco Panamericano

Caixa, a state bank, bought a third of Banco Panamericano in 2009. A fraud of billions came to light a year later. The banks' guarantee fund covered the first part, Caixa kept its stake, and it sold in 2021 at a reported profit.

Government
Lula 2, Dilma 1
What happened
In Dec 2009 Caixa (via Caixapar) bought 35.54% of Banco Panamericano for R$ 739.272 million. Fraud was found in Sep-Nov 2010. Caixa held 49% of voting capital.
Who got it
Grupo Silvio Santos received the price.
Terms
The Central Bank estimated a hole of R$ 2.5 billion. New management put the shortfall at R$ 4.3 billion. Prosecutors alleged balance-sheet fraud of at least R$ 3.8 billion in 2007–2010, and a court convicted seven former directors. The Central Bank's own inspector had flagged R$ 171.5 million of missing provisions on 12 Mar 2010, before the approval.
Mechanism
Equity purchase approved by the Central Bank on 15 Jul 2010. The remaining 30% of the price (R$ 221.8 million) was paid on 26 Jul 2010.
Who paid
The 2010–11 hole fell first on FGC, the banks' deposit-guarantee fund (first R$ 2.5 billion), and on the group. Silvio Santos pledged personal assets as collateral.
What came after
BTG Pactual bought 51% of the voting shares for R$ 450 million in 2011 and Caixa kept its stake. On 6 Apr 2021 CaixaPar agreed to sell its 49.2% of voting shares to BTG's Banco Sistema for about R$ 3.7 billion (R$ 11.42/share). The article reports a net profit of R$ 2.02 billion to Caixa but does not show how it is derived.
Counter-view
TCU Acórdão 987/2020 found the representation against the Central Bank unfounded and no irregular action established, though the MP de Contas argued the approval was rushed. Caixa ended with a gain, although the TCU representation called the deal 'ruinous' at the time.

e5-15
Belo Monte dam (Xingu, Pará)

Belo Monte was won in 2010 by a consortium led by state-owned firms and funded mostly by a R$ 22.5 billion BNDES loan. Costs rose from R$ 19 billion to about R$ 30 billion. Indigenous groups were not consulted first, and plea deals allege bribes of about 1% of contracts.

Government
Lula 2, Dilma 1
What happened
The concession went to Norte Energia, led by Chesf/Eletrobras, at the April 2010 auction. BNDES approved R$ 22.5 billion in Nov 2012 over 30 years, the biggest loan in its history.
Who got it
Norte Energia. The shares quoted in the notes (Eletronorte 19.98%, Eletrobras 15%, Chesf 15%, Petros 10%, Funcef 10%) are from June 2017, not 2010. Others held Belo Monte Participações (Neoenergia) 10%, Amazônia Energia (Cemig/Light) 9.77%, Aliança Norte (Vale/Cemig) 9%. Norte Energia was majority state-owned.
Terms
Winning bid R$ 77.97/MWh versus a ceiling of R$ 83 (6.02% discount); the subtitle of the source says 78.03. Cost estimates rose from R$ 19 billion at the auction to about R$ 26-30 billion. Economist Rogério Werneck argued a cost-reflective tariff was at least R$ 100/MWh (not verified).
Mechanism
A legislative decree (DL 788/2005) authorised works without prior Indigenous consultation, followed by an ANEEL auction and BNDES credit. The MPF suit filed in 2006 lost 2-1 at TRF-1 on 9 Nov 2011; judge Selene Almeida voted to annul the decree until Indigenous people were heard. ILO Convention 169 was ratified in 2003. The final merits outcome was not confirmed.
Who paid
Indigenous and riverine people (the Xingu basin has 24 ethnic groups in 30 Indigenous Lands), the Treasury through BNDES and state shareholders, and the environment.
What came after
Plea deals: Camargo Corrêa executives said 1% of the contract went to PT and PMDB politicians. Andrade Gutierrez's deal cites about R$ 150 million in bribes. A claim of R$ 15 million to Delfim Netto is denied. TCU opened an audit in June 2015 (result not found). The MPF said BNDES showed no evidence of viability and risk analysis (reported via WRM, not opened). Contractors asked for another R$ 1 billion (unverified).
Counter-view
The government and developers say there is no direct impact on Indigenous lands, but MPF disagrees (Outras Palavras guide). The plea-deal bribe claims are allegations from testimony. MDB denied them, Delfim Netto's lawyers say he did consulting work and paid taxes, and he told police he got R$ 240,000 from Odebrecht. The opposing bidder, Belo Monte Energia (Andrade Gutierrez, Furnas, Eletrosul), lost.

    Subtitle says 78.03; body says 77.97.
  • verified BNDES loan approved Nov 2012: R$ 22.5 billion over 30 years (78% of R$ 28.9 bn investment; includes bridge loans of R$ 1.1 bn + R$ 1.8 bn) (BRL) (2012; BNDES via Valor/IHU) source
    The notes' R$ 24.5 bn request could not be confirmed.
  • corrected Project cost estimates: R$ 19 billion at the auction; about R$ 26-30 billion later (R$ 28.9 bn BNDES figure) (BRL) (2011–2012; Norte Energia; TCU-approved budget; BNDES) source
    Notes said R$ 25 bn by 2012 and about R$ 31 bn. Those two figures were not found in the cited guide.
  • unverified Cost-reflective tariff argued by Werneck: at least R$ 100/MWh (BRL) (2010; Rogério Werneck (Estadão)) source
    Not opened.

e5-16
Cessão onerosa and the 2010 Petrobras capitalisation

In 2010 the government gave Petrobras the right to produce 5 billion barrels in the pre-salt without a bid, in return for about R$ 75 billion paid in Treasury bonds. Petrobras later said it overpaid and wanted compensation. It is a transfer between the state and its own company, so it is context for the study.

Government
Lula 2
What happened
Lei 12.276/2010 gave Petrobras the right to produce up to 5 billion barrels of oil equivalent in six Santos Basin pre-salt areas without a bid. The price was about R$ 75 billion (US$ 42.5 billion), around US$ 8.5 a barrel.
Who got it
Petrobras, which is state-controlled with private minority shareholders. The state raised its stake in exchange for the capital. This is a state-to-state-company transfer, not a plain private handover.
Terms
Petrobras later argued it overpaid because oil prices fell and the fields held more oil than assumed. It saw itself as a creditor and sought compensation.
Mechanism
Lei 12.276/2010, with payment in Treasury securities within the Petrobras capitalisation.
Who paid
The Union and Petrobras minority shareholders, through the capitalisation.
What came after
Surplus volumes were offered in a 6 Nov 2019 round: signing bonus R$ 69.96 billion against about R$ 106.5 billion expected. Only Búzios (Petrobras 90%, CNODC and CNOOC 5% each) and Itapu sold. Atapu and Sépia had no bids.
Counter-view
Petrobras's compensation claim is the main counter to the 'giveaway' framing: Petrobras says it paid too much. Critics such as Monitor Mercantil call it a giveaway (https://monitormercantil.com.br/denunciando-a-entrega-da-cess-o-onerosa/, not opened).
Figures
  • corrected Price paid by Petrobras: about R$ 75 billion (US$ 42-42.5 billion), average US$ 8.51-8.56 a barrel (BRL) (2010; Eixos; Brazil Journal; ANP) source
    Notes had US$ 42.5 bn = R$ 74.8 bn. Sources give small variations. Use about R$ 75 bn and about US$ 8.5/bbl.
  • corrected Estimated surplus volume above 5 bn barrels: 6 to 15 billion barrels (ANP/GCA, 2017); 6 to 10 billion (Brazil Journal 2019) (2017–2019; ANP/GCA; Adriano Pires) source
    Notes said 9.8-15.2 bn bbl, which is in neither opened page.
  • disputed Petrobras compensation claim: R$ 12-20 billion floated (2017); US$ 20-25 billion reported under Temer (BRL) (2017; Eixos; Brazil Journal) source
    Range R$ 12-20 bn to US$ 20-25 bn, different dates and reports.
  • unverified 2019 surplus-volume round signing bonus: R$ 69.96 billion (expected about R$ 106.5 billion) (BRL) (2019; ANP round of 6 Nov 2019) source
    Search listing only; page not opened by the fact-check.

e5-17
Pre-salt production-sharing regime (Lei 12.351/2010) and the Libra auction (2013)

Under the 2010 law the pre-salt moved to production sharing with Petrobras as operator. The Libra auction in 2013 drew a single bid at the minimum profit-oil share and a fixed R$ 15 billion bonus. The state kept control, so this is a counter-example.

Government
Lula 2, Dilma 1
What happened
Pre-salt areas moved from concession to production sharing. At the Libra auction on 21 Oct 2013 there was a single bid. A fixed signing bonus of R$ 15 billion was paid on 27 Nov 2013.
Who got it
Consortium: Petrobras 40% (operator), Shell 20%, Total 20%, CNPC 10%, CNOOC 10%. Petrobras bid 10% on top of its mandatory 30%. Eleven companies qualified; Exxon, BP and Chevron stayed out.
Terms
Profit oil to the Union was 41.65%, exactly the minimum in the notice. The bonus was a fixed fee, not bid up, and the auction was decided only on profit oil.
Mechanism
Lei 12.351/2010: production sharing, Petrobras as sole operator with at least 30%, and a Social Fund (art. 47). Lei 12.734/2012 redistributed royalties. Lei 13.365 of 29 Nov 2016 made Petrobras's operatorship a right of preference rather than an obligation.
Who paid
The Union forgoes some upside to the consortium; critics also say the bonus helped balance the 2013 accounts (not confirmed).
What came after
Part of the Libra area was returned in 2021 (not checked).
Counter-view
The government line was that the Union keeps ownership of the oil and Petrobras keeps control. The notes themselves call this a state retaining control, a counter-example rather than a handover.

e5-18
Sete Brasil (drilling-rig company for the pre-salt)

Sete Brasil was a state-backed company created to build 28 drilling rigs in Brazilian yards for Petrobras. It went into judicial recovery in April 2016 with R$ 14-18 billion of debt, and state banks, pension funds and a shipbuilding guarantee fund took the losses. The company blames the Petrobras order cut and Lava Jato.

Government
Lula 2, Dilma 1 and 2
What happened
Petrobras, state pension funds and banks capitalised a company to order 28 drilling rigs from new Brazilian yards under local-content rules. Petrobras later cut the order, with 14 given as the later outcome. Shareholder contributions were R$ 8.3 billion.
Who got it
The Sete Brasil shareholders and the Brazilian shipyards. Shareholders included Petrobras (over 5%), Petros, BTG, Funcef and Previ.
Terms
Local-content rules required rigs from new Brazilian yards. Funds kept investing after the schedule slipped, and the money was fully applied by 2016.
Mechanism
Private-law company funded by state pension funds, FI-FGTS and banks. Financing from BNDES was expected but the notes' claim that it was never released could not be confirmed.
Who paid
Pension-fund participants (Petros, Funcef, Previ, Valia), FI-FGTS (workers' FGTS money), the Union as the largest creditor (about two-thirds, about R$ 12 billion through state banks and funds), private banks and funds, and the shipbuilding guarantee fund FGCN.
What came after
Judicial recovery was filed on 29 Apr 2016. A Greenfield complaint (29 Dec 2019) put the loss borne by pension-fund participants at R$ 5.5 billion and sought R$ 16 billion in reparation.
Counter-view
Sete Brasil later sued Petrobras for R$ 36 billion, arguing Petrobras cancelled the rig orders and local-content policy caused the losses, and shareholders claimed about R$ 8 billion from Petrobras (search summary, BNamericas, not opened). A director blames Lava Jato (Congresso em Foco, not opened).

    Not re-checked: read from the cited page in the gaps research. By investor: Funcef about R$ 500 m; FI-FGTS about R$ 640 m invested; BTG provisioned 25%; Petros 29% cut in value.

e5-19
Payroll tax relief (desoneração da folha)

From 2011 many employers paid tax on revenue instead of payroll. The relief cost R$ 77.9 billion over 2012–2016 and peaked at R$ 25.2 billion in 2015. Government studies found small job gains for that cost.

Government
Dilma 1
What happened
Employers in chosen sectors paid a tax on revenue instead of on payroll. A 2011 pilot was widened in 2012–2015. The cost peaked at R$ 25.2 billion in 2015 and the cumulative cost for 2012–2016 was R$ 77.9 billion.
Who got it
Employers in the covered sectors. Part of Plano Brasil Maior (2011).
Terms
Government studies found small job effects, 30,000 to 132,634 jobs. FGV IBRE says the Treasury cost per job kept was R$ 4,800-5,600 a month against an average admission wage of R$ 1,700.
Mechanism
Tax-law change replacing the payroll contribution with a levy on revenue.
Who paid
Social security, compensated by the Treasury.
What came after
The relief was partly reversed in 2015–2016: cost fell to about R$ 14.5 billion in 2016.
Counter-view
Sector groups said the relief protected jobs and formalisation, and the government presented it as part of Plano Brasil Maior (sources not opened beyond the UFRGS article's note of intent).

e5-20
Airport concessions: Guarulhos, Viracopos, Brasília (2012), Galeão and Confins (2013)

In 2012 and 2013 the government auctioned six big airports and bids ran 66% to 673% above the minimum. Later, Viracopos went into judicial recovery and Galeão was handed back, with the public side absorbing the losses. The government had called the high bids a success.

Government
Dilma 1
What happened
Concessions of 20 to 30 years. The 6 Feb 2012 auction offered R$ 24.535 billion in total. The 22 Nov 2013 auction of Galeão and Confins offered R$ 20.839 billion in total.
Who got it
Guarulhos: Invepar/ACSA. Brasília: Inframerica. Viracopos: Aeroportos Brasil (Triunfo, UTC, Egis). Galeão: Odebrecht Transport with Changi. Confins: CCR 75%, Flughafen Zurich 24%, Munich 1%. Infraero kept 49% of each concessionaire (ITL; Galeão confirmed). Financing for Galeão and Confins was not established.
Terms
Premiums over the minimum were large: Guarulhos 373% (R$ 16.213 billion on a minimum of R$ 3.424 billion), Brasília 673% (R$ 4.5 billion on R$ 582 million), Viracopos 159% (R$ 3.821 billion), Galeão 293.9% (R$ 19.018 billion), Confins 66% (R$ 1.82 billion). The true Galeão and Confins minimums are uncertain: Exame's numbers and the premium maths do not agree.
Mechanism
Federal concession run by ANAC, with a fixed grant (outorga) plus a variable contribution. The Lei 13.448/2017 relicitation framework was later used for Galeão.
Who paid
Users and the public side bore the aftermath: forgone grant payments and Infraero's 49% exposure; BNDES was the main creditor of Viracopos. Odebrecht exited Galeão in 2017.
What came after
Viracopos: shareholders asked to return the concession in 2017 (year unconfirmed), the concessionaire filed for judicial recovery on 7 May 2018 (debt about R$ 2.88 billion, mostly BNDES) and the plan was approved on 14 Feb 2020, leading to Brazil's first airport relicitation. Galeão: Changi (51% after buying out Odebrecht in 2017) asked ANAC on 10 Feb 2022 to return it, claiming a R$ 7.5 billion imbalance; ANAC had denied the rebalancing. A 30 Mar 2026 auction reportedly gave Galeão to Aena for R$ 2.9 billion (not confirmed by the fact-check). Confins was not returned and got a R$ 60.7 million recomposition in Nov 2022.
Counter-view
The government framed the premiums as proof of competition and low taxpayer cost (bids about five times the minimum, EBC). The concessionaires blame the 2014–16 recession and Covid. ANAC held the demand shortfall was the concessionaire's risk. Critics read the big premiums as over-bidding (the winner's curse).

e5-21
MP 579/2012 (Lei 12.783/2013): electricity concession renewals

In 2012 the government forced early renewal of power concessions in return for lower tariffs and indemnities, cutting bills by more than 16%. The cost fell on the Treasury and Eletrobras. It runs against the usual handover pattern, because the state pushed prices down.

Government
Dilma 1
What happened
Generation and transmission concessions were renewed early for up to 30 years at lower revenue, with indemnity for unamortised assets and lower sector charges. The promised bill cut was more than 16%.
Who got it
Consumers and electro-intensive firms got lower tariffs. Concessionaires such as Cesp, Cemig and Copel resisted. This is a reverse case.
Terms
MME expected indemnities of about R$ 20 billion and Eletrobras expected about R$ 30 billion. Eletrobras later got about R$ 14 billion, then about R$ 20.8 billion after MP 591 (search summary).
Mechanism
MP 579/2012, converted into Lei 12.783/2013, with MP 591/2012 correcting transmission indemnities (investments up to 31 May 2000, paid over 30 years, IPCA).
Who paid
The Treasury (through CDE transfers) and Eletrobras. No consolidated Treasury figure was found. Eletrobras's 2012 loss was R$ 6.88 billion and its shares fell about 28% around the announcement (search summary only).
What came after
Critics say the cut was artificial and was followed by a 'tarifaço' in later years.
Counter-view
The opposing view is that the state forced renewal at below-market indemnities (Poder360 and Acende Brasil, via search summary, not opened).
Figures

  • verified Indemnities expected by MME: about R$ 20 billion (BRL) (2012; MME via InfoMoney) source
  • verified Indemnity expected by Eletrobras: about R$ 30 billion (BRL) (2012; Eletrobras via InfoMoney) source
  • corrected Added indemnity for transmission (MP 591/2012): R$ 10 billion (BRL) (2012; Agência Câmara (rapporteur Eduardo Cunha)) source
    Notes cited InfoMoney. The real source is Agência Câmara, 3 Dec 2012, and the correction is MP 591.

    Search summary only.
  • unverified Eletrobras 2012 loss and share fall: loss R$ 6.88 billion; shares about -28% around the announcement (BRL) (2012; Search summary) source
    Search summary only.

e5-22
Forest Code 2012 (Lei 12.651): amnesty for past deforestation

The 2012 Forest Code cut restoration duties for land cleared before 2008, by an estimated 29 million hectares. The Supreme Court upheld most of it in 2018 and said it is not a full amnesty, because penalties return if owners break the agreements.

Government
Dilma 1
What happened
The new Forest Code reduced the penalties and restoration duties for clearing before 2008. Soares-Filho and colleagues (Science, 2014) estimate it amnesties 29 million ha illegally cleared before 2008.
Who got it
Rural landowners, large and small, whose legal-reserve debts for pre-2008 clearing were reduced.
Terms
Restoration needed falls from 50 to 21 million ha (-58%), and 88 million ha remain legally clearable. Protection from penalties applies to infractions before 22 June 2008 if the owner joins the regularisation programme (PRA).
Mechanism
Lei 12.651/2012. On 28 Feb 2018 the STF upheld most of it: of 23 provisions, 18 were constitutional and 5 unconstitutional.
Who paid
The environment, the climate and downstream water users.
What came after
The STF held that it is not a true amnesty, because owners keep penalties if they fail the regularisation terms.
Counter-view
Tereza Cristina (Frente Parlamentar da Agropecuária) called the amnesty partial, with legal certainty for farmers and over 90% of producers in the rural registry (CAR). Agroicone's Rodrigo Lima said pre-2008 penalties are forgiven only if owners follow the 2012 rules. The Science authors say only 1% of cropland sits in areas needing restoration. Environmentalists such as ISA's Nurit Bensusan say it invites future deforestation (Câmara; Brasil Agro).
Figures
  • verified Illegal clearing amnestied (Science 2014): 29 million ha (ha) (2014; Soares-Filho et al., Science 344:363) source
    Confirmed through press reports (IHU, UFMG); the paper itself was not opened.
  • verified Land still legally clearable: 88 million ha (ha) (2014; Soares-Filho et al.) source
    Stated by IHU; the UFMG page does not give it.
  • verified Restoration needed: from 50 to 21 million ha (-58%) (ha) (2014; Soares-Filho et al. via UFMG) source
    Of the remaining 21 m ha, 78% is legal reserve and 22% is protected riparian areas (APP).
  • verified STF ruling (28 Feb 2018): 18 of 23 provisions constitutional, 5 unconstitutional; not a full amnesty (2018; STF via Agência Câmara) source
