Federal highway concessions, third round

In 2013–14 the government auctioned 30-year highway concessions with duplication duties in the first five years. Several concessionaires fell short, and relicitation started in 2021. Few figures could be confirmed, so this case needs a primary source such as an ANTT or TCU audit.

Government
Dilma 1
What happened
30-year toll concessions with duplication obligations in the first five years. Example: Concebra (BR-060/153/262, 1,176.5 km, Triunfo), won in 2014.
Who got it
Concessionaires such as Triunfo (Concebra). Financing via BNDES and a 15% internal return were not confirmed.
Terms
Low-toll-bid model. The notes' signing date of 31 Jan 2014, the five-year duplication duty and the BR-163 details come from a page that is now 404, so they are unconfirmed.
Mechanism
Federal toll concessions awarded by ANTT (Edital 004/2013 for Concebra).
Who paid
Users paid tolls without the promised works. BNDES exposure was not quantified.
What came after
Six concessions of 2013–14 struggled to meet the main duplication requirement. ANTT approved relicitation of BR-060/153/262 in 2021, split into Rota do Zebu (BR-262 MG, auctioned 2024) and Rota Sertaneja (BR-153/262 GO-MG). The remaining 211.6 km of BR-060/153 stays with Concebra in a TCU consensual-solution process (2026).
Counter-view
Not found. The usual argument for low-toll-bid auctions was not sourced. A primary source such as an ANTT or TCU audit of the third round is still needed.

Goias state government and Eletrobras (50.93% holder); Temer federal government

Celg distribution auctioned 30 Nov 2016, after a failed attempt in Aug 2016 with no buyers.

Enel. Eletrobras received R$1.065 bn because it held 50.93%. The proceeds went to the federal holding, not to Goias.

e6-01
End of Petrobras's mandatory pre-salt operator role (Lei 13.365/2016)

A 2016 law ended Petrobras's rule of operating every pre-salt block. Private and foreign oil firms can now operate them. Critics say the country loses control of its reserves; supporters say Petrobras lacked the capital.

Government
Temer
What happened
Lei 13.365/2016 revoked the rule in Lei 12.351/2010 that made Petrobras operator of all pre-salt blocks with at least 30% stake. Petrobras kept a right of first refusal (30 days to answer per block). If it takes the operator role it keeps at least 30%. The first auction under the new rules was held on 27 Oct 2017.
Who got it
Foreign and private oil companies able to operate pre-salt blocks. The bill is linked in the research notes to Sen. José Serra (PLS 131/2015); the ConJur page does not mention it.
Terms
No single price. There is a dispute over the value of the reserves ceded; no estimate was found in these sources.
Mechanism
Ordinary law amending the pre-salt production-sharing regime.
Who paid
Disputed. Critics (FUP, unions, nationalists) say the Treasury and the country lose control of the strategic reserve. Supporters say Petrobras lacked capital to operate everything.
What came after
Petrobras CEO Pedro Parente said Petrobras would use its preference right 'very selectively' (Carta Capital, confirmed). The 2017 auction went ahead after a federal injunction (26 Oct) was challenged by the AGU. A union challenged the law in court; no outcome found. Whether Petrobras took preference in only some blocks is unconfirmed (search says 2 of 4 blocks in the 3rd round).
Counter-view
Supporters: Temer said the old mandatory share was 'exagerada' (ConJur). The Senate bill rationale said Petrobras lacked capital to operate every block.
Figures
  • unverified Signature bonuses of the 27 Oct 2017 auction: about R$ 6.15 bn (BRL) (2017; Search result (Carta Capital fact-check)) source

Petrobras gas pipelines: NTS and TAG (and TBG)

Petrobras sold 90% of its NTS and TAG gas pipelines to private groups. NTS went to Brookfield for about US$ 5.2 bn (US$ 4.2 bn paid at closing). TAG went to Engie for about US$ 8.6 bn. The sales were part of a debt plan and a CADE settlement; unions say the country lost a strategic network.

Government
Temer (NTS), Bolsonaro (TAG)
What happened
Sale of 90% of NTS (Brookfield-led group), announced Sept 2016 and closed 4 Apr 2017. Sale of 90% of TAG (Engie-led group), announced 5 Apr 2019 and closed 13 Jun 2019. TBG (51%) was pledged in the 2019 CADE agreement with a deadline at the end of 2021, but was not completed.
Who got it
Brookfield group (NTS). Engie-led group (TAG).
Terms
NTS: US$ 5.19 bn headline (US$ 3.55 bn shares plus US$ 1.64 bn debt); US$ 4.23 bn actually paid at closing. TAG: about US$ 8.6 bn enterprise value (includes US$ 800 mn BNDES debt); Petrobras received R$ 33.5 bn. No undervaluation estimate was found.
Mechanism
Sale of subsidiary stakes under Petrobras's divestment plan and a CADE settlement (TCC) to end its dominance in the gas market.
Who paid
Unions (FUP) argue loss of a strategic network. Unnamed specialists cited by CUT/FUP say about US$ 1 bn a year in revenue is lost; this is unconfirmed and comes from an advocacy source.
What came after
Not traced beyond the sale. TBG sale required by CADE was not completed (Eixos search result only).
Counter-view
Petrobras argued the sales were for debt reduction and for opening the gas market, as CADE required. CUT/FUP frame it as 'delivering pipelines to foreigners'.

e6-03
Petrobras import-parity pricing (PPI) and dividends to private shareholders

Petrobras priced fuel at import parity from 2016 until May 2023, and paid very large dividends, especially in 2022 (R$ 215.7 bn). The Union received about R$ 79 bn of that. The case is about who gained from the payouts, not a sale of an asset.

Government
Temer, Bolsonaro, Lula 3 (to May 2023)
What happened
Petrobras priced fuels at import parity (PPI). The FUP says this began in 2016 under Temer and was kept by Bolsonaro (labor source, snippet only). On 12 May 2023 CEO Prates confirmed a new formula would replace it; the board approved a new strategy on 15 May 2023. In the PPI years Petrobras paid large dividends, mostly in 2022.
Who got it
Shareholders: the Union (largest single receiver), BNDES/BNDESPar, Brazilian institutions and foreign holders.
Terms
Dividends 2022: R$ 215.7 bn announced, with Brent averaging US$ 101.19. Union got about R$ 79 bn. Union plus BNDES/BNDESPar hold 36.6% of capital.
Mechanism
Company pricing policy and dividend policy. No new law.
Who paid
Fuel consumers (import-parity prices); disputed. The Union is itself the biggest dividend receiver, so dividends are not purely a transfer to private owners.
What came after
New pricing formula announced May 2023 (uses client alternative cost and marginal value). Critics say the formula is not published. Ineep says prices became more stable in 2023-24. In 2023 the payout rule changed from 60% to 45% of free cash flow (snippet).
Counter-view
The Union is the largest dividend receiver, so the open questions are the share paid to non-Union holders and whether the payout crowded out investment. (Money Times / InfoMoney / BP Money, as in the notes.)
Figures
  • unverified Dividends announced for 2022: 215.7 bn (BRL) (2022; InfoMoney) source
    Not covered by the fact-check round; taken from the gap research notes.
  • unverified Union share of 2022 dividends: about 79 bn (BRL) (2022; InfoMoney) source
    Not covered by the fact-check round; taken from the gap research notes.

2016–2020
e6-04
Early renewal of Vale railway concessions (EFVM, EFC) and Rumo Malha Paulista

The government renewed Vale's two big railway concessions early, without a new auction, and renewed Rumo's Malha Paulista to 2058. The payment owed to the state changed hugely with the valuation method, from negative to over R$ 14 bn more. The final grant was R$ 11.8 bn and a new settlement was still being worked out in 2026.

Government
Temer (process), Bolsonaro (TCU approval)
What happened
Extension of the 1997 Vale concessions (Vitória-Minas, EFVM; Carajás, EFC) without a new auction. TCU approved the renewals on 29 Jul 2020. Investment commitments: R$ 8.5 bn (EFVM) and R$ 9.8 bn (EFC), plus Fico R$ 2.73 bn. Rumo's Malha Paulista: TCU Acórdão 2.876/2019 (27 Nov 2019), extension to 31 Dec 2058, addendum signed 27 May 2020.
Who got it
Vale (EFVM, EFC) and Rumo (Malha Paulista).
Terms
The grant (outorga) swung with the valuation method. Vale waived a negative EFC value of about R$ 2.1 bn; EFVM ranged from about R$ 1.52 bn to R$ 3.28 bn after TCU recalculation. TCU staff recalculation with Vale's 2017 EBIT/ROL would add about R$ 14.17 bn on EFC and over R$ 15 bn in total. Vale proposed R$ 639 mn at an 11.04% discount rate; at the Selic of 2.25% that would be about R$ 15.47 bn. Final outorga R$ 11.8 bn; total commitments R$ 24.7 bn to 2057.
Mechanism
Early (anticipated) renewal clause under Lei 13.448/2017 (confirmed by a typo on the TCU page, which says 'Lei 13.488'), with the grant valued by the regulator ANTT.
Who paid
The Treasury (value of the grant); competitors lose the chance for a new bid.
What came after
Repactuation: Dec 2024 protocol of about R$ 17 bn including R$ 11.3 bn of outorgas; the Secex Consenso at TCU failed in Aug 2025; as of 13 Mar 2026 a deal of about R$ 11 bn was near (about R$ 4 bn paid, about R$ 7 bn to go) plus about 400 km of Fico. 'Terms' were under discussion on 1 Apr 2026 (agenciainfra).
Counter-view
Vale and ANTT argue the ore price is internal and that other operators' cost of capital would overstate the value. TCU staff argued the opposite.

    Notes said EFC grant ran from about R$ 14 bn (CADE method) to about R$ 200 mn (ANTT method). The R$ 200 mn is unconfirmable; the negative R$ 2.1 bn and the TCU staff +R$ 14.17 bn are confirmed.

e6-05
Ferrogrão and the cut of Jamanxim National Park (Lei 13.452/2017)

A 2017 law cut about 862 ha out of Jamanxim National Park to make room for the Ferrogrão grain railway. The STF suspended it, then validated it in May 2026. Defenders say the law also added over 51,000 ha of other protected land.

Government
Temer (law); Lula 3 (STF ruling)
What happened
MP 758/2016 and Lei 13.452/2017 removed about 862 ha from Jamanxim National Park for the Ferrogrão (EF-170) railway and BR-163 right of way. PSOL filed ADI 6553; the STF suspended the law (injunction 2021) and sent the case to conciliation (hearing 2 Jun 2023). Judgment began Oct 2025 (Dino vista); postponements 8-9 Apr 2026; the STF validated the law on 21 May 2026 with 7 votes in the majority (Fachin dissented, Dino partly diverged, Cármen Lúcia did not vote).
Who got it
Grain trading companies and exporters via the railway concession. The model was never auctioned (not in sources).
Terms
No price. Land taken out of a protected area.
Mechanism
Provisional measure converted into law reducing a conservation unit.
Who paid
Indigenous peoples in the region (INESC factsheet) and the park area.
What came after
STF validated the law in May 2026, saying there is no environmental regression.
Counter-view
The same MP/law would add over 51,000 ha of APA Tapajós to the park, so net protected area rises (ConJur). The case is told one-sidedly if only the 862 ha cut is cited.
Figures

e6-06
Land regularization: Lei 13.465/2017 and PL 2633/2020 ('PL da grilagem')

Lei 13.465 (2017) made it easier to get title to federal land, and the 2021 'PL da grilagem' would have extended it. The STF is judging the law and leans toward partial invalidation. Reports say over half of 11 million ha of untitled parcels overlapped forests where titling is banned.

Government
Temer (law); Bolsonaro era (PL 2633)
What happened
MP 759/2016 and Lei 13.465 (July 2017) broadened regularization of rural and urban land, including federal land. The PGR (Janot, filed late Aug 2017, then Raquel Dodge) filed ADI 5.771 arguing unconstitutionality. PL 2633/2020 was approved by the Câmara on 3 Aug 2021 (296 to 196) and sent to the Senate; critics say art. 38 and the 22 Jul 2008 cutoff amount to a continuing amnesty. Law 11.952/2009 allows no-bid titling up to 2,500 ha for occupations up to Dec 2011; the original cap was 1,500 ha and Lei 13.465/2017 raised it to 2,500 ha.
Who got it
Occupiers of federal public land, including large holders; critics say it favours land concentration. The MST opposes the title-deed model.
Terms
No price; free or low-cost titling. Free titling up to 1 fiscal module (100 ha in the Amazon); faster track up to 4 modules (400 ha).
Mechanism
Law and provisional measure regularizing occupations after the fact.
Who paid
Public land (the Union) and traditional communities.
What came after
STF: ADIs 5771/5787/5883/6787 are in the virtual plenary. Toffoli voted on 6 Dec 2024; Dino diverged (partial upholding, vista May 2025); Cármen Lúcia followed; a Toffoli complement about Aug 2026 aligns with Dino. No final outcome found. PL 2633 Senate status is in conflict: 'prejudicada/encerrada' vs 'aguardando apreciação' on the Congress page.
Counter-view
Defenders say titling reduces conflict and gives smallholders legal security; the STF majority trend is partial, not full, invalidation.

2017
e6-07
Renca decree: opening a copper reserve to mining

A 2017 decree closed the Renca copper reserve, about 4.7 million ha in the Amazon, to open it to mining. A court suspended it and President Temer revoked it in September 2017. No mining rights are known to have been issued.

Government
Temer
What happened
In Aug 2017 a decree extinguished the Renca (National Reserve of Copper and Associates, created 1984) to open it to mineral exploration. The area is about 47,000 km2, about 4.7 million ha, in Amapá and Pará (about 2.3 million ha in Amapá); gold is the main mineral, plus iron, manganese and tantalum. Decree 9.142 (22 Aug) was replaced by 9.147 (28 Aug), which kept the extinction but excluded Indigenous and conservation areas. A federal court in Brasília (Judge Spanholo, 21st Federal Court) suspended it on 29 or 30 Aug. Decree 9.159 (signed 25 Sep, published 26 Sep) revoked 9.147.
Who got it
Prospective private mining companies. No concession was granted in the sources; the 'transfer' was the opening of the area to private mining rights.
Terms
No price.
Mechanism
Presidential decree.
Who paid
Indigenous and conservation areas, forest. Reversed before any concession was found.
What came after
Reversed. The case shows that mass mobilization and a court stopped a transfer. Whether any mining right was ever issued is not known. One snippet says the September decree revoked 9.147 but kept the extinction (oeco).
Counter-view
The government argued the decree only ended the reserve status and that protected areas inside Renca stayed untouched (specific laws still applied).
Figures
  • corrected Renca area: about 47,000 km2 (about 4.7 million ha) (2017; Agência Brasil) source
    Notes said about 4 million ha (the IHU page says 'more than 4 million ha'). Fact-check corrected to about 4.7 million ha. Decree numbers corrected: 9.142 first, 9.147 second, 9.159 revoked 9.147.

Copagaz / Nacional Gás Butano / Itaúsa. Under the CADE remedy, NewCo 1 goes to NGB and NewCo 2 to Fogás.

e6-09
Garimpo expansion, Yanomami crisis and PL 191/2020 (mining on Indigenous land)

Illegal gold mining on Yanomami land grew sharply from 2018: mining-related deforestation rose 309% by 2022 and malaria cases more than doubled. A bill to legalise mining on Indigenous land (PL 191) was never passed and was withdrawn in 2023. The Lula government declared a health emergency in January 2023.

Government
Bolsonaro; emergency response under Lula 3
What happened
Illegal mining on Yanomami land: Hutukara estimated about 20,000 miners (ISA 2021: 21,000). Mining-related deforestation grew 309% between Oct 2018 and Dec 2022 (1,236 to 5,053.82 ha). Malaria cases rose from 9,908 (2018) to 21,883 (2021). PL 191/2020 (sent Feb 2020) would regulate mining, oil, gas and hydropower on Indigenous lands. The Câmara approved urgency on 9 Mar 2022 (279 to 180/190). Ibram opposed (note of 15 Mar 2022). The bill was withdrawn on 29 May 2023.
Who got it
Illegal gold miners and their financiers; no fiscal benefit to the State.
Terms
No price. No fiscal benefit.
Mechanism
Weak enforcement; a bill to legalise mining on Indigenous land (not passed).
Who paid
Yanomami lives and health, rivers, forest. Bolsonaro's government at one point called the crisis exaggerated ('exagero', Mourão; DOL).
What came after
Federal government declared a national public-health emergency (ESPIN, Portaria GM/MS 28, 20 Jan 2023) and began an emergency response. Hutukara's report says the Uraricoera river holds 52% of the mining-degraded area; Congresso em Foco says over 45% (2020 data).
Counter-view
Miners' associations and bill sponsors argued regulated mining on Indigenous land would reduce illegal garimpo and bring royalties to communities.
Figures

    Notes gave only '309%'; the period and hectare values were added by the fact-check.

BR Distribuidora privatization (now Vibra Energia)

Petrobras sold its fuel distributor BR Distribuidora in two share offerings, in 2019 and 2021, raising about R$ 20 bn in total. The buyer was the open market, so no single owner took control. The price looked market-based. Critics say Vibra stations charged more, but that rests on a single week of data.

Government
Bolsonaro
What happened
2019: Petrobras sold about 350 million shares at R$ 24.50 (R$ 8.6 bn) and went from 71.25% to 41.25% (37.5% with the supplementary lot, R$ 9.6 bn). 30 Jun 2021: it sold the remaining 37.5% at R$ 26 per share (R$ 11.36 bn) and left the capital.
Who got it
Dispersed market through public share offerings; no controlling owner. The company was renamed Vibra Energia (announced 19 Aug 2021; search only).
Terms
Market-priced offerings; no undervaluation estimate was found.
Mechanism
Follow-on share offerings registered with CVM, no control premium.
Who paid
Critics reported that ex-BR stations (Vibra) sold the most expensive gasoline in several capitals. This rests on one week of ANP data (10-16 Jul 2022) and critical framing.
What came after
Petrobras later discussed retaking part of the brand/stake (Money Times, Eixos).
Counter-view
Vibra says pump prices are set by individual stations (Brasil de Fato page). The sale rationale was debt reduction and a focus on pre-salt.

e6-11
Federal airport concession rounds 2019-2022 (5th, 6th, 7th) and the returns of Viracopos and Galeão

Three airport auctions from 2019 to 2022 handed dozens of airports to private groups for 30 years. Bidders paid many times the minimum price, but the 7th round had a single bidder for Congonhas. Earlier-round concessions such as Viracopos and Galeão were handed back, and risk returned to the public side.

Government
Bolsonaro (all three auctions); Lula 3 (relicitações)
What happened
5th round (2019): 12 airports in 3 blocks. 6th round (2021): 22 airports. 7th round (18 Aug 2022): SP-MS-PA-MG block with Congonhas, Norte II, and a General Aviation block (11 airports plus). Private concessions carried 77.5% of passengers in 2011-2021, rising to 91.6% with the 7th round.
Who got it
5th round: Aena (Nordeste), Zurich Airport (Sudeste), Consórcio Aeroeste (Centro-Oeste). 6th: CCR (Sul block, Central block), Vinci (Norte). 7th: Aena (SP-MS-PA-MG, sole bidder), XP Infra IV FIP (General Aviation, no competition), Consórcio Novo Norte (Norte II). Financing of bidders is not published. CCR (6th round winner) was a Lava Jato target and had paid about R$ 800 mn under two leniency agreements (R$ 81.5 mn with São Paulo prosecutors in Nov 2018; R$ 750 mn with Paraná prosecutors in Mar 2019) before bidding.
Terms
5th round total R$ 2.377 bn against a minimum of R$ 219 mn (average ágio 986%), investment promise R$ 3.5 bn over 30 years. 6th round R$ 3.3 bn (ágio about 3,822%), investment R$ 6.1 bn. 7th round: SP-MS-PA-MG R$ 2.45 bn, ágio 231.02%. The large ágios can be read two ways: low reserve prices set by the state, or bidders pricing risk and investment duties. No independent valuation was opened.
Mechanism
ANAC auctions at B3 for 30-year concessions with initial outorga plus annual variable fees; relicitação under Lei 13.448/2017.
Who paid
Taxpayers carry the legal and TCU process of the 2010-2014 round hand-backs (Viracopos, Galeão, Natal) after demand fell. Galeão's return was announced 10 Feb 2022.
What came after
Viracopos: relicitação started 2020; the TCU deadline of 2 Jun 2025 passed unmet; an autocomposição commission was created Oct 2025; talks still open on 10 Jun 2026 (agenciainfra snippets). Galeão (Changi): TCU approved a repactuação in Jun 2025; new-concession bids on 24 Mar 2026 from Aena, Zurich and RIOgaleão (snippets). 7th-round contracts signed 29 Mar 2023 (unverified). No opened source on the winning bid of the 2026 Galeão round.
Counter-view
The defenders' view is that the ágio is paid up front for risk and investment duties. The sole-bidder 7th round shows limited competition.

Federal road concessions 2019-2025 (Dutra 2021, relicitação and repactuação)

Federal road concessions were auctioned with toll discounts as the main bid. By mid-2023, 16 of 24 federal concessions were in hand-back or serious imbalance. The government then renegotiated terms to unlock new investment.

Government
Bolsonaro (Dutra); Lula 3 (2023-25 rounds, repactuação)
What happened
Dutra / Rio-Santos auction on 29 Oct 2021: 625.8 km, 30 years. Ministry balance 2023-24: 9 auctions, about 4,300 km, more than R$ 111 bn of potential investment. On 28 Jul 2023, of 24 federal concessions, 16 were in devolution/relicitação or had serious imbalance; only Rota do Oeste had reached an agreement under the 2017 law.
Who got it
CCR won Dutra with the maximum 15.31% toll discount; EcoRodovias offered 10.6%. Only two bidders were admitted.
Terms
Dutra: outorga R$ 1.77 bn, investment about R$ 14.83 bn. Paraná lot 3 won with about 70% off the average toll. A new policy redirects outorga into works.
Mechanism
ANTT auctions with toll discount (and outorga) as the bid; relicitação by Lei 13.448/2017; the 2023 'otimização' program (Portaria 848, Aug 2023).
Who paid
Road users (tolls, delayed works on stalled stretches), the state in renegotiation, and lenders. Causes given: recession, pandemic (about R$ 250 mn loss) and Lava Jato financing problems. Whether aggressive discounts caused the failures is not stated in the opened article; analysts often claim it, unverified here.
What came after
Four advanced negotiations could unlock about R$ 20 bn, and at least R$ 60 bn more if the other 12 agree; terms capped at 15 years, investments in the first 3 years, lower tariffs. 14 contracts joined the optimization program; TCU approved 3. 2025 cycle: 13 auctions, about 6,200 km, R$ 135 bn (agenciainfra snippet, unverified). First relicitação under Lei 13.448 on BR-040 in 2024 (unverified).
Counter-view
The Ministry's own balance is used as the positive case (Tribuna PR); it is not an independent source.

Distrito Federal government, with BNDES modelling the sale
What happened
CEB's distribution unit auctioned 4 Dec 2020. CEB risked caducidade; liquidating it could have cost the DF about R$1 bn (the article's own estimate).
Who got it
Bahia Geracao (Neoenergia, controlled by Iberdrola). CPFL bid R$2.508 bn and Equatorial opened at R$1.485 bn.

Who paid
Not stated.
What came after

A court injunction from the night before was lifted by STJ president Humberto Martins, who found that the sale did not need prior enabling legislation. The STF (Nunes Marques) kept an injunction.

e6-13
Orçamento secreto (relator amendments, RP9)

Relator amendments, called the secret budget, moved tens of billions of reais in 2020-22 to recipients chosen by Congress leaders, with little traceability. The STF ruled the practice unconstitutional in December 2022 (6-5). Estimates of the paid amount range from about R$ 28 bn to R$ 30 bn.

Government
Bolsonaro, with Congress (Lira, Pacheco) controlling indications
What happened
Relator amendments (RP9) were decided by the budget rapporteur with no set criteria; the visible name is the rapporteur's, not the requesting member. This is a channel through which public budget flowed to private contractors via politically picked recipients, not a sale of an asset.
Who got it
Health took 57.4% of the R$ 28.79 bn paid, then urbanism 11.53%, social assistance 5%, education 4.68%. Six parties (PP, PL, PSD, MDB, União, Republicanos) hold 81% of the 2022 executed amount attributed to party indications; external users (non-members who sponsored) controlled about 31%. Lira tops the 2022 list (R$ 134.5 mn indicated). An NGO (ICA) received R$ 98 mn in 2020-2022. Data cover Jan-Oct 2022 only with manual matching, so are partial. PL, PP and Republicanos took R$ 2.86 bn in 2020-2021.
Terms
Amounts are given as ranges because sources differ (see figures).
Mechanism
Budget amendments with no traceability. Rosa Weber suspended execution in Nov 2021 (upheld 8-2). On 19 Dec 2022 the STF ruled RP9 unconstitutional 6-5 (ADPFs 850, 851, 854, 1014).
Who paid
The public budget, through lost traceability. Proven losses are not stated here.
What came after
The 2023 budget reserved R$ 19.4 bn for relator amendments, and Congress passed a stopgap resolution days before the ruling. A merits decision on 19 Dec 2024 declared the practices incompatible with the Constitution; RP8/RP9 execution partly resumed; R$ 12.6 bn of unpaid items were paid in 2025 (snippets, unverified; the Senate note was unreadable).
Counter-view
Congress argues the amendments are its legitimate budget prerogative. The criticism is lack of traceability, not that congressional amendments exist.

Codevasf: relator amendments and contracts

Codevasf, a regional development agency led by Centrão nominees, handled billions in relator amendments in 2020-22. Audits found overpayments of a few million reais, small against the money routed. The main issue is traceability.

Government
Bolsonaro; Centrão-nominated leadership
What happened
R$ 7.3 bn passed through Codevasf in 2020-21, of which R$ 3.6 bn were relator amendments. In 2022, R$ 610 mn of relator amendments were approved, raised to R$ 1.2 bn after a May portaria; the total went from R$ 2.1 bn to R$ 2.7 bn (about 44% relator amendments). In 2021 the budget started at R$ 1.3 bn and rose to R$ 3.5 bn; about one third had no identified author.
Who got it
Contractors such as Construservice, Engefort and JT. President Marcelo Moreira Pinto was a PP nominee (Lira, Ciro Nogueira per CUT, a partisan source). Operation Odoacro (PF, 20 Jul 2022): Construservice had at least R$ 140 mn reserved since 2019; 16 search warrants.
Terms
Auditors could not opine on a R$ 2.7 bn balance (Russell Bedford audit via Folha, relayed by CUT). Loss R$ 358 mn in 2021.
Mechanism
Budget routing via relator amendments and public works contracts.
Who paid
The public budget. Proven overpayments are small (millions) against the billions routed; the case is mainly about traceability and loss of control.
What came after
CGU found R$ 7.3 mn of damage on asphalt in 10 of 12 states. TCU found R$ 7.8 mn overpayment in 12 contracts (a drainage item never built) among 23 contracts with Engefort, Construservice and JT (11 Aug 2023), without a link to the orçamento secreto in the article.
Counter-view
Codevasf says appointments follow technical requirements. No wrongdoing has been established against named politicians in the opened sources.

Marco Legal do Saneamento (Lei 14.026/2020) and the CEDAE auctions

A 2020 federal law forced sanitation services to go to bidding. Rio's CEDAE auction in April 2021 raised about R$ 22.7 bn for three of four blocks, more than double the minimum. The costs fall on tariff payers over the concession period.

Government
Bolsonaro; CEDAE auction by Rio de Janeiro state
What happened
The law (July 2020) requires bidding for sanitation services previously handed to state companies without competition. CEDAE auction on 30 Apr 2021: three of four blocks sold for about R$ 22.7 bn in grant payments against a minimum of R$ 10.6 bn (ágio 113.2%).
Who got it
Aegea consortium: Block 1 (R$ 8.2 bn, 103.13% premium) and Block 4 (about R$ 7.2 bn, about 188%). Iguá: Block 2 (R$ 7.286 bn). Block 3 (minimum R$ 908 mn) had no winner.
Terms
The premium over the minimum looks high, but the grant is paid up front and recovered through tariffs. No independent valuation was found.
Mechanism
Federal framework law plus state concession auctions.
Who paid
Tariff payers and service quality over the concession period; critics (Outras Palavras) claim hidden risks. A 2025 sector review (acionista.com.br) discusses the aftermath; details were not extracted.
What came after
Aftermath not traced in detail.
Counter-view
Government and the industry cite investment and universalization targets; critics (Outras Palavras, academic) raise tariff and public-control concerns. Neither was independently opened in the fact-check.

Cedae (Rio de Janeiro) water and sewage concessions

Rio's water and sewage service was auctioned in 2021 for R$22.7 bn, more than double the minimum. Four years later the buyers were fighting over payments and tariffs, and a conciliation deal was suspended by a court.

Government
Rio de Janeiro state government; BNDES designed the model
What happened
Water and sewage concession of the Rio metropolitan region in four blocks, auctioned 30 Apr 2021 on B3. Cedae stays as bulk water seller; about 30 municipalities stayed out.
Who got it
Block 1: Aegea (R$8.2 bn). Block 2: Iguá (R$7.286 bn). Block 4: Aegea (R$7.2 bn). Block 3 had no winner and was re-auctioned to Aguas do Brasil for about R$2.2 bn (InvestNews snippet, unverified).
Terms
R$22.7 bn total for three blocks against a R$10.6 bn minimum outorga. Block 1 minimum R$4.036 bn (agio 103.13%); Block 2 minimum R$3.172 bn (agio 129.68%); Block 4 agio about 188%. 35-year contracts, about R$30 bn of investment, about 13 million people.
Mechanism
Concession auction. BNDES was structurer, not financier, as far as found.
Who paid
Not stated beyond tariff effects below.
What came after
Iguá owed a final outorga installment of R$1.8 bn due early Feb 2025, sought arbitration to deposit only R$828 million citing losses and social-tariff counts above the tender estimates, and the state regulator Agenersa denied suspension ('calote' is the outlet's word). In Oct 2025 a conciliation term cut the wholesale water cost by 24.13% over the sewage-coverage gap; Cedae withdrew in Dec 2025 and the TJ-RJ suspended the agreement. A 7.10% rebalancing increase was approved; the Feb 2026 adjustment was 9.75% (Block 1) and 8.09% (Block 4). Aguas do Rio serves about 10 million people in 27 municipalities. TCE-RJ suspension dates, and 10.97%/15.89% increases from Dec 2025 that conflict with the above, are unverified.
Counter-view
Supporters read bids at more than twice the minimum as competition. Critics read them as a promise that tariffs or renegotiation would have to pay for it.

The loss-making distributor CEEE-D was sold in 2021 for a symbolic R$100,000 to the only bidder, along with about R$3.5 bn of debt. The state avoided losing the concession; critics point to job cuts and poor service after the 2024 storm.

Government
Rio Grande do Sul state government (Governor Leite)
What happened
The rump distributor left after the 1997 split, sold at an auction in 2021. Contract signed 8 Jul 2021.
Who got it
Equatorial, the only bidder. CPFL did not bid, citing risk and return.
Terms
R$100,000 (symbolic). Analysts assumed about R$3.5 bn of debt; ICMS debt alone exceeded R$3.3 bn. Equatorial must invest R$1.6 bn. The 2015 renewal to 2045 depended on quality indicators that CEEE-D missed two years running. Analysts put value at 1.5x-2x RAB.

Share sale. No BNDES money found.
Who paid
The state shed the debt and the caducidade risk. Critics cite layoffs and outsourcing.

Equatorial serves about 1.7 million consumers in 72 municipalities. After the 16 Jan 2024 storm, Governor Leite threatened the concession. The Porto Alegre council opened a CPI. A May 2021 court suspension of the share sale (Sul21 snippet) and its outcome are unverified.

Leite says private firms should deliver the service and the state could not fund the needed investment. The sale was needed to stop a caducidade risk (Brazil Journal).

RLAM refinery (Bahia) sold to Mubadala / Acelen

Petrobras sold the Bahia refinery RLAM to Abu Dhabi's Mubadala for US$ 1.65 bn in 2021. Critics say it was worth about twice that. The audit court approved the sale, and a CGU audit found weak valuation methods. Petrobras has since talked about buying it back.

Government
Bolsonaro (buyback talks under Lula 3)
What happened
Sale of the Landulpho Alves refinery (RLAM, Mataripe, Bahia) to Mubadala Capital (Abu Dhabi), operating as Acelen. Concluded Nov 2021. It ended Petrobras's regional refining monopoly and created a private regional monopoly in Bahia.
Who got it
Mubadala Capital (Abu Dhabi), operator Acelen.
Terms
US$ 1.65 bn signed (closing announcement said US$ 1.8 bn subject to adjustment). In the 2021 TCU case, Petrobras's own base scenario was US$ 3.04 bn, so the price was about 45% below it. INEEP (union-linked think tank) estimates US$ 3-4 bn, 'half price'. TCU authorized the sale in 2021 and rejected challenges; CADE approved without restrictions. A CGU audit (Jan 2024) found weak valuation method but did not conclude there was a clear economic loss.
Mechanism
Competitive sale of an asset by a state company, under a CADE commitment, with TCU and CADE review.
Who paid
Bahia buyers of fuel (private regional monopoly), and the Treasury if the price was too low. CADE opened an investigation into Acelen for alleged price discrimination against Bahia buyers of gasoline A and diesel S10; Acelen accuses Petrobras of the reverse. The CADE probe was opened in 2022 (a Brasil Energia headline says archived, page not opened). A current Bahia gasoline price series was not found.
What came after
Petrobras resumed talks to buy the refinery back: due diligence reported Jul 2024 (Reuters), and on 24 Mar 2026 Petrobras reaffirmed interest in a CVM letter, with no deal. A Mubadala partnership proposal was disclosed on 22 Dec 2023. Sindipetro-BA appealed to CADE.
Counter-view
Petrobras says it followed its rules, TCU found compliance, due diligence was done, and goals were debt reduction, the CADE commitment and pre-salt capital (Bahia Notícias 287859).

e6-17
Eletrobras privatization (capitalization)

Eletrobras was privatized in June 2022 by a share offering at R$ 42 per share, cutting the Union to about 37% of capital. A TCU minister said the plants were undervalued by tens of billions of reais, but the court majority approved. The law also forced the contracting of 8 GW of gas plants, which critics say consumers will pay for.

Government
Bolsonaro
What happened
Law 14.182/2021 (from MP 1031) turned Eletrobras into a corporation by a capital increase and share offering that diluted the Union. Offer priced on 9 Jun 2022. Union total capital fell from 58.7% to about 37%; direct voting share fell to 40.29% before a 10% cap on any holder's votes. The law also forced the contracting of 8 GW of gas thermal plants ('jabutis'), even where there are no gas pipelines.
Who got it
The market (share offering, no controlling owner). Voting power of any shareholder is capped at 10%.
Terms
R$ 42 per share, R$ 29.29 bn base and about R$ 33.7 bn with the supplementary lot. TCU minister Vital do Rêgo (dissent) said the plants were worth R$ 130.4 bn against the government's R$ 67 bn and listed six alleged illegalities (e.g. Itaipu valued at R$ 1.2 bn). TCU technical staff flagged R$ 16.2 bn of failures in the valuation model. TCU plenary approved 6-1 (15 Feb 2022, first stage) and 7-1 (18 May 2022).
Mechanism
Law 14.182/2021 converting a state company into a corporation via dilution (no direct sale).
Who paid
Consumers through tariffs (thermal plants, CDE-related items); the Treasury through lower value.
What came after
Company renamed Axia (ticker AXIA3, from ELET3; per snippets). Three years on (Eixos, 2025): PMSO costs down 18%, headcount down 27%, investments up from R$ 4.6 bn (2021) to R$ 7.7 bn (2024), shares about R$ 41 against the R$ 42 offer, with analysts having projected R$ 60-70. AXIA3 closed at R$ 47.30 on 31 Oct 2026, about 13% above the offer before dividends (researcher arithmetic). Net income R$ 3.64 bn (2022), R$ 10.38 bn (2024), R$ 6.56 bn (2025).
Counter-view
TCU majority approved; the government estimated a R$ 67 bn value and said the bonus plus CDE flows benefit consumers. Defenders say the capital goes to the company, not the state. Critics: TCU staff, Vital do Rêgo, unions.

  • corrected Undervaluation claimed by TCU minister Vital do Rêgo: plants worth 130.4 bn vs government 67 bn (gap about 63 bn); 46 bn is the capacity component that would raise the outorga (BRL) (2022; Vital do Rêgo (TCU, dissent)) source
    Notes said 'R$ 46 bn undervaluation'. Fact-check: 46 bn is only the capacity component; the total gap he stated is about R$ 63 bn.
  • corrected TCU technical staff: valuation failures: 16.2 bn (MME accepted 5.6 bn; CDE transfer could fall from 29.8 bn to 26.9 bn) (BRL) (2022; TCU technical unit (Seinfra Elétrica)) source
    Not a booked loss; it is an estimate of flaws in the model. The labor-union document is not the source. Search only; page not opened.

Petrobras refinery sales 2021-2023 (Reman, Lubnor, SIX; failed Refap, Repar, RNEST)

To meet a 2019 CADE agreement, Petrobras sold or tried to sell several small refineries. Reman and SIX were sold; the Lubnor sale was cancelled in 2023 after Ineep said it was priced 55% too low. Critics say regional monopolies moved from public to private hands.

Government
Bolsonaro (sales); Lula 3 (cancellation)
What happened
The 2019 CADE agreement (TCC) obliged Petrobras to sell 8 refineries. Reman (Manaus, 46,000 b/d) was sold to Ream; Lubnor (Ceará, 8,000 b/d) to Grepar (cancelled); SIX (shale unit, São Mateus do Sul, PR) to Forbes & Manhattan Resources. Repar's first sale attempt was halted over low offers; RNEST got no proposals. Ultrapar's reported Refap interest (about US$ 1.2-1.4 bn) ended in Oct 2021.
Who got it
Reman: Ream (Atem's Distribuidora). Lubnor: Grepar (linked to Greca; competing asphalt distributors opposed). SIX: Forbes & Manhattan Resources (closed early Nov 2022 to Forbes Resources Brazil Holding). Private buyers gain regional fuel monopolies in small markets.
Terms
Reman: US$ 189.5 mn headline (Eixos) to US$ 257.2 mn total (US$ 28.4 mn deposit in Aug 2021; US$ 228.8 mn at closing on 30 Nov 2022). Lubnor: US$ 34 mn (signed 25 May 2022). Ineep (union-linked) says market value was at least US$ 62 mn, so 55% below, with no method detail and no Petrobras reply. SIX: US$ 33 mn.
Mechanism
CADE TCC 2019; sales without a new law, through Petrobras board and binding rounds.
Who paid
Regional fuel consumers if monopolies move to private hands (FUP, Ineep). Petrobras (federal and private shareholders) gets cash. CADE says the sales open competition.
What came after
Lubnor contract terminated 27 Nov 2023 over unmet conditions precedent about land involving two federal entities; Grepar says it waived them and will sue. Lubnor stays with Petrobras. CADE asked for further diligence on Reman in Mar 2022. The messy outcomes (one cancelled, one price adjusted) show the process was uneven.
Counter-view
Defenders (CADE) say the sales open competition. Critics (FUP, Ineep) say they move regional monopolies from public to private hands.

Petrobras field and gas asset sales and divestment totals (Polo Bahia Terra, Carmópolis, Gaspetro/Bahiagas)

Petrobras sold gas and onshore field assets in 2021-23 and then stopped its field divestments in September 2023. Bahia bought a Gaspetro stake for about a quarter of what Compass paid for a bigger stake. Some buyers had payment or contract problems, and totals come mainly from labor-aligned sources.

Government
Bolsonaro (sales); Lula 3 (end of E&P divestments)
What happened
Polo Bahia Terra (28 onshore concessions, Recôncavo and Tucano, about 13,500 b/d oil and 660,000 m3/d gas): binding phase began 19 Mar 2021; Petrobras ended E&P divestments on 4 Sep 2023 and dropped Bahia Terra, Urucu, Manati and Argentina. Carmópolis (11 Sergipe concessions) was sold to Carmo Energy (Cobra group), closed Dec 2022. Gaspetro: Compass (Cosan) bought Petrobras's 51% and Bahia bought Gaspetro's stake in Bahiagas.
Who got it
Carmo Energy (Cobra group) for Carmópolis. Compass (Cosan) for Gaspetro. The Águila consortium offered above US$ 1.5 bn for Bahia Terra but was disqualified for not proving financial backing and started arbitration; PetroReconcavo/Eneva made a binding offer in Mar 2022 of about US$ 1.4 bn (unverified).
Terms
Gaspetro: Compass paid R$ 2.03 bn for 51%; CADE approved unanimously and required Compass to sell stakes in 12 of 18 distributors. Bahia paid R$ 540 mn for Gaspetro's Bahiagas stake, about a quarter of the Compass price; the Bahia secretary called the price 'very low'. Mitsui had bought 49% in 2015 for about R$ 1.9 bn (unverified). Carmópolis: US$ 1.1 bn in total.
Mechanism
Asset sales by Petrobras under its divestment plan, with CADE conditions where required.
Who paid
The Union and private shareholders of Petrobras if prices were low; no independent valuation was found.
What came after
Carmópolis: Petrobras says US$ 296 mn was due and unpaid (reported 26 Dec 2023). Several sold assets came back onto Petrobras's agenda after buyer problems (Mataripe pricing, Carmópolis payment default, Lubnor cancellation). Petrobras reconsidered a Bahia Terra sale in 2025 (unverified).
Counter-view
Defenders say the sales reduced debt and focused Petrobras. The only totals found come from labor-aligned sources (OSP, DIEESE/FUP); a non-union estimate is a gap.

Correios: privatization attempt and 2025 financial crisis

Correios was not privatized: the Câmara passed the bill in 2021 but it stalled in the Senate. In 2025 the company lost R$ 8.5 bn and took a R$ 12 bn bank loan backed by the Treasury. The public, not private owners, now carries the risk.

Government
Bolsonaro (PL 591/2021); Lula 3 (2025 crisis)
What happened
No privatization was completed. The Câmara approved PL 591/2021 on 5 Aug 2021 (286 to 173, 2 abstentions; rapporteur Gil Cutrim) and sent it to the Senate (rapporteurs Oriovisto Guimarães, then Marcio Bittar; ADIs at the STF; outcome unconfirmed). In 2025 the company posted a net loss of R$ 8.5 bn (2024: R$ 2.6 bn), about R$ 6.4 bn of it court liabilities, with negative equity of R$ 13.1 bn.
Who got it
Nobody: the company stays public. The company's president (Rondon) ruled out privatization in Oct 2025 (Carta Capital only; unconfirmed).
Terms
Loan: board approved R$ 20 bn on 28 Nov 2025; the Treasury rejected that version and authorized R$ 12 bn on 18 Dec 2025 (Caixa, BB, Bradesco R$ 3 bn each; Itaú and Santander R$ 1.5 bn each; about 115% of CDI; 3-year grace; 15-year term). Signed 26 Dec 2025, runs to Dec 2040. No R$ 10 bn figure was found.
Mechanism
Privatization bill (stalled); a Treasury-guaranteed bank loan.
Who paid
The Treasury, as guarantor. A public company, not sold, with the public bearing the risk.
What came after
H1 2026 net loss R$ 5.55 bn (up 30.36% from R$ 4.26 bn); Q2 loss R$ 2.39 bn, Q1 R$ 3.16 bn. The government committed a R$ 6 bn capital injection by end 2027, linked to the R$ 12 bn five-bank loan; debt term extended from 18 to 180 months. Restructuring of up to 15,000 voluntary dismissals and 1,000 agency closures to save R$ 2.1 bn (snippets, unverified).
Counter-view
Defenders of privatization point to the losses and the need for the loan. Opponents say the crisis comes from legal liabilities, pension costs and competition rules.

    Notes had R$ 12 bn, R$ 20 bn and R$ 10 bn. Corrected: the board approved R$ 20 bn (28 Nov 2025); the Treasury authorized R$ 12 bn (18 Dec 2025). No R$ 10 bn figure was found. Signing date comes from a search result.

    Not covered by the fact-check round; taken from the gap research notes.

Corsan (Rio Grande do Sul), 2022

Corsan was sold to the only bidder, Aegea, for R$4.151 bn, 1.15% over the minimum. The buyer reports higher investment, while the union side says the price was too low and some 2,000 jobs were lost.

Government
Rio Grande do Sul state government (first state sanitation sale under the 2020 sanitation law)
What happened
B3 auction on 20 Dec 2022 of the state water company. Corsan served 307 municipalities and about 6 million people, with 5,995 employees and a R$943 million pension liability.
Who got it
Aegea, sole bidder. Iguá, Aguas do Brasil and Equatorial visited but did not bid.
Terms
R$4.151 bn, a 1.15% agio over the R$4.1 bn minimum. Aegea must invest R$12 bn to reach universal service by 2033. 198 of 317 municipalities had not signed regularization terms (38% of revenue). A union request to postpone was rejected by the TST.
Mechanism
B3 auction under the 2020 sanitation law. No BNDES role found.
Who paid
Not stated.
What came after
Aegea took control in Jul 2023 with 5,600 employees; about 2,000 had left by Mar 2024; 18 months of job stability was agreed. Investment about R$2 bn a year against about R$500 million a year under the state. More than 200 contracts renegotiated. A TCE case seeks annulment. Tariff adjustments of 6.46% (Jan 2025) and 4.68% (Jan 2026), and a TJ-RS suspension of a 23.01% adjustment (undated), are unverified.
Counter-view
Jerson Kelman: profit funds expansion (NeoFeed). The Sindiagua president (advocacy) says the TCE/RS rapporteur found the price underestimated and the 1a Camara recommended annulment.

After the privatization the Union kept about 42% of the shares but only 10% of the votes. In December 2025 the STF approved a deal that gives the Union 3 of 10 board seats. The 10% voting cap stays.

Government
Lula 3
What happened
The Union holds about 42-43% of common shares but votes only 10%. The AGU filed suit in 2023. On 11 Dec 2025 the STF plenary homologated a settlement (rapporteur Nunes Marques; PGR supported it). The Union nominates 3 of 10 board members (2 if its stake is below 30%, none below 20%) and 1 of 5 fiscal council members. Eletronuclear: R$ 2.4 bn investment in Angra, negotiated over 15 months. The cap stays at 10%.
Who got it
The Union gets governance seats, not proportional votes. The private shareholders keep the 10% cap.
Terms
No price. The terms are governance rights.
Mechanism
Settlement in the STF conciliation centre, homologated by the plenary.
Who paid
Treasury / public control: the Union holds about 42% of common shares but cannot vote them in proportion.
What came after
Vote reported as 6-4 (CNN Brasil): majority Nunes Marques, Fux and others; dissenters Moraes, Cármen Lúcia, Dino and Fachin (on the Court's competence). A conflicting Eixos report says Moraes proposed a constitutional-conforming interpretation and that three justices voted to approve before a pause; both are given. The term 'golden share' does not appear in the sources.

Citi analyst via Eixos: the deal leaves political risk. Eletrobras treats the deal as legal certainty.

Desenrola Brasil and Novo Desenrola (household-debt relief)

Desenrola is a debt-relief program, not a sale of public assets. In 2023 it renegotiated R$ 32.5 bn of household debt; the 2026 version uses a public guarantee of up to R$ 15 bn. It is included as a counter-case.

Government
Lula 3
What happened
Not an asset transfer: a household-debt relief channel, included as a counter-case and as private-credit relief. Desenrola Brasil 2023: lenders' auction offered R$ 126 bn in discounts (average 83%, credit cards 96%, 654 companies), debts up to R$ 20k, and R$ 32.5 bn was renegotiated for about 11.5 million people by Dec 2023. Range 2 had no Treasury guarantee. Novo Desenrola (4 May 2026): discounts 30-90% (average 65%), FGO guarantees up to 50% of defaults.
Who got it
Indebted households (income cap of 5 minimum wages, R$ 8,105 under Novo Desenrola) and lenders, who recover part of bad debt with a public guarantee. Maximum interest 1.99% a month over 48 months.
Terms
Novo Desenrola: guarantees up to R$ 15 bn; R$ 2 bn from the FGO, R$ 5-8 bn from forgotten funds, up to R$ 5 bn from the Treasury if needed.
Mechanism
Federal program with FGO guarantee (Lei 14.690/2023 details from a snippet, unverified).
Who paid
Banks (write-downs) and a small public guarantee. A critic's view is that the state subsidizes credit-card interest practices.
What came after
Tax waivers (Refis, Carf voto de qualidade, Perse) were not researched here; they are partly covered in the tax-expenditure case.
Counter-view
The R$ 126 bn is face value offered, not a cost to the state.

Marco Temporal (Lei 14.701/2023 and STF ruling)

In 2023 Congress imposed a 1988 cutoff date for Indigenous land claims, overriding Lula's vetoes. The STF struck the cutoff down in December 2025 with a 9-justice majority. Congress is still pushing a constitutional amendment (PEC 48), so the risk is not over.

Government
Congress overriding Lula's vetoes (2023); STF 2025
What happened
Law 14.701/2023 imposed the 5 Oct 1988 cutoff for Indigenous land claims and 'renitente esbulho' requirements. After the STF Tema 1.031 ruling (Sep 2023), a conciliation commission drafted a bill (23 hearings, ended 23 Jun 2025 without conclusion); APIB left the table on 28 Aug 2024, calling it forced conciliation (snippet). The STF (rapporteur Gilmar Mendes) declared the marco temporal and the renitente esbulho requirement unconstitutional, concluding on 19 Dec 2025.
Who got it
Had it stood: landholders, agribusiness, mining and energy interests on claimed land.
Terms
No price. Land rights.
Mechanism
Ordinary law passed by Congress after overriding vetoes; reviewed by the STF.
Who paid
Indigenous peoples, had the law stood.
What came after
Nine justices were in the majority against the marco; Mendonça was the lone dissent on the marco; Fachin dissented on the deadline and Cármen Lúcia partly on other provisions. Tribuna do Sertão gives 9-1, names Nunes Marques and dates it 18 Dec (wrong). PEC 48 was approved by the Senate on 9 Dec 2025; the Câmara status was not found. Legislative risk remains.
Counter-view
Congress and agribusiness argue the Constitution fixes 5 Oct 1988 as the reference; PEC 48 and Lei 14.701/2023 express this.

Sabesp privatization (São Paulo)

São Paulo sold about 32% of Sabesp in July 2024 at R$ 67 per share, raising about R$ 14.8 bn, and gave the company a single long concession. Critics say the price was below market; the governor says the investment plan justifies it. Complaints against Sabesp are high.

Government
State of São Paulo (Tarcísio); federal context Lei 14.026/2020
What happened
Offering closed 22 Jul 2024. The state sold about 32% of shares (from 50.3% to about 18.3%) at R$ 67 per share. A new single concession replaces the municipal contracts (371 of 375 municipalities adhered). Investment commitment R$ 260 bn through 2060, R$ 69 bn by 2029; universalization target moved from 2033 to 2029.
Who got it
Equatorial Energia bought 15% (R$ 6.9 bn) and became the reference shareholder (no formal control).
Terms
R$ 67 per share for about R$ 14.7-14.8 bn. R$ 85 was an all-time high, and the close on 17 Jul 2024 was R$ 83.20. The discount is 'almost 20%' per one source and 10-14% per others. Independent valuations of R$ 85.58 and R$ 103.90 per share exist (Valor, search snippet). Tarcísio says the high investment commitments justify the price and that the share rose after the sale (R$ 74 on 28 Jun vs R$ 33-46 in 2022).
Mechanism
Share offering plus a new concession contract (de facto a regulated monopoly).
Who paid
Consumers. Initial tariff cuts (1% residential, 10% social, 0.5% other) apply to the first tier only; the funding source is not stated, and a search says the FAUSP fund receives at least 30% of proceeds, which critics say breaks the LRF. Sabesp had 6,879 Procon complaints in the 2025 ranking, 69% unresolved, against Enel's 5,373. In 2026 Haddad criticized the opaque criteria of the sale.
What came after
Critics (Apública, Haddad) cite service problems. The governor's claim that tariffs are 15% below the no-privatization path was not found and is unconfirmed. The 'Enel of water' phrase was also not found.
Counter-view
Tarcísio says high investment commitments justify the price and the state says the share rose after the sale.

A 2025 law loosened environmental licensing, adding self-declared licences and a fast track for strategic projects. Lula vetoed 63 provisions but Congress overrode most of them in November 2025. Environmental groups have taken the law to the STF.

Government
Lula 3
What happened
The law overhauled licensing with self-declared licensing (LAC) and a Special Environmental License (LAE) for 'strategic' projects. Congress approved it on 17 Jul 2025 (Câmara vote 267 to 116 per snippets); Lula sanctioned it on 8 Aug 2025 with 63 vetoes (of about 400 provisions), including limiting LAC to low-pollution projects. Congress overrode vetoes on 27 Nov 2025; promulgation is dated 5 Dec (Mayer Brown) or 8 Dec (CBIC snippet). LAE items (32-38) were held back for an MP (MP 1.308/2025), converted into Lei 15.300/2025 on 22/23 Dec 2025 with no vetoes (snippets).

Developers of infrastructure, agribusiness and energy projects.

No price.

Law approved by Congress, with vetoes overridden.
Who paid
The environment and Indigenous and traditional communities. Observatório do Clima called it the biggest environmental setback in history, and ADIs were filed at the STF (Monitor Mercantil).
What came after
Number of overridden vetoes differs: 52 (press) or 56 of 63 (Observatório do Clima); the attribution to Observatório is unconfirmed. NGOs went to court.

Industry and government say the law ends licensing paralysis. Critics (Observatório do Clima, MPF) call it the 'devastation bill'.

Braskem control sale (Novonor to IG4)

Novonor sold control of Braskem to an IG4-backed fund in 2026, paid in debentures with no cash price. Petrobras kept its 47% of the votes and co-control. This is a private-to-private transfer, so it is not strictly public to private.

Government
Lula 3
What happened
Novonor (ex-Odebrecht, in judicial recovery) sold its controlling stake to the Shine I FIP (Vórtx, advised by IG4 Capital). Deal indicated 15 Dec 2025; contract signed 17 Apr 2026 and announced 20 Apr. Petrobras (47% of voting capital, 36.1% of total) did not exercise preference or tag-along (material fact 23 Apr 2026) and remains co-controller. After closing: IG4/Shine 50.1% of voting shares (34.3% of total capital), Petrobras 47%. CADE's general superintendence approved without restrictions on 6 Mar 2026. Closing was announced on 3 Jun 2026 (euqueroinvestir), but the fact-check found no closing page. Court approvals and an EU Foreign Subsidies Regulation review were conditions; a tender offer (OPA) for minority shares is required.
Who got it
Shine I FIP (Vórtx / IG4). IG4 bought about R$ 20 bn of Novonor debts held by banks (December 2025 deal), secured by Braskem shares. The Alagoas geological problem (mine subsidence in Maceió) is inherited by the buyer.
Terms
No cash price: paid in NSP debentures (2 first-series plus 1 second-series NSP debentures per Braskem share; 547,257,590 first-series and 273,628,795 second-series in total). BTG says the implied price is probably very low. Citi flags judicial recovery risk. Braskem ended 2025 with adjusted net debt of US$ 7.5 bn.
Mechanism
Debt-for-equity structure; control passes between private owners with Petrobras as co-controller (new shareholder agreement requires consensus).
Who paid
Minority shareholders take the risk. The public-to-private angle is whether Petrobras pays or protects Braskem; not found in opened sources.
What came after
The OPA price per share is a gap. Snippet only: CVM approved the OPA registration but the notice was unpublished as of 21 Sep 2026; TJ-SP rejected a Safra request to suspend the sale in July. Petrobras CEO Magda Chambriard was reported to chair the board (unconfirmed).
Counter-view
Novonor and creditors present the sale as a rescue of a distressed asset. Petrobras waiving rights is framed by some as avoiding fiscal exposure, not as a transfer. Not strictly a transfer of public assets.

1967-2073
x-01
Zona Franca de Manaus: cost estimates

Manaus has had tax breaks since 1967, now protected in the Constitution to 2073. The cost depends on who counts: the Receita's figure swung from R$24.2 bn to R$55.26 bn, while FGV says the real cost of the industrial pole is about R$7.5 bn. Critics and defenders disagree on the counterfactual.

Government
Military regime (1967); the extension to 2073 is a later constitutional amendment whose year and government were not verified
What happened
Tax exemptions for firms in the Manaus Industrial Pole. The Receita's own estimate swings: R$24.2 bn (2021), R$45.59 bn (2022), R$55.26 bn (2023), R$32.7 bn (2024). The effective-base table gives R$25.2 bn for 2021.
Who got it
Firms in the pole, whose 2024 turnover was R$204.9 bn: informatics 23.06%, electronics 18.08%, two-wheelers 17.8%. Financed by other taxpayers and, for ICMS, by other states. Federal expenditure flows mostly outside the North.
Terms
The dispute is the counterfactual. The Receita counts all PIS, Cofins, IPI and import tax waived. FGV argues the real cost of the industrial pole is only about R$7.5 bn (2021). Industry-only range: R$5.94-9.89 bn potential in 2024 by FGV against the Receita's R$8.74 bn projection. The headline R$22.95 bn (2024, 4.1% of federal expenditure) includes commerce, services and agriculture.
Mechanism
Exemption of IPI, import tax, PIS/Cofins and others for firms with approved projects under Suframa (DL 288/1967); constitutional entrenchment (ADCT art. 40) and extension of benefits to 2073 (ADCT art. 92-A). The 1967 decree itself was not opened.
Who paid
The federal budget. FGV says Amazonas returns more federal tax than it receives in benefits (1.74%), and that firms add about R$6.0 bn a year in required counterparts, lifting the Union's return to 2.24%, plus about R$6.0 bn a year of ICMS to the state. FGV's method for the 1.74% was not checked.
What came after
Constitutional protection to 2073 means no sunset before then. The 2023 tax reform kept the advantage (not confirmed).
Counter-view
The FGV report is itself the favourable side: it argues the real cost is lower than the headline. Critics (Senate TD 126 and cost-per-job arguments) say the cost per job is high; the cost per job was not opened.

Scale of grilagem: Livro Branco, INCRA 1999/2001 and parliamentary inquiries

Official estimates put 93 to 100 million ha of Brazilian land under suspicion of grilagem around 1999-2001, mostly in the Amazon. These are suspicion figures, not court findings. The land was taken without payment.

Government
Medici-era Chamber inquiry (1970); FHC government (1999-2001)
What happened
Suspected land-grabbing of public land. The 1970 inquiry: Para had the most complaints (17 cases) and 8 million ha sold illegally. Livro Branco (INCRA 1999): about 100 million ha nationwide under suspicion. INCRA 2001 update: 93 million ha, of which Amazonas 55 million ha and Para 31 million ha.
Who got it
Large claimants holding forged or inflated titles. INCRA's re-registration of holdings above 10,000 ha cancelled records covering 20 million ha of irregular holdings (Barreto et al. 2008).
Terms
Not applicable: appropriation with no price. The public estate was taken for free.
Mechanism
Forged titles, inflated areas, registry collusion, later regularization of the occupations.
Who paid
The Union and the states (loss of land); posseiros, Indigenous and traditional peoples (violence).
What came after
INCRA re-registration, Provimento 13/2006, CNJ cancellations 2009-2010. The 2001 inquiry report is available but was not read in full. A search summary says it cites 'more than 50 million ha' improperly appropriated; not confirmed.
Counter-view
'Area under suspicion' is an estimate, not an adjudicated finding. The 100 million and 93 million figures are not additive with the Para registry totals (different bases and years).

North Mato Grosso: private colonizers, Otsar/Cotriguacu and the Sharp episode

In the 1970s and 1980s INCRA authorised about 36 private colonizers in northern Mato Grosso, with holdings of up to one million ha. Little was colonised on time and the land did not return to the public estate. A fraudulent land transfer aimed at the firm Sharp brought down a minister.

Government
Medici-Geisel (incentives, SUDAM); Figueiredo
What happened
INCRA authorised about 36 private colonization firms in northern Mato Grosso. Largest holdings: Rendanyl (later Otsar) 1,000,000 ha; Indeco (Ariosto da Riva) 400,000 ha; Colniza (Lunardelli) 400,000 ha; Juruena (Joao Carlos Meirelles) 200,000 ha. The Otsar land passed to Cotriguacu 'in a fraudulent operation' aimed at a later transfer to the multinational Sharp, the episode that brought down minister Amaury Stabile.
Who got it
Colonizers from Parana and Sao Paulo capital and a Parana cooperative (IBGE names the Sao Miguel do Iguacu cooperative; another document names a different one). Fiscal incentives (SUDAM) helped finance them.
Terms
Not stated.
Mechanism
State land sales to colonizers, grilagem over Indigenous land, then resale or transfer between firms. The one million ha was redistributed as 400,000 ha Cotriguacu, 400,000 ha Juruena and 200,000 ha Indeco.
Who paid
Indigenous peoples, posseiros, and the public estate. Only Indeco implemented its colonization on time; the others did little and the land did not return to the public estate.
What came after
Colonizers sold lots to settlers from the South. A named 'Fazenda Cotriguacu' grilagem case was NOT found; only the colonizer is documented.
Counter-view
Colonizers describe themselves as 'Bandeirantes of the 20th century', building towns on empty land (Travessia quotes this self-image).

x-06
State takeover (estatizacao) of the private external debt

In the 1970s and early 1980s the central bank guaranteed the exchange rate on private foreign loans, so the public side ended up owing the dollars. Foreign banks were repaid and Brazilians paid through inflation. No single headline amount is quoted in the sources.

Government
Geisel and Figueiredo (military regime); Delfim Netto at planning/finance
What happened
Private and state-firm foreign debts under Lei 4.131 and Resolucao 63 loans were taken onto the public side. No single headline figure for the private-then-public share could be quoted safely; the two papers give series.
Who got it
Private Brazilian borrowers and state firms were relieved of dollar risk. The foreign creditor banks were made whole through the 1982 rescheduling backed by the IMF.
Terms
The central bank sold exchange cover below the cost of the later devaluations (Cruz 1995).
Mechanism
Central bank and CMN circulars and resolutions, not laws passed by Congress: Circular 230/1974 and Resolucao 432/1977 (the BC guaranteed the exchange rate on foreign loans), DRME deposits, and project deposits so that private debtors paid cruzeiros to the BC while the BC owed the creditors dollars.
Who paid
The Treasury and the central bank (money printing, internal debt), so inflation and the lost decade fell on wage earners.
What came after
The debt was later converted into the Brady bonds of 1994 (not opened).
Counter-view
The state took the debt to avoid a wave of private bankruptcies and a payments default during the 1982 crisis (argued in the IPEA text).
Figures

Millions of hectares in Para were registered to a 'phantom' owner, Carlos Medeiros, who never appeared. Estimates range from 1.8 million ha blocked to 9-12 million ha claimed. The people behind it were never identified.

Government
Military regime (1975); Sarney through Itamar (1984-1993); Judiciary of Para
What happened
Land registered in the name of a person who never appeared. Papers dated to about 1800 first appear in an official document in 1975. Sources disagree on area: about 9 million ha in 32 municipalities, about 12 million ha at one point, and 1.8 million ha of his titles blocked.

Sold on to loggers and cattle ranchers; only one buyer is named (Marinho Gomes de Figueiredo). The real backers were never identified; his lawyers (Viegas) were the only known figures.
Terms
No price information in the opened pages.

An 'adjudicacao' letter built from inventories of two Portuguese men. In 1993 'lost' inventory records were restored without consulting Iterpa, the Union or prosecutors.
Who paid
Para and the Union (public land); forest and communities on the land.
What came after
The federal prosecutors found the fraud after a logging plan was approved on Union land near Santarem and sought blocks in all registries. The Corregedoria chose provisional blocks instead of cancellation. The 2001 inquiry called it the largest grilagem case seen. 1995-1997
x-10
PROER: the Nacional, Economico and Bamerindus operations

In 1995-97 the central bank lent to banks buying failed lenders, so buyers got healthy assets and the state kept the bad ones. The Chamber inquiry put the net loss at R$7.1 bn; another estimate says R$71 bn. Supporters say it prevented a bigger run.

Government
Fernando Henrique Cardoso; BC presidents Gustavo Loyola, with Gustavo Franco as BC director (who signed which operation not confirmed)
What happened
Federal credit to buyer banks taking over failed banks (MP 1.179 and 1.182 of Nov 1995, CMN Res. 2.208). The Chamber inquiry report says R$20.4 bn lent and R$7.1 bn net loss to the Union around 2002.
Who got it
The BC lent to the buyer bank; Itau-type buyers took Economico's good assets, Unibanco took Nacional's, HSBC took Bamerindus in March 1997 (date from snippet). Healthy assets went to the buyer; bad assets and housing-fund (FCVS) credits stayed in the liquidated estate. The Union financed it through BC credit and bond sterilisation.
Terms
The loans were at below-market terms and long maturities (inquiry chapter VI). At Nacional the hole was hidden by fictitious loans for years.
Mechanism
MPs 1.179/1.182 and CMN Res. 2.208. Lei 9.447/97 later made controllers jointly liable and allowed their assets to be frozen.
Who paid
The Treasury, through BC provisions that flow into its balance. Controllers largely kept personal wealth, hence decades-long collection fights.
What came after
The Proer inquiry concluded intervention was necessary but criticised controls; the BC attorney-general argued losses of R$40 bn or R$69.5 bn were avoided (exact attribution to be re-checked). FGC and the sale of the estates continued into the 2020s.
Counter-view
A systemic run in 1995 would have cost more; supporters point to avoided losses of R$40 bn or R$69.5 bn (BC attorney-general, cited in the inquiry chapter; attribution to be re-checked).

Lei Kandir: ICMS exemption on exports of primary goods

In 1996 Brazil waived the state ICMS tax on primary-goods exports. States say they lost between R$269 bn and R$637 bn. A 2020 law pays them R$58 bn over 17 years, a fraction of the estimates.

Government
Fernando Henrique Cardoso government (signatory not confirmed from an opened page); the compensation fight ran under every later government
What happened
The state tax ICMS was waived on exports of primary and semi-finished goods (LC 87, 13 Sept 1996). Loss estimates differ: R$268.9 bn accumulated 1997-2016 (R$25 bn in 2016 alone) versus R$637 bn since 1996 as of 2019.
Who got it
Exporters of ore, soy, meat, pulp and similar goods (named companies not opened). Financed by states and municipalities. By 2016 the biggest absolute losses were Minas Gerais R$64.6 bn, Rio R$60.7 bn, Para R$35.7 bn, Mato Grosso R$30.8 bn, Espirito Santo R$28.3 bn. As a share of revenue: Mato Grosso 26.01%, Para 14.58%.
Terms
Compensation to states was never based on measured loss. The STF found Congress had failed to regulate ADCT art. 91 for more than ten years after EC 42/2003.
Mechanism
LC 87/1996 art. 3 exemption; transitional compensation in art. 31 and annex, amended by LC 115/2002; EC 42/2003 wrote the exemption into the Constitution and created ADCT art. 91. ADO 25 was filed in 2013 by Para and 15 other states (rapporteur Gilmar Mendes). On 30 Nov 2016 the STF unanimously found the omission and gave Congress 12 months; the TCU would set the amount if Congress failed.
Who paid
The states. LC 176/2020 pays R$58 bn from 2020 to 2037: R$4 bn a year to 2030 (R$1 bn to municipalities), then falling R$500 mn a year for 2031-2037. Extra R$7.6 bn brings the total to R$65.6 bn. States had to drop lawsuits against the Union to receive it.
What came after
The R$58 bn is far below either loss estimate, so on those numbers the settlement repays a fraction. Whether the exemption brought more exports than it cost is not documented.
Counter-view
The Union argued it already transfers large sums to states and that the temporary scheme is constitutional (Conjur, 13 Dec 2016). The rapporteur replied that social contributions, which are not shared with states, rose from 29% to 54% of federal revenue between 1994 and 2016. A Folha Vitoria headline says the Fazenda held that the law does not oblige full repayment; that page returned 403 and was not read. The economic defence (exports and the trade balance rose) is not documented.

Dividend tax exemption

From 1996 Brazil did not tax dividends paid to owners. Ipea estimated a 15% tax would raise about R$43 bn a year. Lei 15.270/2025 ended the exemption in part from 2026.

Government
FHC (law of 26 Dec 1995, date from a URL slug); Lula III for Lei 15.270/2025
What happened
Profits distributed to owners escaped personal income tax from January 1996. Ipea (Gobetti and Orair) estimated in 2015 that a 15% tax on profits and dividends would raise R$43 bn a year (R$50 bn in another version).
Who got it
Owners and shareholders of companies. 71,440 Brazilians earning over R$1.3 million a year declared an average of R$4.2 million and paid 6.7% in tax. A senator compared a civil servant paying 27.5% on R$5,000 with an owner receiving R$300,000 in dividends paying nothing. Financed by employees and consumers through payroll and consumption taxes.
Terms
Ipea estimate of revenue forgone. The claim that 'only Brazil and Estonia fully exempt dividends' is a senator's hearing statement; a search did not confirm Estonia. An OECD comparison was not opened.
Mechanism
Art. 10 of Lei 9.249/1995 exempts distributed profits from withholding and from the recipient's tax base. The same law's art. 9 created interest on equity (JCP), deductible from corporate tax (text not opened). Lei 15.270/2025: 10% withholding when a company pays one resident individual over R$50,000 a month; non-residents pay 10%; a minimum tax starts at R$600,000 a year and reaches 10% at R$1.2 million.
Who paid
Wage earners (labour income taxed up to 27.5%) and the Treasury.
What came after
After about 30 years, Lei 15.270/2025 reintroduced a withholding, effective 1 Jan 2026 (date from a snippet). Dividends from profits up to fiscal year 2025 stay exempt.
Counter-view
The defence reported by IHU is that the exemption avoids taxing profit twice, at the company and again as personal income. The opposing argument, that the 1995 corporate rate cut and the JCP deduction already lower the corporate burden, was not sourced.

PROES and Banespa

In the late 1990s the Union issued about R$61-73 bn in securities to clean up state banks and refinance state debts before sales such as Banespa's. Buyers got cleaned banks and the Union absorbed the bad assets. The BCB says the real fault lay with earlier state-bank management.

Government
Fernando Henrique Cardoso
What happened
The Union issued federal securities to states to clean up state banks (MP 1.514/1996, CMN Res. 2.365/1997) and refinanced state debts (Lei 9.496/97). Banespa was federalised in Dec 1994 and sold to Santander in Nov 2000. The BCB book counts R$61.4 bn in securities issued under PROES.
Who got it
State governments (debts refinanced), state-bank creditors, and buyers (Itau, Bradesco, Santander, ABN) who received cleaned banks. The Union financed it with federal securities.
Terms
States federalised or privatised banks and the Union absorbed the bad assets. The price paid for Banespa was not opened.
Mechanism
MP 1.514 and Lei 9.496/97; state-debt contracts with the Union indexed to IGP-DI plus fixed interest.
Who paid
The Union and so taxpayers; states bore it through long debt service to the Treasury.
What came after
See the privatization notes for the sales. Federal-bank follow-up (BB recapitalisation 1996-97 under MP 1.504, 1.553/1.555 with an R$8 bn ceiling; PROEF 2001 and Emgea): amounts not confirmed, only search snippets seen.
Counter-view
The BCB book argues the cleanup cost belongs to past state-bank management (politically driven lending), not to the program that closed the banks.

1969-2025 (main law 1997)
x-14
Oil royalties and the special participation

Brazil's oil royalties grew about 53 times from 1999 to 2025 as production rose, reaching R$58.22 bn in 2024. The fight is over how the money is shared between producing and non-producing states. Some legal details (the 2013 STF suspension, the 10% rate) were not confirmed.

Government
Military regime (1969), Sarney (1989), FHC (1997), Lula (2010), Dilma (2012); signatories not verified
What happened
The question is how much of the oil rent the state kept. Lei 9.478/1997 raised the basic royalty from 5% to up to 10% (snippet only); the ANP says the field rate can vary from 5% to 15% by contract. Royalties plus special participation grew 5,204% from 1999 to 2025 and in 2022 first exceeded ICMS on fuel. The TCU reports R$58.22 bn paid in 2024.
Who got it
The state kept more as production rose. Distribution is concentrated: ten municipalities hold half of the municipal share and have under 9 million people; some get over R$20,000 per resident per year. Lei 12.734 cut the 'confronting states' share from about 30% to 20% and 'confronting municipalities' from 20% to 4%.
Terms
In the concession regime the rent is split by rate, not by auction price alone. Bonus, royalty and special participation by field were not opened. In 1997 the 5% rate produced only about R$208 million in today's values.
Mechanism
Concession contracts (Lei 9.478/1997); production sharing in the pre-salt (Lei 12.351/2010); redistribution under Lei 12.734/2012. The STF suspended the redistribution rules in 2013 (ADI 4917), with the final status not confirmed.
Who paid
Non-producing states and municipalities under the old distribution; producing ones after Lei 12.734 if it takes effect. The TCU found weaknesses in how the ANP calculates and distributes.
What came after
More revenue as production rose 61% between 2015 and 2025 and prices moved. The ANP projects R$68 bn for 2025. The Petrobras corruption context is in other notes.
Counter-view
FGV IBRE (an opinion piece by the authors) argues royalties are not ICMS compensation, so producing states cannot claim them as a replacement. The producing states argue the opposite, but their position was not documented in an opened page.
Figures

    A second search snippet gave a much higher figure that could not be sourced and is not used.

    The annual table in the blog was an image and not extracted.

    Range 5-15% per ANP contract terms; the 10% ceiling is snippet-only.
  • verified 1997 royalty in today's values: about R$208 million (about 0.2% of today's revenue) (BRL) (1997; FGV IBRE opinion piece) source

Repetro: customs regime for oil and gas equipment

Repetro waives import and federal taxes on oil and gas equipment, and runs to 2040. INESC counts R$260 bn of benefits to the 267 listed firms in 2015-2023, though part is not Repetro itself. The Receita keeps the regime out of its official tax expenditure report.

Government
FHC (1999) and Temer (2017) by date in office; the sources do not name the president
What happened
Relief from import tax, IPI, PIS and Cofins on equipment for oil and gas exploration. INESC crossed Receita data with the 267 firms listed under Repetro: R$260.08 bn of incentives, exemptions and immunities in 2015-2023.
Who got it
Most of the 267 firms are transnationals; the top three include MODEC and Ventura Petroleo. Petrobras-operated fields produce 88-89% of Brazilian oil, so some benefit reaches Petrobras. Financed by the Treasury.
Terms
The Receita says it is technically impossible to compute Repetro as a deviation from the reference system, so it is not in the official tax expenditure report. INESC says the Receita holds robust data and could publish it.
Mechanism
Special customs regime: suspension of II, IPI, PIS/Pasep and Cofins on goods for oil, gas and hydrocarbon activities, becoming exemption or zero rate once used as required. Decreto 3.161/1999; Lei 12.276/2010 and 12.351/2010 (pre-salt); Lei 13.586/2017 extended it to 31 Dec 2040. LC 215/2025 kept it among relieved regimes.
Who paid
The federal budget.
What came after
INESC says values grew significantly from 2017, though the table peaks in 2020 and declines to 2022, so the table alone does not prove cause.
Counter-view
The regime is defended as a way to avoid taxing imported capital goods that would be re-exported (position not documented in an opened page). The Receita's own treatment, that Repetro is not a deviation from the reference system, is the verified form of the same argument.

Marka and FonteCindam rescue (Cacciola)

In January 1999 the central bank sold dollars forward to two banks below market just after a devaluation. A 2012 court ordered repayment of billions, but the ruling was annulled and a 2017 appeal court held the rescue legal. The figures vary widely between sources.

Government
Fernando Henrique Cardoso; BC president Francisco Lopes (took over days before)
What happened
On 11-14 Jan 1999 the BC sold dollar futures to Marka and FonteCindam below market after the 13 Jan devaluation. The 2012 civil sentence ordered repayment of R$1.05 bn plus R$0.52 bn.
Who got it
Marka (Salvatore Cacciola) and FonteCindam. The Union financed it through the BC.
Terms
Futures were sold at a rate below the market rate of the day (JB report on the 2012 sentence).
Mechanism
BC discretion over exchange operations; civil improbity action.
Who paid
The BC and Treasury, per the 2012 sentence, until it was reversed.
What came after
The 2012 civil condemnation was annulled and TRF-1 held the rescue legal in 2017. The Cacciola criminal case (embezzlement, fled to Italy, extradited from Monaco 2008) was not opened; its figures must not be mixed with the civil case.
Counter-view
No loss at all: the BC and TRF-1 held the rescue legal in 2017 (ConJur).
