REFIS and tax amnesties (special instalment programs)

Between 2000 and 2017 Brazil ran about 28 tax-debt instalment programs (40 by the Receita's count), each forgiving fines and interest. Pert and Refis da Crise alone forgave R$108.3 bn. The TCU says the repeats reward people who do not pay.

Government
FHC (Refis 2000), Lula (Paes 2003, Paex 2006, Refis da Crise 2009), Dilma (reopenings), Temer (Pert 2017); signatories not in the TCU chart
What happened
Repeated special instalment programs for tax debts. The TCU counts about 28 programs in 2000-2017; the Receita counts about 40 in 18 years costing R$176 bn. Pert forgave R$47.4 bn and Refis da Crise R$60.9 bn.
Who got it
Debtors, including large firms; named beneficiaries not in the opened pages. Pert covered 131 thousand taxpayers. Taxpayers who joined three or more programs owed over R$160 bn and about half defaulted afterwards. Financed by compliant taxpayers and the social security budget.
Terms
The TCU says the payment terms 'find no parallel in the world'. Pert gave discounts up to 70% off fines and 90% off interest, and up to 175 instalments. The exact month counts in the TCU comparison chart were not extractable.
Mechanism
Each program is a medida provisoria converted into law, with discounts on fines and interest and long instalment plans. Lei 9.964/2000 (from MP 2.004-6/2000) created the first Refis; Paes 2003 is Lei 10.684/2003; Refis da Crise is Lei 11.941/2009.
Who paid
The Treasury and social security funds. The TCU argues repeated amnesties reward non-payment and punish those who paid on time. The Pert and Refis da Crise forgiveness sums to R$108.3 bn (my sum from press figures); it overlaps with the Receita's R$176 bn and cannot be added.
What came after
More programs followed after 2017, including 2020-2021 transaction regimes (not confirmed). Refis 2000 amounts were not opened.
Counter-view
The usual defence is that a collectible stream beats an uncollectible stock (no page opened to source it). The Receita itself is quoted as opposing a new Refis (Netcpa), so the tax authority does not back the practice.

Para registry with more land than the state, and the CNJ cancellations

Para's property registries held far more land than the state itself, including one 410-million-ha entry. CNJ-driven cancellations removed 91.1 million ha of registrations. Some of the land later reappeared in federal databases.

Government
Lula government; the Judiciary (CNJ, TJ-PA Corregedoria, with Iterpa and INCRA)
What happened
CNJ-driven cancellations hit at least 10,728 registrations in 88 municipalities covering 91.1 million ha in Para. Separately, one registration of 410 million ha in the Vitoria do Xingu registry was cancelled in 2009, '3.9 times the size of Para'.
Who got it
Claimants through 'phantom' owners and fake inventories; the people behind most chains are not identified. Where later sold, buyers were logging and cattle interests.
Terms
No price; purchases were mostly registry entries.
Mechanism
Duplicated or inflated registrations, forged adjudication letters, notary collusion. Lei 6.739/1979 allowed administrative cancellation of null registrations; Provimento 13/2006 blocked registrations by size and date criteria. TJ-PA ordered only blocks, so the matter went to CNJ.
Who paid
The state and the Union (land lost, years of litigation); innocent third-party buyers when registrations were cancelled.
What came after
Imazon found some blocked or cancelled holdings re-entered INCRA's Sigef (1.5 million ha), including 332 properties of 2.5 million ha with 34% of the original forest (811 thousand ha) already deforested. 89% of lawsuits started before the CNJ decision.
Counter-view
The cancellations were administrative and based on size and date proxies, so some legitimate titles may have been caught; critics call it a legal-certainty problem (a jus.com.br article, listed in search and not read).

Federal tax expenditures (gastos tributarios) series

Federal revenue given up through tax breaks grew from R$114.8 bn in 2008 to R$519.0 bn in 2023, about a quarter of federal collection. The official series leaves out some of the biggest regimes, so it understates the total. International comparisons show Brazil is near the regional average, so the debate is about pace and beneficiaries.

Government
Lula II, Dilma, Temer, Bolsonaro, Lula III (the series grows under all of them)
What happened
Revenue not collected through exemptions, deductions, reduced rates and deferrals. In the Receita Federal series it rose from R$114.8 bn (3.82% of GDP) in 2008 to R$519.0 bn (4.78%) in 2023. The 2024 value of R$512.3 bn is a projection.
Who got it
In 2021: Simples Nacional 21.70% (R$91.3 bn), agriculture and agroindustry 12.12%, exempt personal income 8.85%, regional development 7.91%, non-profits 7.56%. Manaus and free-trade areas got R$25.2 bn (5.98%). 62% of federal tax expenditure flows to the Southeast and South. Financed by all other taxpayers.
Terms
The figure is the Receita's own estimate, not a market valuation. It leaves out several large items (Repetro, dividends, interest on equity, presumed profit) because the reference system treats them as normal or too hard to compute. So it is a floor, not a ceiling.
Mechanism
Hundreds of separate norms: Simples (LC 123/2006), PIS/COFINS zero rates, income tax exemptions, regional regimes. The legal basis of the report itself was not opened. Portaria RFB 319 (2023) and LC 187/2021 allowed publishing beneficiaries by company.
Who paid
Other taxpayers. In 2021 federal expenditure equalled 24.03% of federal collection. FGV IBRE puts state expenditures at 2.4% of GDP in 2024, so federal plus state may reach 7.2% of GDP.
What came after
The 2024 tax reform (EC 132/2023) and later proposals targeted tax expenditures (not confirmed from an opened page). The report still excludes the largest special regimes.
Counter-view
Brazil is not an outlier. For 2021 the Receita table puts Brazil at 4.67% of GDP against a Latin American listing average of 5.26%; Canada 7.94%, US 6.06%, Colombia 7.73%, Chile 2.49%, Peru 1.82%. The Receita notes each country uses its own method. FGV says Brazil's 2002-2022 average was 3.0% of GDP against Italy 7.0% and US 6.9%. The dispute is about the pace of growth and who benefits (Receita Federal DGT; FGV EESP report).

Terra Legal: prices charged versus market value, and the TCU audits

Brazil sells occupied public land in the Amazon at 10-50% of an already low official table, and some states at far less. Imazon estimates this forgoes R$62-88 billion on 19.6 million ha. A TCU audit found titles given to holders above the legal limit and on areas that should not have been regularised.

Government
Lula (2009); Temer (2017 changes); Bolsonaro (MP 910/2019); also state governments (Para, Amapa, Roraima)
What happened
Federal titling of occupied public land in the Amazon. Imazon: privatising the 19.6 million ha of undesignated federal land at current legal values would cost society R$62-88 billion, about a quarter of Petrobras's 2019 market value. In Para the gap between market value and state price reaches R$9 billion across 8,053 properties.
Who got it
Occupants of federal land in the Amazon, including holders above the legal limit. TCU audited R$58.6 billion of land; 62 holders above 2,500 ha occupy 540 thousand ha.
Terms
Lei 11.952 art. 11: free titling up to 1 fiscal module; art. 12: larger areas at 10% to 50% of the INCRA minimum land-value table, paid over 20 years with up to 3 years of grace. That table is itself below market. Amapa sold areas for as little as 4% of market value and Roraima allowed up to 85% discount for those who deforested (both search summaries).
Mechanism
Dispensation of bidding; discounts by size; instalments; self-declared occupation with remote checks. State land agencies (Iterpa in Para, and in Amapa and Roraima) used discounted price tables; Roraima Lei 976/2014 as changed by Lei 1.351/2019.
Who paid
The Treasury (forgone revenue), state treasuries, the forest, and legitimate small occupants who wait.
What came after
The TCU ordered recovery of irregular areas; no complete recovery was found. TCU 627/2015 price findings not confirmed. Title production fell to almost zero in the first half of 2019.
Counter-view
The government argued the subsidy helps poor occupants and low land values reflect poor access and lack of infrastructure. Imazon replies that most area goes to large claimants and that the subsidy brings no socioenvironmental return (Imazon, 10 facts).

    Search summary only.

Amnesty laws and moving cutoff dates

Brazil's land amnesties keep moving the goalposts: a 2008 cutoff, a limit raised from 1,500 to 2,500 ha, and a 2019 proposal covering 55-65 million ha. Each change rewards earlier occupation and signals to new grabbers to wait. Proponents say it gives legal certainty.

Government
Lula (Lei 11.952/2009); Temer (MP 759/2016, Lei 13.465/2017); Bolsonaro (MP 910/2019)
What happened
Lei 11.952 set a cutoff of 22 July 2008; later occupations can be sold at the maximum land value. Lei 13.465/2017 raised the regularizable limit from 1,500 ha to 2,500 ha. MP 910/2019 would have allowed 55 to 65 million ha of undesignated Union land to be regularised, including occupations with illegal deforestation after 22 July 2008.
Who got it
Occupants with up to 2,500 ha and, under MP 910, larger claims; large claimants dominate the area.
Terms
See the Terra Legal case.
Mechanism
Statutory amnesty by date. The Chamber commission rejected PL 8411/17, which would have restored the 1,500 ha limit, on 11 April 2018. When MP 910 lapsed is not confirmed. Lei 14.757/2023 was not researched.
Who paid
The Treasury and the forest; honest occupants who respected earlier cutoffs.
What came after
ADIs against Lei 13.465 were filed (a former prosecutor-general, Raquel Dodge, reportedly argued unconstitutionality; not opened).
Counter-view
Proponents say regularization brings legal certainty and enables compliance with the Forest Code. MPF Nota Tecnica 8/2020 argues it rewards past crimes.
Figures

  • verified Land under MP 910/2019: 55 to 65 million ha of undesignated Union land (2019; MPF Nota Tecnica 8/2020) source
  • verified Regularizable limit: 1,500 ha raised to 2,500 ha by Lei 13.465/2017 (2017; Chamber of Deputies news) source

    Both recorded; the 2011 claim was cited from memory and not confirmed.

Undesignated public forests and CAR self-declarations

By 2020, nearly a third of the Amazon's undesignated public forests (18.6 million ha) had been registered in the CAR by private claimants. The CAR is not a title, but it works as a first step toward regularization. Counts of undesignated land differ between IPAM and Imazon.

Government
Dilma (CAR created with the Forest Code 2012); Temer and Bolsonaro (registrations rose)
What happened
Undesignated public forests cover 57.5 million ha in the Amazon. By 2020, 18.6 million ha of them (32%) were illegally registered in the rural environmental registry (CAR). Imazon counts 86.1 million ha (17% of the Amazon) still awaiting a destination.
Who got it
Claimants who file a CAR on public land; IPAM says 44% of 2020 CAR entries were large areas.
Terms
The CAR is free and self-declared. It is not a title but is used as proof of possession for later regularization.
Mechanism
The CAR is self-declaratory and does not check ownership; overlaps with public forests can be registered, which feeds speculation and later regularization.
Who paid
The Union and the states; the forest (deforestation and fire higher in CAR areas inside public forests).
What came after
Ongoing. Imazon recommended blocking CAR on these forests in 2021 (not verified in the pages opened).
Counter-view
Defenders say CAR is only an environmental registry and confers no ownership. IPAM answers that it works as a de facto land document.
Figures
  • disputed Undesignated public forests in the Amazon: 57.5 million ha (2020; IPAM, Amazon on Fire 7) source
    Range 57.5 million ha (IPAM) to 86.1 million ha (Imazon); different definitions and dates, not reconciled.
  • verified Undesignated forests illegally registered in CAR: 18.6 million ha (32%) (2020; IPAM, Amazon on Fire 7) source
    CAR inside these forests rose 232%.
  • disputed Public land awaiting destination: 86.1 million ha (17% of the Amazon) (2021; Imazon, 10 facts on land regularization) source
    See range on the 57.5 million ha figure.
Sources

CFEM mining royalty and the 2017 reform

Brazil's mining royalty (CFEM) was charged on net revenue until 2017, when the base became gross revenue and some rates rose. Collection reached R$7.45 bn in 2024. Industry says the problem is enforcement, while others say miners keep too much of the rent.

Government
Michel Temer (2017 reform)
What happened
The public share of mineral rent. Before 2017 the royalty was charged on net revenue: iron ore 2%, gold 1%, bauxite/manganese/potassium 3%, precious stones 0.2%. Collection was R$7.45 bn in 2024 on R$270.8 bn of mineral operations; iron ore supplied 75.01% of it.
Who got it
Miners keep the rent after the royalty. Petrobras plus mining make up 51.2% of 18 'super-profit' companies listed in the slides (profit year not stated). Company-level payments were not extracted. Financed by producing municipalities and the public that bears the environmental cost.
Terms
Lei 13.540/2017 moved the base from net to gross revenue less sale taxes, and raised the iron ore ceiling from 2% to 3.5% (can be cut to 2%), gold 1% to 1.5%, diamond 0.2% to 2%, niobium 2% to 3%. Other systems tax margin or profit: Ontario 10% of net profit, Quebec 12%, Newfoundland 16%, Peru 1-12% of operating profit, Chile 1% of sales plus 8-26% of operating margin, South Africa 0.5-7%, Western Australia 7.5% of sales on iron ore (official page not opened).
Mechanism
Lei 13.540/2017 (from MP 789/2017). Old distribution: 12% Union, 23% state, 65% producing municipality, with a 50% landowner share under Lei 8.901/94. The pre-2017 net base let firms shrink the amount due.
Who paid
Public revenue lost to under-payment. The TCU found about 69.7% of titleholders did not pay voluntarily in 2017-2022, and those who paid under-reported by 40.2% on average (cited by industry lawyers; the TCU PDF itself was unreadable). Lawyers estimate better enforcement could lift collection to about R$16 bn with no rate change.
What came after
Collection grew about fourfold between 2017 and 2024, but how much comes from the new base versus price and volume is not separated. A Chamber hearing on 12 Aug 2025 shows the fight is still open.
Counter-view
The industry side (Eixos, by FPA Advocacia) says nominal rates cannot be compared across regimes, a rate on gross revenue can be as onerous as higher rates elsewhere, and the problem is enforcement not rate. The opposite view (Giliad slides to the Chamber) frames sector profitability as the base for a higher take. The effective-rate comparison could not be settled from the pages opened.
Figures

Pandemic credit lines and guarantee funds

In 2020-21 the Union put money into guarantee funds so banks could lend to small firms with default risk covered. The loss is hidden in fund equity and no total was found.

Government
Bolsonaro; Guedes
What happened
Union equity contributions to the guarantee funds FGO (Pronampe), FGI (Peac-FGI) and the Pese payroll line.
Who got it
Small businesses and the banks that lent against the Union guarantee; the guarantee shifts default risk to the funds.
Terms
Not covered.
Mechanism
Equity contributions to guarantee funds that honour defaulted loans.
Who paid
The Union via the funds. The total of honoured guarantees and losses so far was not found.
What came after
Pronampe debts honoured by the FGO were renegotiated by Banco do Brasil.
Counter-view
The programs kept firms alive and the loss rate depends on guarantee design; no verified figure for either (researcher's note).

Which transfers the data ties to later disasters

22 of 94 disasters on the disasters page name a transfer in their ownership history.

A link is not a cause. It means the operator got the asset through a sale or concession before the disaster. Several rows say outright there is no causal link (the old Eletrobras dams, for example).

Biggest open questions

  • Colony: the total cost of railway guarantees to 1889, the Amazon steamship subsidy actually paid, tobacco and tithe contractor profits, and who bought the Jesuit estates.
  • Republic: coffee-burning totals, the Norte do Paraná land company's prices, Santos docks profits, and the Amforp buy-out figures (no usable source link).
  • Dictatorship: the total private debt the Central Bank took over in 1979–85, the Albras subsidy, Proálcool's total cost, and the 1983–85 bank-rescue costs.
  • 1985–2002: one total of BNDES loans to privatization buyers, several state-sale prices, the seguro-apagão total, and the Banestado CC5 mechanism.
  • 2003–2016: local-content waivers per oil round, leniency-deal terms, the TCU cost of the PSI, and losses on Sete Brasil.
  • 2016–2026: hectares titled under the land laws, the Correios sale value, airport minimum bids, and tax waivers (Refis, Carf, Perse).
  • Cross-cutting: primary law texts were blocked; the CFEM audit and Kandir counter-arguments are thin; the Cuiabá registry fraud was not found and was dropped.

Choices made when building the data

  • Signs on each entry are the data builders' judgement from the notes. They were not fact-checked.
  • 3 entries have no figures (e1-18, e1-21, e2-05). 21 figures have no source link.
  • Some deals appear twice, once in an era and once in the cross-cutting group. "See also" links join them.
  • Weak fits for "public to private" (Cubatão, Serra Pelada, Itaipu, the nuclear deal, Calha Norte) are kept and say so in their text.
